A flirt's heart is like an omnibus—it always has room for one more. Ann Eliza writes to ask why a poor man invariably keeps dogs. We have not given the question much consideration, but we have concluded that a poor man supports a dog to keep "the wolf from the door." Is it fair always to forget all the good, or kindness, shown to us, by those with whom we live' for the sake of one little pain they may have caused us, and which, most likely, was quite unintentional on their part? Do you wish to live at peace with all the world? Then practise the maxims of an influential man, who when asked, after the revolution' how he managed to escape the execu- tioner's axe, replied, "I made myself of no reputation, and kept silence." A Scotch boy had delivered a message to a lady, but did not seem in a hurry to go. Being asked if there was any- thing else his mother bade him say, he whimpered out, "She said I wasna' to seek anything for coming, but if ye gave me anything, I was to take it." ADVICE TO YOUNG MEN.—My advice is—Go and pro- pose to the most senible girl you know. If she accepts you, tell her how much your income is, and from what source derived, and that you will love her with all your heart into the bargain; and then keep your promise. Just you be true taller—lore her sincerely, and a more fond, faithful, foolish slave you will never meet anywhere. You will not deserve her, I know; but she will never know it. THE " CZAR " RwreuEs !—There was a company of gen- tlemen engaged ha a little game of cards in a prominent gentleman's parlour one night lately. It grew late, and fears were expressed by the party that they were trespass- ing upon the kindness of the mistress of the house, who, by the way, was not present. "Not at all, gentlemen—not at ali ! Play as long as you please. I am Czar here," said the master of the house. "Yes, gentlemen, play as long as you please," .said a silvery voice, and all rose as the mistress of the house stood before them. "Play as long as you please, gentlemen ! But, as it is nearly one o'clock, the Czar is going to bed i" He went. WHAT A WIFE SHOULD BE.—Burns, the poet, in one of his letters, set forth the following as the the true qualifica- Cone of a good wife:—" The scale of good wifesbip I divide into ten parts: Good nature, four; good sense, two; wit, one; personal charms—namely, a sweet face, eloquent eyes, fine limbs, gracefulearriage (I would add a fine waist, toe, but that 13 soon spoilt, you know), all these, one; as for the other qualities belonging to or attending on a wife, such as fortune, connection% education (I mean education extraordinary), divi le the remaining two degrees between them as you please, only remember that all these minor proportions must be ex- pree;ed by fractions, for there is not any one of them in the aforesaid scale entitled to the dignity of an integer.' A LUNATIC IN THE CLOUDS.—Godard used to tell the story. A wealthy private gentleman offered him one thou- sant franca if he could be allowed to ascend with him, and thee., accordingly started on their voyage together, no one else being in the car. The aeronaut soon found that he had a dengerous lunatic fore companion. The madman insisted upon being allowed to climb up outside the balloon by the rop and netting, and Godard was obliged to let him have his eely, though he induced him to fasten a rope round his waist, which the former cut as soon as he saw his oppor- tan!`.y. Next the lunatic commenced cutting away the core which held the car, and which now, only partially supported, inclined seriously on one side. The end of a long story IVA 3, that Godard at last contrived to let out so much gas around his tercible companion that he became asphyxi- ated end insensible, and the balloon was speedily brought to earth once more. The madman was restored to animation, and epeedily conveyed to the nearest police-station.—" A- dventures above Vie Clouds," in "Good Words." JOHN HENRY NEWMAN PREACHING IN ROME.—It wa my L-20:1 fortune to hear John Henry Newman preach in Roeee It was in the chapel of the English Roman Catholic Colleae. I believe I was the only Protestant present, h iv:.); gained admission through my friend, the vice-rector. The chapel was filled with English Romanists of all ranks and descriptions. Never will I forget the aspect of the preacher—that weird countenance of his—as he hurriedly entered from the sacristy, nor the intensity of his obeisance as he passed the altar on the way to the pulpit. It was not that he knelt, but that he seemed to crush himself down before it in brief, earnest prayer. His sermon was touching in the highest degree. Its theme was the experiences of St. Peel on giving up all his former associations, beliefs, and friendships, in order to be true to his new convictions. As addressed by such an audience, the bearing of the dis- course was obvious. More than once, as he read illustrative passages from the Acts and the Epistles, the half-suppressed sob showed how deeply the preacher was moved. However widely he might differ from Newman, his would have been a &loos nature which could refuse its sympathy, or not feel all that was best in him quickened by the self-revela- tion given by this sincere and pure-hearted man.—Donald 311Leod, Good Il'ords. _- - - -

_ , A GOLDEN RULE AND ITS ADVANTAGES.—I find that the Gale thing is to believe all the kind things that other men are reported to have said about me, and hardly ever to be- lieve the unkind things. This is a pleasant rule as well as a safe one. Why should we be ready to think that people are always speaking against us? If we are conscious of not d serving to have the hard words said about us which reach us on currents of idle gossip, we ought to suppose it very improbable that good men who really know us were guilty of saying them. As for strangers, they often speak, not aeainst us, but against some dismal simulacrum of us—a mere phantasm created by imagination and rumour—which they have mistaken for us; and though the mistake may hive its inconveniences there is no reason for being hot and indignant about it. A quiet, honest man may sometimes see in his newspaper at breakfast-time that some scoundrel heylnz, real flesh and blood, of the same name as himself has beee brought up before the magistrates for burglary. He does not fume, and fret, and get angry with the wit- neasee tescause they say such hard things against the man that happens to bear his name. He does not denounce the magistrates for committing him. He knows that the wit- nesses eeid nothing against himself, and that the magis- trates have done him no wrong. It was another man that was concerned in the affair, not he. And some reports that reach Us of what has been said about us ought to be received leth the same equanimity.—R.W. DALE, in "Good Words." A LONDON ROOTIERY.—The streets are narrow, and they are also ill-paved, badly drained, and over-guttered, for practically the entire roadways are turned into gutters. And in these gutters the children of the rookeries may be seen aisporting themselves at all hours of the day—the School Board notwithstanding—comparatively happy in their dirt -aud freedom: The adult inhabitants, also, show Out of doers a good deal; not, of course, tumbling about the gutt3rs, but sit9ng on the door-steps or window-sills, or lounging or reclining upon the pavement. This is most markedly the case in the summer months, when the multi- tudinous insect colonists of the dwellings are given to show themselves tormentingly active in the struggle for exist- wee. Donkeys and goats are quartered pretty much as ' members of the families to which they belong, and the fowls, which are numerous though not choice, have about a 8 free a run of the houses by night as they have of the streets by day. All sorts of odd and obscure industries are .also carried on indoors, so that upon the whole these rarn. shackle dwellings are very fully and variedly ntilised. The parish L:st-cart is rarely seen in the district, but the parish fever a:-,I smallpox cabs find a good deal of their work there; so likewise do the parish doctor and the relieving officer; while the wife beatings, violent assaults, street rows, and public-house scrimmages, for which the quarter is notorious, furnish neighbouring hospitals and police courts with some ef their most interesting cases.—The RiversL: Tisitor, in "Good Words." div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES,

SANITARY EXHIBITION AT GLASOOW.—It is intended in September and October next to hold an exhibition in Glas- gow of sanitary apparatus and articles of domestic use and economy in connection with the autumn Congress of the Sanitary Institute of Great Britain. Medals and certificates for approved exhibits will be given. The British Museam has recently acquired a manuscript of the Old Testament of extraordinary beauty and great value. It is in three volumes, large quarto, and was made about 1483 in the city of Lisbon. It is believed to be a careful copy of an ancient and model codex, and designed itself to be also a model codex. It has beautifully and richly illu- minated borders, and the first words of sections are written in letters of gold on a charming basis of delicate pen-and- ink workmanship. THE BALLOON ASCENT FROM MARSEILLES.—The at- tempt to cross the Mediterranean to Algeria has failed. The three travellers were taken by the wind towards Cor- sica. The balloon descended into the water, and the party of aeronauts were nearly drowned. They threw out all their apparatus, provisions, &c., and afterwards rose again to 9,000 feet. Then a violent wind drove them to Italy at a speed of 90 miles per hour. At nine o'clock on Sunday they reached the Italian coast, and came down safely at a Tuscan hamlet near Brescia. They were heartily welcomed by the inhabitants. The distance traversed was more than 1,2)0 miles. A SO-CALLED NEW "GEM." Mr. Bryce-Wright writes from 204, Regent-street :—" A. so-called new gem' (vio- lane) has been lately introduced into the London market from Paris. Many collectors of pierres de fantasie ' have purchased these precious stones' at very high prices, per- haps thinking they are a new and transparent variety of the mineral violan, a dark violet blue variety of pyroxene. Such is not the case. They are simply imitations of the I amethyst, made of glass, with an admixture of potash and. borax. The metallic oxides are nearly absent, the specific gravity of these precious stones' being only 2.26. They are easily scratched with quartz, and under the dichroiscope show naturally no extraordinary ray. I have just received for examination a specimen, for which the sum of £5O was given; its true value is about 25." FOR aanz FAMILY SCRAP-BOOE.—Never let tea boil.—For rough hands, use lemon juice.—Tepid milk and water cleans oilcloth without soap.—Turpentine applied to a cut is a preventive of lockjaw.—A hot shovel held over furniture removes white spots—Sprinkle sassafras bark among dried fruit to keep out worms.—A handful of hay in a panful of water neutralises smell of paint.—To make a carpet look fresh, wipe with a damp cloth after sweeping.—ln sewing and winding carpet rags, double them with the right side out.—Clean tea or coffee cups with scouring brick; it makes them look as good as new.—Remove ink-stains on silk, woollen or cotton by saturating with spirits of turpentine. —Washing pine floor in solution of one pound of copperas dissolved in one gallon of strong lye gives oak colour.—Re- move flower-pot stains from window sills by rubbing with fine wood ashes and rinse with clean water—A paste of equal parts of sifted ashes, clay, and salt, and a little water, cements cracks in stoves and ovens.—Mixture daf two parts of glycerine, one part ammonia, and a little rose-water whitens and softens the hands.—Cover plants with news- papers before sweeping. Also put a little ammonia upon them once a week.—Cabbage is made digestible by first slicing and then putting in boiling water, with a pinch of soda and some salt, and boiling just fifteen minutes. THE ARK.—When Mr. Bryce ascended Mount Ararat he did not actually discover the remains of the Ark. But Ararat is a large mountain, and as Mr. Bryce's motto was excelsior (in Mr. Longfellow's sense of the word), he was content with reaching the summit. He did find a piece of wood, however, and he "was not prepared to assert that it was not gopher wood," and a portion of the Ark. There is now every reason to believe that the wood was gopher wood, and a fragment of the very structure in which Noah escaped from the deluge. The Turkish Government has recently appointed Commissioners to examine into the causes of avalanches on Mount Ararat. This is highly creditable to the Porte, which is sometimes thought rather to neglect the interests of its Armenian subjects. In a glacier of the mountain the Commissioners have discovered the Ark in very fair preservation, though not quite sea- worthy. Much of the Ark remains to be excavated out of the ice, and if Dr. Schliemann means to get a concession to dig, and pouroir excluszf, he had better take time by the forelock. It will surprise us if Hittite inscriptions are not discovered on the venerable relic. The tradition of the Deluge is practically universal—Uncle Remus shows (what M. Le Normant doubted) that it occurs among the negroee. But the quaintest form of the story is the Lithuanian tale —that as men were being drowned Perkua (the chief deity of the race) was eating nuts. He dropped the shells in the raging waters, and in the shells men escaped. Hence, doubtless, the term " walnut-shell " applied to small round boats patronised by freshmen.—Daily News.

The progress of rivers to the ocean is not so rapid as that of man to error. A pretty anecdote is told of an old man who, as the Queen was taking one of her drives, attempted to throw a bouquet of simple flowers into the carriage. He missed the mark, and they fell into the road. Her Majesty at once ordered the coachman to stop, in order to give the old man , the opportunity of a second shot. This time he was suc- cessful, and the flowers were accepted with a smile. A Chatham-street merchant was shipwrecked while re- turning to his home with the hard-yarned fruits of his labours in this country. He had tossed about for three days in a small boat, when he was waked from a drowsy fatigue by his companion shouting, "A sail! a sail!" Starting up with despair written on every feature, he ex- claimed," A sale! a sale! and I have no catalogue !" CROOKEIO COINCIDFNCES.—A pamphlet, published in the year 1703, has the following strange title The Deformity of Sin Cured: a Sermon preached at St. Michael's, Crooked Lane, before the Prince ef Orange, by the Rev. S. Crook- shanks. Sold by Matthew Denton, at the Crooked Billet, near Cripplegate, and by all Booksellers." The words of the text are :—"Every crooked path shall be made straight," and the Prince before whom it was preached was deformed in person. In a road leading to the cheese-famed Dunlop, a half- witted creature named Andrew Gillies was employed to break stones, and to keep the hedges in order. One day a well-known doctor in that quarter, while passing along the road on which Andy was engaged with his hammer, think- ing to raise a joke at the daft stonebreaker's expense, said, "Man, Andrew, some day when I have time, I'll have ye a' ta'en doon and set up anew; wha will I mak ye like?" " Mak' me like wha ye please, doctor, only see y dinna mak' me like yersel." As EXAM. ANECDOTE.—A correspondent writes us as follows :—ln the Christmas week of 1871 I was undergoing my final examination at one of the London Colleges. I must mention that it was at the same time that his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales was battling with typhoid fever at Sandringham, and thg heart of the whole nation was round that sick bed; even the medical students, harassed and fatigued by an examination which extended over five days, used to find time, morning and evening, to rush to the General Post-office and read the latest bulletins. My exam. was over, and-I was sitting in comparative comfort, listen- ing to the answers of a Bartholomew's man, who followed me, and whose cool self-confidence I greatly envied. The ex- aminer took him on the treatment of typhoid; and after the candidate had exhausted all the means of treatment he could think of, without satisfying his questioner, the latter said. "Have you never heard of the treatment by cold baths ? "Certainly I have, sir," replied the candidate; "but the treatment is so very novel that I scarcely thought it worth mentioning. " Nonsense!" retorted the great physician; "I have been usingit with the best results at the—Hospital The Bartholomew's man replied that, in spite of that, he should hesitate to adopt it in private practice, as in case of a fatal result occurring from any other cause, it would infallibly be attributed to the new treatment, and damage the practice. The examiner demurring to this, the young man at length said, " Pardon me, sir; but if the Pance of Wales were under your care now, do you think you would feel inclined to treat him with cold baths?" The examiner looked annoyed for a moment, then began to smile, then to laugh outright at the man's impudence; and at last, shrugg- ing his shoulders, replied good-naturedly, "Well, upon my word, lam not quite certain that I should."—Chambersis Journal.

ALARM CAUSED BY BALLOONS—Many are the stories told of the alarm caused by the descent of balloons. "Diana ye think the world will soon be at an end ?" was the remark of an old Scotchman, when one descended near Glasgow in the year 1785. "Eh, missus, but he's come at last, and no mistake!" was the observation of an old countryman one night, when Coxwell descended near Croydon. "Who's come at last?" cried his better half, running out with another light. "Look ye, Sally," said he, pointing to the dim, dark outline of the mysterious visitor, " that's the old gem'man himself, or else I'm a Dutchman." Coxwell tells another story of descending near a village late at night, and being absolutely denied shelter or refreshment at several houses, two of them inns. He had to sleep in the car, with ballast-bags for pillows, and curtains—silk curtains— formed by the folds of the balloon, in the middle of a field. Next morning some workmen approached, and he lay still purposely, to see how they would behave. "On jumping up, like Jack-in-box, the worthies looked perfectly be4il- dered ; two ran off, and the rest were powerless aito speech. 'Why, lads, it's a balloon,' said I, 'don't be frightened.' And what be you,' inquired the bravest of the lot. Why the aeronaut to be sure; the party who goes up.' 'Ah; said he, I thought you wa'ant a mortal man.' 'But lam though, feel me,' said I. 'No, da'angd if I come any closer;' and immediately a side movement was made for the gate." The landlords who had denied him the night before apologised, but one of them said, " Lord love ye, sir, a man coming out of the clouds, what could he expect on this here wicked earth?" Looking at the matter in this light, one can understand the alarm of a young girl, tending sheep, who, from no apparent source, once saw a deal chair de- scending from the skies! Arago tells us that Gay-Lussac, when he had reached twenty-two thousand and odd feet, wished still to ascend, and the chair being readily available, over it went. Its workmanship was sufficient to prove that it was not of celestial origin!--__nid.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 4, lBB3.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 4, lBB3.
NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, &c.

A reserve of 1,280 acres for a Governmental farm has been proclaimed on the Central Railway, 180 miles from Rock- hampton, Queensland. The Minister for Lands of Victoria has temporarily reserved 2,500 acres in South Gippsland for the purposes of an aFicultural college. The Minister contemplates mak- ing a similar reservation in the west district. The large cattle show recently held at Berlin was by far thelargest at ptesent held in Germany this year. There were 180 exhibitors and altogether 1,200 animals, comprising 451 oxen, 310 sheep, and 439 pigs; while last year only 886 ani- mals in all were shown. Ram IN DEVON.—On the north coast of Devon the coun- try is overrun by rats which have been doing immense damage to the crops and hedges for more than a year, and still swarms in thousands in spite of all the efforts of the landowners and farmers to keep them under. A CORPORAL BURIED IN A. HAYRICIC.—A remarkable accident is reported from Portsmouth. A ship's corporal of the Himalaya, a few nights ago, got upon a half-made hay- rick. While he was asleep upon it the haymakers resumed their work, and, ignorant of his presence, buried him. He was not rescued till Wednesday night, and is in a prostrate condition. Tits COLORADO POTATO BEETLE.—The Colorado beetle has been seen on board a ship trading between America and England, and strict injunctions are given to officers of Cus- toms at the ports of the United Kingdom relative to the course they are to pursue in the event of the beetle being found in any vessel arriving in this country. The instruc- tions issued at the time of the previous scare are to be rigidly carried out. To KEEP BUTTER Coon.—Lay the butter on a plate, which is to be placed in a milk-pan with just enough water to reach the edge of the plate without touching the butter. Take a piece of thin, soft cloth, dip it in water and lay it on the butter, with the sides falling into the water all around; then place the pan in some window where there is a draught of air. The evaporation constantly carried on as the water is drawn alp by the porous cloth will keep the butter cool and firm even on a very warm day. Weems' SEEDS IN YORICSIYIRE.—The whole of the Prizes, value £3OO (and commendations), given by the Royal Agri- : cultural Society, at their annual meeting last week, for the Best Cultivated Farmlin Yorkshire, were awarded to cus- tomers of Messrs. Webb and: Sons, the Queen's Seedsmen, Wordsley, Stourbridge, who used Webbs' celebrated Grass, Clover, and Root Seeds, Cereals and Bone Manures, for the production of their Prize Crops. Class I.—For grazing or dairy farms above 150 acres in extent, with at least two- thirds in Permanent Grass: First Prize, £75, Mr. R. E. Turnbull, Twyers Wood, Hedon, Hull; Second Prize, £25, Mr. W. H. Davis, Holme House, Gargrave ; Commended, Mr. H. Holden, Halton East, Skipton. Class 2.—For arable farms above 150 acres in extent, with less than two-thirds in Permanent Grass: First Prize, £75, Mr. T. H. Hutchin- son, Manor House, Catterick; Second Prize, £25, Mr. J. Watson, Wood House, Brough ; Commended, Mr. W. Cover- dale, Lund Cote, Kirby Moorside. Class 3.—For farms under 150 acres in extent: First Prize, £75, Mr. B. Beevers, Clay Shed Farm, Escrick; Second Prize, £25, Mr. Joseph Horner, Marton, Bingley. ADULTERATION 01, MIL/C.—DEALERS AND FAANIERS.—A case of some importance to milk dealers and farmers was heard before Mr. T. S. Daniel, QC., and a special jury, at Keighley County Court, on Wednesday. John Waterhouse, milk dealer, of Keighley, sought to recover the sum of £8 is. 11d. from James Smith, farmer, of Keighley, being the amount of penalty inflicted and damages sustained by the plaintiff selling defendant's milk, which was found to be adulterated. The case for the plaintiff was that he re- ceived milk from the defendant which should have been pure, but it was found to contain water at the rate of one gallon in seven. The plaintiff was fined before the magis- trates, and now claimed the penalty and costs.—Mr. Neill, for the defence, submitted that the milk was unadulterated when supplied to the plaintiff.—The jury at first disagreed, but eventually returned a verdict for the amount claimed with costs. A new trial was applied for and granted. A NOTEWORTHY AGRICULTURIST.—SIR B. T. BRANDRETH GIBBS, PRESIDENT OF THE ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. OF EtioLawn.—Sir Brandreth Gibbs' agricultural career is exactly contemporary with that of the society itself. In office at the first show in 1839, he has been in office ever since. Then appointed, at the suggestion of Earl Spencer, who had seen him at work as a volunteer, he soon succeeded his late brother as the general manager of the society's shows, an office which he continued to hold till 1874. He has all through his public life acted As member of the Coun- cil of the society, and in 1859, on a sudden vacancy, he un- dertook the office of secretary, when the Council voted him the society's large gold medal, accompanied with an en- grossed yote of thanks. He has latterly been elected to a vice-presidency of the society, and now his official connec- tion culminates in the presidency. Sir Brandreth Gibbs has also been honorary secretary of the Smithfield Club since 1843. He was one of the organisers of the Great Ex- hibition of 1851. In 1855 he represented the English Agri- cultural Department at the Paris Universal Exhibition. In 1862 he was again in office at the Great Exhibition at South Kensington. In 1867 he was Special Commissioner for all matters relating to agriculture in the Paris Universal Exhi- bition of that year. In 1873 he acted for the agricultural portion of the Great Exhibition at Vienna. The honours he has received from foreign Governments for services ren- dered on these great occasions have been fitly crowned by the knighthood which he has received at the hands of the Queen. It has certainly been a most fruitful career—one of great and most useful activity; nor have Sir Brandreth's services been confined to this country alone, although here his services have been most constant and most noteworthy —nor confined even to the agricultural field. His powers of organisation have been sought and employed on other occa- sions, as in the fishery exhibitions of late years, and espe- cially in the one now so successfully before the public, of which he had been appointed director and secretary, offices, however, which he had at length to resign, owing to failing health. Sir Brandreth takes office now as president of the Royal Agricultural Society, whose pusperity he has wit- nessed and promoted during the whole of its exiatenee: There is not one of its members more loyal to the great interests which it represents—not one capable in his own person of more fitly representing the society itself—whether its splendid history, its magnificent present position, or its capabilities for the future. A past to which he has so largely contributed is certain to direct him aright in guiding it towards a future of still greater utility and success.— Agricultural Gazette. Tie E AGRICULTURAL STATISTICS OF IRELAND.—These statistics for 1882, collected by the officers of the Royal Constabulary, have just been issued, and they show that on the whole Irish farmers had not a very gratifying experi- ence last year. The meteorological report, which fully accounts for the want of prosperity, is prepared from ob- servations made in Dublin. Rain fell on 227 days, against 1977. days per annum, the average of the twelve years 1870-81. The amount of rainfall was 31.184 inches, whilst in 1870-81 the average was only 28.851 inches. During the seventeen years 1865-81 the average annual rainfall was only 28194 inches in 193 5 days. It is evident, therefore, that last year was an unusually wet one in Ireland. Of a total cultivated area, amounting to about 15,300,000 statute acres, 10,109,625 acres were devoted to pasturage and 5,081,336 acres to grain and other crops and to meadow and clover. The quantity of land under potatoes was 837,918 acres. In 1871 the potato area was 1,058,287 acres. The process of natural selection is evidently establishing the "champion" variety as not only the least liable to disease but also the most prolific, and the Irish farmers have not been slow to profit by its evident fitness for their uncertain climate. Last year 70-7 per cent. of the land given to potatoes was planted with this description, and the yield per acre largely exceeded that of any other. In the county of Dublin as much as 93 cwt. per acre were gathered, but else- where the yield varied from 35 cwts. to 71 cwts. per acre. Very little wheat is grown in Ireland, and oats is the prin- cipal grain crop. Of this the yield last year was poor, only 18,286,495 cwts. having been reaped from 1,397.307 acres of land, against 19,703,074 cwts. from 1,393,312 acres in 1881. Next to that of pasturage the acreage under hay crops is the largest. Last year it was 1,962,152 acres, and 2,001,029 acres in 1881. The estimated produce was 2.1 tons per rcre, against 2 tons in 1881. The export of cattle from Ireland to Great Britain was last year the largest on record. Not fewer than 722,581 oxen, bulls, and Cows were sent, of which 427,798 were "store" cattle destined to be fattened in England. It is worth noticing, too, that this increased export has not diminished, the number held by the farmers of Ireland—the stock being 3,987,211 in 1882 and 3,956,595 in 1881. It appears, there- fore, that although the grain crops were poor in the sister island last year there were substantial compensation in the good yield of potatoes and in the increased export of cattle. For these the prices obtained were, as every one knows, un- precedentedly high.

div.p: Passion is the drunkenness of the mind.—Spenser. Temper is nine-tenths of Chriatianity.—Btehop Wilson. What in life is more beautiful than happy human faces? Not what, I have, but what I do, is my kingdom.— Carlyle. The noblest quality wherewith nature has endowed woman for the good of the world is maternal love. A cheerful temper, joined with innocence, will make beauty attractive, knowledge delightful, and wit good- natured. A recent obituary notice says:—" Mr. Smith was an estimable citizen. He died with perfect resignation. He had recently been married." A Yankee farmer recently advertised for a runaway wife, and called particular attention to the meanness of her deser- tion just as the spring work was coming on, after he had had the expense of wintering her. "PLUCKED IN THE ERANIN&TION."—This phrase bad its origin in an ancient custom, by which anyone, who objected to a degree about to be conferred in congregation, notified his dissent by plucking the sleeve of the proctor's gown. What stronger breastplate than a heart untainted! Thrice is he armed that hath his quarrel just; And he but naked, though locked up in steel, Whose conscience with injustice is corrupted.—Sitaksticre.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

BROAD BEANS of the successional crops will require the tops pinched, and if there is any black fly lodging in them , carry the whole away and put them on the fire. LETTUCE may still be sown, and may become serviceable before the frost injures it. We rely chiefly on the Alexan- dria Cos. Those who prefer the cabbage varieties will find a good one in "All the year round." We should prefer sowing them very thin, so that they may remain in the place they are sown. . TURNIPS.—Few people are aware what a *ice dish the tops of these make when boiled. In the spring, when the flowering shoots have attained the height of fin, or Bin., they may be pinched off close to the turnip, and cooked similar to other green vegetables. For this purpose we sow at this time of the year on any spare piece of ground, which we make moderately firm by treading. Veiteh's Red Globe is the variety we select. The Chirk Castle Black Stone is also a good one for standing the winter. STRAWBERRY BEDS, under the best conditions, will not continue prolific over the fourth year. Now is the time to set about preparing plants for a new bed, and it is possible to have them so that they will bear fruit next year far superior to plants of three or four years' standing. Gene- rally there are plenty of runners round the outside of the bed, and as they are the strongest they should be made use of. The soil round the bed is usually very hard, conse- quently We advise the introduction of soil from some other part of the garden, which should be placed four inches thick, and on this lay the runners, with a stone on each to keep it in its place. They will take root in 10 or 14 days, by which time the ground should be ready for their recep- tion. To give an idea of what plants will be required we will touch slightly on planting. We plant in rows 21t. apart, and the same between the plants, but on each side of the plant in the line we put another, the three forming a triangle. As soon as the fruit is gathered the first season, the two lateral plants are cut off with the spade, which allows space for the other plant to develop itself. By this method it will be found that finer and probably more fruit will be produced the first year than in any year after. Another method that may be adopted is to plant in rows as stated, and set the plants Bin. apart in the row, cutting out two out of three the second year. Varieties of strawberries are numerous, and most of them have something to recom- ' mend them—their size, flavour, prolificness, and suitable- ness to soils. President is a general favourite, and suits this • locality well. Vicomtess Heeicart de Thury is a prolific cropper; bright red skin and well flavoured. Sir J. Paxton has been one of the best with us this season. The fruit is very large and handsome, and the crop heavy. Keen's seedling is an old well-known kind; few excel it in flavour, and we should be sorry to do away with it. Sir Chas. Napier is on trial with us, but it is highly spoken of as a suitable kind for this locality. The cottager will do well to select from the three first named. THE FRONT GARDEN.—We have cut away all the flower- ing stems of that beautiful old plant, the Double Rocket, which was cherished by our grandmothers. We did not throw the stems away, as our man "Friday" declared they would root if put in the ground, and make good plants. Consequently they were cut in suitable lengths and inserted in the shade (not under) of an old apple tree. We were further informed that that was the way old country folks always propagated them. We have always depended on the young shoots at the base for cutting, to which reference was made two or three weeks back. A GARDEN OF ANNUALS.—Turning into a by-lane near Farington the other day, we were gratified to see such a one in front of a cottage. There were Lupins, Chrysanthe- mums, Burridgi, Marigolds, crimson and white Candytuft, Nasturtium of sorts gilia tricolour, linum grandiflora, and others. Many more were to come on, especially Everlast- ings. Virginian stock formed an edging for the centre bed. The flowering season of this plant may be prolonged if the ends are clipped off with a pair of shears or scissors. One or both sides may be done first, and the top after, or vice versa, so as to avoid depriving it wholly of its beauty, how- ever temporary it maybe. Beyond this miniature hedge, the garden appeared natural and pleasing. All that is required in such a garden are a few perennials, to impart more solidity to the whole. THE WINDOW of the cottage alluded to had some plants above mediocrity for a cottage, and some had been in their possession for a period of two or three years. Cottagers lose more window plants than they need. We once knew an old Waterloo veteran who kept Tom Thumb geraniums for twelve years, until they at last required boxes to grow in. I never saw a garden produce a better display with the same kind. Now, everyone engaged in plant-growing has experienced how difficult it is to preserve old geraniums over the winter. We shall endeavour to instruct the cot- tager how to accomplish this as the season wines round.

div.head: SUICIDE OF A LUNATIC AT IL INiIILL. CHARGE AGANST THE ATTENDANT,
div.p: THE SUICIDE OF A LUNATIC AT IL INiIILL. CHARGE AGANST THE ATTENDANT,

At a meeting of the Committee of Visitors of Rainhill Asylum, held on the 18th instant, Mr. E. Gibbon in the chair, Dr. Rogers, the medical attendant, having reported that James Parry, an inmate of the asylum committed sui- c'de by hanging on the 3rd instant, and that he had sus- pended the attendant, Charles Burrows, who was in charge of Parry, it was ordered that Mr. Swift, the clerk to the Committee of Visitors, prosecute Charles Burrows before the justices. A summons was accordingly issued against Charles Burrows, and on Friday he appeared at the St. H-lens Police Court to answer the charge of wilfully neg- lecting James Parry. Mr. H. D. Riley appeared on behalf of the defendant. Mr. Swift in his opening statement said under the Lunacy Act the Bench could for the offence charged against defendant fine him in any sum not exceed- ing £4O nor less than £2, but under the Summary Jurisdic- tion Act they could fine him in any lower amount they pleased. He (Mr. Swift), however, thought if they found defendant guilty of the charge they wall think £2 little enough. The circostances were shortly these : Parry was a night attendant at the asylum. On the 2nd inst. he went on duty about eight o'clock to watch a numbtr of patients, some eight of whom were suicidal, and he was placed in the room so that he could see them all, with in- structions not to lose sight of any of them. Althoueh he was the only attendant actually on duty, close by, a yard or two away, there were two other attendants sleeping, so that in case of any emergency he had nothing to do but arouse one or both of those attendants. The chief night attendant visited the ward two or three times during that night and found all correct, but between three and four o'clock in the morning he was called by a patient who was assisting Burrows, and on arriving he found the dead body of a p,ttient named Parry lying on the floor. The neglect, therefore, that was charged against Burrows was that he was on duty, that he had strict orders not to lose sight of this man, but that he allowed him to leave his bed, although it was within two yards of where he (Burrows) was supposed to be sitting, go into another room, bring out a brace and hang himself to a door close by; that he did not prevent the man in any way from committing suicide, nor did he call those attendants who were sleeping in the next room. Mr. Swift then said a plan of the rooms had been prepared, and this was handed to the Bench.—Dr. Rogers, the medical superintendent of the Asylum, said that a written list of the patients under his charge was given to the defendant, the suicidal patients' names having the mark of a cross opposite them. The name ef the deceased man Parry was marked with a double cress, which meant that he ought to be very carefully watched. Defendant bad to look into three other bedrooms, but he had a patient to assist him. Witness did not think it was possible for a man to have committed suicide if defendant had been properly watchful. —ln answer to Mr. Riley, Dr. Rogers said there was a patient named Barker, who took fits, under the care of Bur- rows, and slept in a room different to that in which the de- ceased man Parry slept. On the night in question defen- dant had to be with five persons who had suicidal determin- ation, and had charge of six in other rooms who had a suicidal tendcncy. If a night attendant heard a disturbance in another room where there was a patient with suicidal tendency he would certainly be expected to go and see what it was. It was Burrows's duty to go to the other rooms four times each hour, but while he went a person was left to act as assistant. Parry was one of the 26 patients under defendant's care that night, and he (Dr. Rogers) thought it reasonable or he would not have ordered it. De- fendant had been at the asylum about 18 months. Re-ex- amined: On this night defendant had not left an assistant in charge. Jos. Irving; a day attendant, spoke to haying seen Parry undress on the evening in question and to the fact that there had been no brace or anything of that kind concealed about his person or in his bed.— Mr. Riley, in defence, said he did not think mere had been any case made out against the defendant. The matter had been examined by a coroner's jury, and they refused to make any presentment against Burrows. The question which the Bench had really to decide was as to whether the defendant had in an emergency adopted the wrong alternative. He had five patients to mind in one room and several others distributed through other rooms, and he (Mr. Riley) was in- structed to say that during the night the patient Barker had had a fit and it was whilst defendant was attending him that the suicide had been committed.—After some consider- ation the Bench decided to impose a fine of £2 and costs.— Mr. Riley gave notice that an appeal would be made.

A labourer lately called on one of the local registrars to register the birth of a child. After this was completed he coolly remarked, "The child's very poorly, sir, and I may as well register its death while I am here, to save me the trouble of coming here." The work that is performed only for the sake of what it will bring, not for what it is to carry forth, is like cloth of shoddy, which may please the eye, but will not wear. It is cheap, flimsy stuff, woven with no nobler purpose than to hold together long enough to be bought and paid for. When the celebrated Beau Nash was ill, Dr. Cheyne wrote a prescription for him. The next day the dostor coming to see his patient, inquired if he had followed his prescription. "No, truly, doctor," said Nash ; "if I had I should have broken my neck, for I threw it out of a two-pair of stairs window."

A reverend sportsman was once boasting of his skill in finding a hare. "If I were a hare," said a Quaker who was present," I would take my seat in a place where I would be sure of not being disturbed by thee from the first day of January to the last day of December." "Why, where would you go ?" asked the sportsman. "Into thy-study," replied the Quaker.

MINERS' DEMONSTRATION AT IIAYDOCK PARK. SPEECHES BY 51R. BRADLAUGH M.P. AND MR. BURL' M.P. The first demonstration and athletic festival in cennection with the Ashton and Haydock Miners Trade Union, took place on Saturday afternoon, under favourable auspices. ['he union has beers la existence for some years, but it is principally during the past year or two it has made any groat progress. So late as January 1882, the organisation had only a list of some 615 members, but at the conclusion of the great strike last year, the membership roll was greatly lengthened, and since that time other members have joined at every meeting. In January last the number on the books was 2,240, but at the present moment there are 2,311 persons connected with the society. A month or two ago, the Committee thought the interests of the union would le till further advanced if a popular demonstration took place each year, and it was decided that the first gathering should be.held on a portion of ground near to Haydock Park (Dr. Beaman having kindly granted the privilege of holding it there). Fortunately the weather was all that could be de- sired, and the brilliant sun, with the cool refreshing breeze, were no small or inconsiderable adjuncts to the success of the meeting. The colliers of Earlestown, Haydock, Ashton, Gel borne and surrounding neighbourhoods were early astir, and cozld be seen, attired in their Sunday best, wandering along the roads in the direction of Ashton Heath. In the forenoon the North Ashton, the Haydock, the Goose Green, and the Billings brass bands paraded districts allotted to them by the committee, and there proved an attraction to many of the men, who followed the bands. The official programme set forth that the members were to meet at their lodges not later than 10 a.m.' and walk two deep behind the bands to Asliton Heath. On arriving there a monster procession—the men, each of whom wore a medal commemorative of the event suspended by a safety pin and blue ribbon—being formed three abreast. Altogether some 2,000 or 3,000 colliers were present, and as they marched through the streets of Ashton they presented an imposing spectacle. In front was the North Ashton brass band, under the conductorship of Mr. Singleton, who led the members of the Park-lane, Miners' Rest, Waggoners' Rest, and Triumphant Lodges. Next followed a waggonette containing Mr. Thomas Burt, M.P., Mr. Charles Bradlaugh, M.P., Miss Bradlaugh (daughter of Mr. C. Bradlaugh), Mr. Isherwood, and Mr. Samuel Woods (miners' agent for the district), and the gentlemen named were loudly cheered on making their appearance. The Haydock brass band (con- ducted by Mr. Forshaw) headed the Pewfall Grand, the Poor Man's Friend, the Star in the East, and Labour in \ ain Lodges; while preceding the men connected with the Britains Glory, British Queen, Hope of Ashton, England's Glory, Ever Firm, Hinge of Industry, and Alexander lodges was the Goose Green brass band, under the leadership of Mr. Mullineaux; the Billinge brass band (conducted by Mr. Lomas) followed, and the rear of the procession was brought up by the members of the Pride of Golnorne, Light of Ashton, Min.ers' Defence, Rising Star, True Blue, Pear Tree, Glory of Longshaw, Pride of Billinge, Live and Let Live, Pride of Pemberton, ' and Pride of Garswood lodges. On arriving at Haydock ! Park, the men were drawn up around a platform which had ' been erected, and a public meeting was held. The chair I was occupied by Mr. Samuel Woods, of Park Lane, and he was supported by Mr. Burt, M.P., Mr. Bradlaugh, 31. P., Miss Bradlaugh, Mr. Edwards (North Staffordshire), Mr. Gerrard and Mr. Tinker (Manchester), Mr. Parkinson and ' Mr. Wogan (Wigan), Mr. Partington (Park Lane), and a , number of other delegates. There would then be an attend- ance of some 5,a00 or 6,000 persons. The CHAIRMAN, in the course of his opening rem irks, said that in January, 1882, the organisation in the Ashton and Haydock district comprised only about 615 members. Shortly afterwards they had a very hard struggle against an unjustifiable attempt to reduce wages, and by the united efforts of the various districts in Lancashire they were enabled to win a victory and compel the coalowners to allow them to return to work at the old rate of pay. The action of the district in that struggle gave an impetus to unionism , which had been of a permanent character, and at the present time they had not less than 2,311 members in the union. There were, however, something like 8,000 or 9.000 men in the dietrict, and he asked all who had not already joined the union to do so at once. Mr. THOMAS HOWARD then moved, Mr. WALTER HOLMES seconded, and Mr. JOHN HIBBERT supported the following resolution :—" That this meeting of miners of Ashton and 1; Haydock offers a hearty welcome to Thos. Burt, E.,q.eal.P., . and Charles Bradlaugh, Eeq., M.P., to our annual demon- stration, and hereby desires to tender unto them our entire sympathy, confidence, and support in their noble and per- sistent efforts to improve and elevate the position of the in- dustrial teeming mutitudes of this country." The motion was enthusiasticilly carried. Mr. THOMAS Dix then proposed "That this meeting is of opinion that the working classes of this country suffer great privation in consequence of the injurious law of en- tail and primogeniture, the non-cultivation of land, and the heavy taxation on the country on account of perpetual pen- sions to those who never rendered any service to the State. ! We therefore call upon her Majesty's Government to pass :1 some measure of land reform for the good of the I people and also for the abolition of perpetual pensions." (Applause.) Mr. EDWARD WALIKDEN seconded the resolution. I Mr. CHARLES BRADLAUGH, M.P., who rOB3 to support ! the motion, was received with loud and continuous cheer- ing. He said he was pleased to dnd that the miners of that district were beginning to concern themselves about poli- tical questions. It was his belief that the working men of this country had hindered their improvement for many ! generations by fancying that politics ought to be left to • other classes, and that political questions formed no busi- ness of theirs. Political life, however, ought to be a part I of their daily life. They made up the citizenship of the ! country. They were its saldiers, its police, and its wealth creators, so that it was to their interest, more than to the , interest of any other class, to see that they were well ! governed, peaceable, and happy. He regarded it as a shame that those who lived in country districts should have no Parliamentary vote, as was the case of most of those pre- sent. It was a mystery he could not comprehend, and an absurdity he would do his best to I abolish. There was especial need for trades unions I of all classes to utilise political weapons. Some time ago the complaint was made that trades unions had no right to exist, and the law declared they should not exist. That, however, was not so now, and trades unions were entitled to I use all political weapons which would tend to improve the I position of the working people of the country. But they I were not only entitled to use them; they were bound to use I them. (Hear, bear.) The suffrage was a weapon of offence , and defence ; and if the members of Parliament for that dis- trict had to look to those who at present had no votes, for ' their votes at the nextelection, they would be more thought- ! fal as to what their wishes were. Employers were organ- ised, and the employed should organise also; em- plovers had political power, and the employed ! should have it as well. It was said that be pleaded ! for class legislation; but if Parliament legislated ! for railway companies, for banks and such objecere I and not for human beings, it was a mockery to talk of class legislation. As to our present representative institutions, we had one House that was not representative at all or that represented the landed interests alone. It stood in the way of everything that it thought too rapid, and it considered every measure of progress too rapid that touched its own interests. In the House of Commons the landlords had more representation than any other body, and they nominated their sons or relations to seats where they had local influence. What he desired to see was far more men in the House who were barn amongst the people. (Applause.) A subject which concerned those present, and, indeed, all working people very deeply, was the expenditure of the country. It was of no use for them to clamour for a rise of five per cent or stand out against a reduction of 10 per cent if 15 per cent were taken out of their pockets to meet the national ex- penditure. There was great need for working men to organise themselves into strong unions. If every workingman had had a vote he did not believe the large employers of labour in the House of Commons would have attempted to coun- teract the beneficial effect which the Employers' Liabitity Act sought to confer upon the people. The action of employers in forcing men to sign themselves out of the Act was dishonourable, and if the workmen had attempted any such practice it would have been denounced as wicked and cowardly. Employers, however, could only put pressure upon men when the latter were disorganised and did not know their own strength, and when they were drunken and unreliable. But if they were sober and industrious, and banded together, the employed were stranger than the em- ployers, for their labour was the wealth of the country. (Applause.) Condemning the law of entail and primogeni- ture, Mr. Bradlaugh pointed as prominent amongst its evil effects to the large quantity of uncultivated or half cultivated land in the country, the proper utilisation of which would result in a cheapening of food and a reduction in the burdens which the people had now to bear. He would not make a speech upon the pension list, because when Mr. Chaplin moved his motion in the House of Com- mons with respect to it, his friend Mr. Bart would second the motion if he (Mr.Bradlaugh) was not in his place-(laugh- ter)—and he did not want to anticipate Mr. Bart's speech. One of the local members had honoured him by mentioning him in a speech—members of Parliament generally did mention him. (Laugher.) That member (Mr. Knowles) had said the pension list was only a small matter. Well when he told them that three dukes—the Duke of Rich- mond, the Duke of Grafton, and the Duke of Marlborough— got pensions amounting to as much as the national debt, they would then see whether it was a small matter or not. (Cheers.) If that was a small matter, he (Mr. Bradlaugh) thought it was enough for him and he would try his hand at the big one after he had seftied it. (Laughter & applause). His only objection to perpetual pensions was that they were for too long a time. (Laughter). It had been said, too, that he was attacking property. Why should he not? The employers were attacking property—the miner's labour was , his property—when they stood between the miner and the cupboard and said, "No food in this district if you do not give up your property." Moreover, he was attacking pro- perty which did not rightly belong to those who had it, for it came out of the wages of the working men. In conclusion, he said that he was very glad indeed to be at so large and enthusiastic a meeting, and the reception which he had met with would encourage him in his struggle with the House of Commons, and when he took his seat there he hoped to be of some service to the working men of the country, in order to repay the debt he owed them. (Loud and prolonged cheering). The resolution was then enthusiastically carried. Mr. J. PARTINGTON moved, and Mr. E. PRAYER seconded, 1 the following:—" That this meeting strongly condemns the

coercive action of many employers (especially in Lance; shire) in depriving the miners of the benefits of the Em- ployers Liability Act, 1830, and hereby pledges itself to support any legislative measure that may be brought before the House of Commons at any time, giving the mining class the full benefits of the Act; and also that we entirely agree with the proposed amendments of the Mines Regulation Act, to be brought before Parliament by Thomas Burt, Esq., M.P., at the earliest opportunity, and as we believe that a strong intelligent legislation is necessary for this purpose, we hereby agree to join the union for the accomplishment of these desirable objects." Mr. THOMAS BURT, M.P., supported the resolution, and was very warmly received. He said the Employers' Lia- bility Act was only passed after years of earnest agitation, The Act was especially passed in behalf of the miner, and although it had only been in operation for two years it had done an immense service to the working-classes of the country. (Applause.) They had obtained, in the aggre- gate, some thousands of pounds of compensation every penny of which was a result of the Act, That, however, was not the chief benefit that had accrued. It had had the effect of inducing greater care on the part of careless, negli- gent, and reckless employers. The whole of the miners in Lencashire—over 30,000—had been compelled to contract out of its provisions. Contracting out of the Act tended to make employers less careful than they otherwise would Ibe of the safety of the men. That the men had been com- pelled to contract out of the Act was, however, their own fault. Had they possessed an organisation the masters would never have attempted it. In the districts of Durham and Northumberland, where the miners had an organisation 40,000 strong, no attempt had been made to force the men to contract out of the Act, but a locality had been selected where the union was weak. At the request of the Parlia- mentary Committee of the Trades Union Congress he under- took to bring in a bill to prevent employers from compelling their workmen to _contract out of the Act. He only received a very small amount of support in the House, and therefore it was for those outside to make their voices heard, and to bring pressure to bear upon their members. He challenged the truth of the statement that had been made that the majority of the coal miners were opposed to his I measure. Those who made the statement knew perfectly well that it was at the united request of the miners that he had been induced to take the matter up. (Applause.) Miners followed a very hazardous occupation. During the preceding year no fewer than , 1,126 miners lost their lives, while during the past ten years the number killed amounted to 11,294 or an average of 1,029 per year. It would be impossible to state how many had been injured and maimed. There was no doubt, however, that great improvements had been made in the working of different mines. If they took into consideration the quantity of coal raised and the number of men employed it would be seen that there had been a continuous decrease lin the number of deaths and accidents since the Regulation ' Acts came into force. Still there were defects in its machi- nery, as, for instance, the position of the check weighman, which was not altogether satisfactory. If the Act had done nothing beyond the protection of young chil- dren in mines it had put working people under an obligation of eternal gratitude. (Hear, hear.) I What was to be the future of the future of the working classes was a more important question than what was to be I the future of the House of Lords or the Bench of Bishops, because working people were the back bone of the national wealth and independence. He would ask them, tberefore,to be true to themselves, and the future was theirs. Our country would be great as she had been in the past, net only in her I army and navy, not only in her liberal resources, but if they I were true to themselves she would be great in a higher, Ipurer, and nobler sense—in her intelligence, virtue, wisdom, land justice, as she already was in the skill and energy of her people, and rising higher and higher in all that really I ennobled and dignified a people she would stand at length— _

Like some tall cl ff, that lifts its awful form, Swells from the vale, and midway leaves the storm; Though round her base the rolling clouds are spread, Eternal sunshine will settle on her head." (Loud cheers.) Mr. WOOAN (of the Wigan Radical Club) moved a resolu- tion of thanks to Mr. Bradlaugh, and pledging the meeting to support him in his efforts to gain admission into Parlia- ment.

Mr. EDWARDS seconded the resolution, which was carried. After a vote of thanks had been accorded to the speakers, a similar compliment was paid to Dr. Beaman for granting them the use of the park, and the meeting concluded.

THE OUTRAGE ON AN OLD WOMAN AT GOLBORNE.

On Thursday, at the Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Justice Stephen, Hobert Boland (26), collier, pleaded net guilty to violently and criminally assaulting Betsy Ball, an old woman 68 years of age, at Go'borne, near Wigan, on the 14th May. Mr. M'Connell prosecuted; and Dr. Commins, M.P., defended. Evidence was given that the old woman was heard screaming on the high road at Go'borne, and upon a policeman coming up he found her lying on the roadside, and that she had been shockingly illtreated. A man was seen running away, ancton the policeman following him he discovered it was the prisoner. The defence was that the old woman had been attacked by two men, and that the prisoner on hearing her scream came up and ran after them. It was while running after them that the policeman, thinking he was the delinquent who wasjunning away, set off in pursuit and arrested him. Hence the mistake. The jury found the prisoner guilty, and his Lordship sentenced him to penal servitude for tea years, remarking in severe terms on the enormity of the crime. On hearing the sentence the prisoner in pitiful tones protested his innocence. The warders proceeded to remove him, but Ws lordship directed that he should be heard. The prisoner then made a statement to the effect that he only went to the rescue of the old woman, and was taken by the officer. It was only nine months since he lost his wife, and since he had been in prison awaiting his trial his child had died.—His lordship said the jury did not be- lieve his story and he himself did not.—The prisoner was then removed.

ANOTHER TRAMCAR ACCIDENT AT Sr. HELENS.—OR Sunday night, another tramcar accident took place at St. Helens' though fortunately without fatal results. A boy named James Foy, of 30, Higher Parr-street. was riding on the front of one of the cars running between Haydock and St. Helens, and en passing the points in Higher Parr-street he sprang off, but fell near the wheels, which caught one of his arms and lacerated it in a shocking manner. Medical aid was at once obtained and the injuries dressed, sand the lad is now, we understand, progressing favourably. AN OBSTINATE PA.RENT.—Antbony Bannister, who was said to keep a fruiterer's stall in the Market, was summoned before the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, to show cause why he should n9t be committed to gaol in respect of non-payment of arrears.—lt was stated by Superinten- dent Johnston that the defendant had been ordered to con- tribute towards the maintenance of a son in the reformatory schocl, but had failed to comply with that order, in conse- quence of which arrears to the amount of £2 9s. had accu- mulated.—Defendant had before been committed to gaol for neglecting the orders of the court.—Bannister, who did not appear, was committed to gaol for six weeks.

.. - ALL THE MOTHER-IN-Law.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, a young man named Wrn. M-cSawley was charged in custody with having assaulted Ann McSaw- ley, his wife, on the 26th March.—lt appeared that the pri- soner and the complainant were livisg apart, and, according to the latter, prisoner met her on the day in question when crossing Hardshaw fields, and assaulted her. A young woman who was called as a witness by complainant did not, however, corroborate this statement, but said the complain- ant used provoking language to her husband, and that the latter never struck ber.—Prisoner said the accusation was false, and was got up to drive him out of the town. His mother-in-law was at the bottom of it.—The case was dis- missed.

PREscoT CHURCH ScnociLs.—The scholars attending the Sun.lay schools in connection w:th the Parish Church, Prescot, had their annual outing on Tuesday. Having as- sembled at the schools, the young folk, to the number of about 700, and marshalled by their teachers, walked in pro- cession to a field belonging to Mr. W. L. Evans, at Park- side, and enjoyed themselves with cricket, football, and other amusements. The greatness of the procession which as it filed through the streets was imposing from its tnagni- tude, and graceful from the neatness of attire and cheerful bearing of those who took part in it, was enlarged by the presence of the flourishing Bible class of young women, conducted by Mrs. McNaughton, and the equally success- ful young men's Bible class, of which Mr. Bartley has charge. The weather was delightful, and tea was served in the fiald under the best auspices by Mr. Eaton. Among those who took part in promoting the festivities were the Vicar (Rev. H. A. Macnaughton) and the Rev. F. R. Lee, and the superintendents of both the day and StmdaY schools.

Early on Wednesday morning a serious subsidence of land Look place at a village in the Cleveland district, near Dar- lington, resulting in the total destruction of 17 dwelling- houses. The inmates were, asleep when the. subsidence be- gan, but was awakened by a police constable, and had only just succeeded in saving their effects when the buildings

collapsed. A gentleman afflicted with the aquatic athletic mania which cost poor Webb his life started from Dover, on eiatur- day, on a voyage to Paris in a marine tricycle of his own construction. The machine is described ass collapsible boat made out of a tricycle tined with canvas. It is about nine feet long and four feet wide, and is propelled by a pair of sculls. The enterprising traveller left the harbour at nine o'clock in the morning, and arrived safely in Calais early in the evening. About 400 persons witnessed his departure. GREAT POST OFFICE HOBBERY.—A very serious robbery of Bank of England notes from Leamington Pest Office is reported to the police, the notes having teen extracted from registered letters addressed to local bankers. The officials decline to give information as to the robbery, but the amount is currently reported at £1,500. A clerk on duty when the missing registered letters arrived failed on Monday to at- tend for duty, and has disappeared from his home. The police are actively prosecuting inquiries, anti have some in-

formation. _ _ TORPEDOES AND IRONCLADS IN SHAM BATTLE.—A Queenstown correspondent reports that toe ships of the channel squadron went to night quarters at eleven p m. on Tuesday off Castletown Bere. Guns were manned, and the ships cleared for action and armed ready for an expected attack by torpedo boats. Six torpedo boats bad left the Hecla in the afternoon, and procaeded into Glengarriff. After dark they come down to Berehaven. Three of them entered the bar from Castletown entrance and commenced attacking the Neptune. Each boat was received with a volley of musketry as soon as it was perceived, and electric lights ware thrown around the harbour during the

attack. - TEE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS BILL.—The Daily News says: TLe Government have been consistent in deal- ing with Conservative and Radical amendments. The most serious alteration proposed by Mr. Balfour was on Tuesday night reconsidered and rejected; and Sir Michael Hicks-Beach's proviso—rather strangely adopted—while it will certainly do no good, is less practical than Mr. Bat- four's, and may not do much harm. Sitting tenants get nothing. The arguments that to compensate the man who is receiving interest on his capital is paying him twice over is, however, not quite applicable; for it was not proposed that the landlord should pay unless he raised the rent on the tenant's improvements. bill is acceptable. THE NOBILITY AND THE STAGE.— The Observer says: We are informed that Viscount Garinoyle, the eldest son of ' Earl Cairns, is engaged to be married to Miss Fortescue, of the Savoy Theatre. An element of romance attaches to the fact of the fairest of the fair fairies—whose hands for the last six months have been sought nightly in marriage by the stage peers of lolanthe—being wooed and won before Messrs. Gilbert and Sullivan's piece has run through its first season, by the son of one of the most. distinguished of English earls. During her short theatrical career Miss Fortescue has won the regard and esteem of her acquaintances and associates ; and Lord Garmoyle is to be congratulated on having-secured the hand of a lady, who, gifted with singular grace, chatm, and beauty, has contrived in the world behind the footlights to make herself not only admired and popular, but respected. A IEWSPAPER OFFICE ON FIRE: THREE CHILDREN SUFFOCATED.—On Sunday morning a fire broke out on the. premises of Mr. Dunsford, Mercury Office, Bridgewater' and spread so rapidly that the family, consisting of Mr. and Mrs. Dunsford and four children, were driven into the upper rooms of the house. Three little girls, the youngest about three years old, were suffocated by smoke, and Mrs. Dues- ford jumped out of the third storey window, and, falling heavily upon the pavement, received such frightful injuries that she subsequently died. Mr. Dunsford clung to the window sill for several minutes. an excited crowd below being unable to render any assistance, the fire escape being locked up. Mr. Dunsford was finally rescued by means of a ladder, and one child was handed through a window and caught by a man below. The servant girl, who had suc- ceeded in getting upon the leads, was rescued by means of a fire escape, which arrived when the conflagration had been almost subdued. The premises were gutted. IMPORTANT 17 ECISION AFFECTING A ROMAN CATHOLIC PRIEST.—Mr. Justice Kay gave judgment on Monday in the interesting case Eyre v. Eyre, which arose under the will of the late Count Eyi e. The plaintiff is the Rector of Stony- ! hurst, and Archbishop Eyre, of Glasgow (brother of the plaintiff), and Lord Arundel', of Wardour, the defendants. Count Eyre, the father of the plaintiff, left all his property, subject to certain legacies, to the defendants, in trust for the benefit of his four children, but with a general power of ap- pointment in the full confidence that they would deal the estate fairly and justly. Lord Arundell had renounced the trust, and Archbishop Eyre had paid the £60,000 into a bank as a separate trust, refusing to pay it over to the plaintiff on the ground that he would not be able to hold it for his own benefit, being bound by his views to hand over all his property to the Society of Jesus. His Lordship held that the trust remained, and that the residuary estate could .not be distributed during the life-term of the trustees unless they joined in making an irrevocable appointment. He, however, ordered the income of the £60,000 to be paid to the plaintiff. RAILWAY COLLISION AT PERTH: PASSENGERS INJURED AND A DRIVER ARRESTED.—An alarming collision oc- curred at the General Station. Perth, on Saturday morning, by which a large number of passengers were injured. A Londen and North-Western tourist train ran at a high speed into a six o'clock train standing at the south ticket plat- form, smashing!the end compartment of a composite car- riage in the London train, and badly damaging the saloon and carriage following. Both trains were filled with pas- sengers. Among those more seriously ',tuft are Mr. and Mrs. Milne, Forfar, the former sustaining internal injuries and nervous shock. Mrs. Milne was cut about the head. Mrs. Lethbridge, from Hampshire, was cut about the bead, and two of her servants, Helen Victory and Harriet Stevens, were also badly bruised. Mr. Gideon tirown, of the firm of Messrs. William Brown and Son, Willerbank Mill, Gala- shiels, sustained cuts and bruises about the head. Three servants of the Duke of Sutherland are among the injured. A careful investigation is being made into the caus3 of the accident, and the driver of the Euston mail has been ar- rested on a charge of culpable neglect of duty. The injured passengers are said to be progressing favourably.

AN EXTRAORDINARY STORY.—An extraordinary story conies from Paris. It is said that a gentleman in weak health arrived in the French capital the other day, and after taking up his quarters in an holel went out to buy cigars. Like many other explorers in strange places, be lost his way, and, not knowing a word of French, found it impossible to obtain any information as to his way back again. After wandering about for a couple of miles, he found himself too exhausted to go any further, and implored help in English from the passers-by. No one understood him, and a crowd began to collect round him. Some policemen then came up, and, taking him for a lunatic, led him to the nearest police station. The officials, quite ignorant of English, passed him on to the Prefecture of Police. Here again the English tongue was a language not comprehended by the officials. A great lunacy doctor exitnined the patient, and unhesi- tatingly pronounced that his voluble protestations in English were the ravings of a dangerous lunatic. The unfortunate individual was accordingly handed over to a lunatic asylum. By the merest accident his friends, who had been distracted by his mysterious disappearance, discovered his name in the list of the inmates of the asylum. He had been under treatment for his extraordinary mental weakness in not un- derstanding French, for three days. Negotiation Were en- tered into which lasted for four-and-twenty hours, and ulti- mately he was set at liberty. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—.Tb e market on Tuesday was well attended. Both local and district makers of pig iron are still very iedifferent about booking orders except at full rates, and buyers are unable to obtain conces- sions. Where business is done it is at the full list rates. Delivered equal to Manchester the prices at which sales are made remain at 45s to 45s 6cl for Lancashire; 44s 10d to 455 101 for Lincolnshire forge and foundry, less ; with a few transactions in Derbyshire foundry at about 48s 6d per ton, less 2. The manufactured iron makers in this district are mostly fully employed, but there is no great weight of business coming forward generally, the only actual pressure being for sheets, in which consumeis have been thrown be- hind in their deliveries by the Staffordshire strike. In this class of goods orders for prompt delivery are difficult to place, and makers are stiffening in their pi ices, .£8 to £8 5s being now the average figures for local made sheets, with very few Staffordshire made sheets to be bought under £8 7s 6d per ton delivered here. Hoops are in moderate demand at about £6 12s 6d, but for bars there is only a slow sale, and ior ordinary qualities not more than £6 2s 61 to £6 5s per ton for delivery into this dist-ict is obtained.- -The pits generally throughout the Lancashire coalfield are being kept running about four to five days a week, sad generally it may be said that a fairly good bbsiness is being done considering the season. For house-fire purposes the demand is moderately active; considerable quantities are evidently being taken for stock, and a good deal of coal is being sent to the London market, which, although largely from the Yordshire coalfield, is also to some extent being dravin from the West Lancashire district. The shipping bade has also been tolerably brisk, and this has helped to take away the seconds and common classes of round coal. The local demand for ircnmeking and general trade pur- poses is not more than moderate, and engine classes of fuel are still somewhat of a drug, common qualities of slack being offered in the market at very low figures. There has been no material change in prices with the commencement of the month, but on the basis of late rates a very steady tone is maintained, and quotations for contracts are only made at advanced prices. The average rates at the pit mouth remain at about 9s. for best coal, is. for seconds, ss. 61 to Os. for common round coal, 4s. 61 to ss. for burgy, 3s. 01. to 48. 3d. for good slack, with common qualities to be bought at 3s. to 3s. 3d. per ton. The prices obtained for shipment are still comparatively low, and delivered at Gersten or Liverpool steam coal averages is. 3d. to 7s. 61, and seconds house coal Bs. 6d. per ton.
