It is clean in tre. All furs and woollens should be well powdered before putting away. Be- ware of imitations.--Adtt.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 4, 1883. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Motereesr. The Cornwall Sunday Closing Bill csme on for the third reading, and the Earl of Wemyss moved the rejection of the measure. The bill was suppoited by the Earl of Kimberley and opposed by the Marquis of Salisbury. After consider- able discussion their lordships divided. The votes for and against were equal-38 on each side—and the Lord Chan- csllor. in accordance with rule, declared that the " non-con- tents " had it, and the hill was thrown out. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. THE SUEZ CANAL QUEgIION.—Sir STAFFORD NORTH- COTE proposed his motion on the Suez Canal in favour of the Government declining to recognise any cairn to such a monopoly as would exclude the possibility of competition on the part of any other undertaking designed for the purpose of opening a water communication between the Mediter- ranean and the Red Sea. He deprecated anything like an irritatieg debate on a delicate question, and disclaimed any desire to make party capital out of the question, although he would point out that the Opposition might have caused the Government great embarrassment if in the early part of the question they had insisted upon its being brought before the House. He wished by his motion to free the House from any tacit acquiescence in the words which had been used by some members of the Government implying that the Suez Canal Company had an exclusive monopoly for the construction of means of water communication between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. He denied that the Com- pany had any such exclusive right either across the Isthmus at Suez or any other part of the world. They had an ex- clusive right no doubt to control the administration of their own canal, but they had no right to forbid the making of a second canal by persons other than those forming their own company.— Mr. NORWOOD moved as an amendment that the House de- sired to maintain its entire freedom of judgment in regard to all matters cennected with the question of water com- munication between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, and the House in consequence declined to pass any resolu- tion as to future negotiations or proceedings respecting the same.—Mr. C. M. PALMER seconded the amendment.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the Government were in complete harmony with the reasons given in support of the amendment.—While admitting that Sir S. Northcote spoke with moderation and reserve, he still maintained that the discussion was likely to do more harm than good. He contended, in reply to Sir S. Northcote's speech, that the Khedive had no power to give an exclusive company. M. de Lesseps could form an exclusive company without the Khedive, and so far from the claims of M. de Lesseps being only heard of in last September, he affirmed that M. de Lesseps's exclusive claim, and a larger claim than that made last September was in possession of the late Government when they purchased the Suez Canal shares. As to clearing up the question of exclusive right, he con- tended that it was not in the power of the House of Com- mons to clear up the rights of the company. It was a judical matter, that could only be settled by some competent tribunal. Would the House of Commons take upon itself to set as an example to other legislative chambers the practice of laving down opinions and doctrines with regard to the Suez Canal Company P He deprecated the raising by such discussions of the bitter memories of the past, and especially of the opposition which the Government of this country gave to the formation of the canal. As to the future of the question, he felt confident that if we only acted with prudence there was an absolute union of interest and a substantial union of views. In a splendid- peroration Mr. Gladstone spoke of the ques- tion as one of high policy. He had not a doubt nor an apprehension as to the future, provided they acted with prudence, with equity, and consideration. "I own," said the Prime Minister, in conclusion, "I have never more clearly seen a conclusion before me as stamped with right and with justice than now when I entreat the House not to accept a motion which asserts nothing that any of us would desire to deny, which establishes nothing that any of us has the least cccasioa to question, which is said to aim at vindi- cating a freedom which at this moment is absolutely unimpaired, and which would set a pernicious ex- ample fraught with the gravest inconvenience were we unhappily to be led in a moment of weak- ness to give our affirmative voice on its behalf." Mr. Gladstone was followed by Baron de Worms, Mr. Monk (who delivered a portion of his speech in the presence of a single member), Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, Mr. Cohen, Mr. Bruce, Mr. Horace Davey. (who though he gave a legal opinion against M. de Lessep's claim of monopoly strongly opposed the resolution), Mr. Giles, and Mr. Childers, who, speaking just before midnight, had a full audience for his review of the history of the negotiations with M. de Les- seps and his defence of the arrangement.—Sir HARDINGE GIFFARD, proposing to continue the legal argument, was re- ceived with impatient cries from the Liberal side.—Sir H. James rose with Mr. Goschen and Sir G. Elliot.—There being cries for the Arrouemer-GnentnaL, he proceeded to address the House, protesting against having been drawn into the debate by Sir H. Giffard, though once in be made a long speech.—Shortly before one the House divided on Sir S. Northcote's resolution. It was rejected by 282 to 183— a Government majority of 99.—Mr. Norwood's amendment was agreed to. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Earl of DERBY explained the nature of the negotia- tions with the Government of Canada respecting the scheme of emigration prepounded by Mr. Stephen, and stated that, though the Canadian Government at present declined to ac- cept the plan suggested by the Home Government, the ne- gotiations were by no means abandoned, and there was still a hope that the scheme would be carried out. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIESDaT. MISCELLANEOUS —Mr. CROSS, in reply to Mr. Hopwood, said the Government of India had asked the consent of the Secretary for India to the repeal of the Contagious Diseases 'Acts of 1868, on the ground that it was a measure that had never, in practice, been a complete success,which was odious in the eyes of our native subjects and in those of a large and influential class of Europeans. He understood it had been suspended for a year.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL, replying to Sir R. A. Cross, said he could not conceive for one moment why the Government should not proceed with the Court of Criminal Appeal Bill. It had been discussed for many days in committee, and he hoped to take it at any time.--Sir R. A. CROSS said he would oppose the second reading.—Replying to Sir M. Lopes, Mr. GLADSTONE stated that the Government intended to go on with the National Debt Bill, notwithstanding the numerous notices against it, as it was essential to the efficiency and healthiness of our financial system. Tne INFORMER CAREY.—Sir RICHARD CROSS inquired if the accounts in the newspapers were true about the assas- sination of Carey the informer, and whether the Home Secretary could tell the House whether at the time Carey was under police protection, or when the police protection ceased.—Sir W. Hsocounr said the Government had re- ceived no direct information on the subject, but the agent of Messrs. Currie (the owners of steam vesselsgoing to the Cape of Good Hope) communicated on Monday afternoon a telegram stating that Carey, the Irish informer, was shot dead on the Melrose Castle, on the 29th July, by a passenger named O'Donnell. That was all the information he (the Home Secretary) bad bad. In reference to the protection of Carey he had no information ; the matter was in the hand of the Irish police. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. On the order for the third reading of the Agricultural Holdings (England) Bill, Sir M. HICKS-BEACH said the Government had provided that landlords and tenants might contract themselves out of the bill by an agreement giving "fair and reasonable compensation," but they had not de- fined "fair and reasonable compensation," and he should not vote for the third reading, but-for the hope that this matter would be considered and set right in the House of Lords. The bill was then read a third time and passed, and the Scotch Agricultural Holdings Bill afterwards passe d through Committee.—Sir A. HATTER informed Viscount Folkestone that a telegram had just been received from Egypt which showed that there was no foundation for the alarming rumonre published that morning respecting the health of our troops. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIiIIRSDAY. The Royal assent was given to 81 pueilic and private bills.—The Bishop of ROCHESTER explained the interest t'ee Ecclesiastical Commissioners have in public-house property, with a view to show that they were doing all they could to suppress such houses on their estates.—The Merchant Ship- ping (Fishing Boats) Bill passed through Committee and was reported, and the English Agricultural Holdings Bill was read a first time, the second reading being fixed for Monday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TEIIIRSDAY. After the Home Secretary had declined to revise the sen- tence passed on the rioters in the Strome Ferry case, the POSTMASTER-GENERAL stated to the HORS§ the terms of the new contract for the conveyance of the Irish mails.—The PRIME MINISTER stated that the prospects of an early ter- mination of the session were not altogether what they could wish, yet they were rather more favourable than they were three or four weeks ago. He hoped ,the session might be brought to a elose some day in the week ending August 25. The right hon. gentleman intimated that the Irish Police Bill would be withdravin, but that the National Debt Bill would be pressed forward.—The PRESIDENT of the BOARD of TRADE informed the Irish members that there was such a general concurrence of opinion in favour of extending the provisions of the Bankruptcy Bill to Ireland that the Government would make every exertion to extend it to that country.—The House then went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates.

THE RESULT: or THROWING A SromE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, OR Saturday last, Alfred Ball, of Newton, was summoned for assaulting Henry Chorley (a lad), on the 24th ultimo.—Mr. Moore appeared for the defendant —The complainant stated that as he was passing the defendant's garden, the defendant threw a stone and hit him on the side of the head.—The defendant was ordered to pay the costs. THE HOPE OF EARLESTOWN LODGE OF GOOD TEMPLARS. —The weekly meeting of the members was held on Monday evening last when there yetis a good attendance. Brother George E. Warburton, P.W.C.T., presided. Arrangements were made in connection with the annual pic-ni: to Frod- sham next week and also in connection with the United Temperance demonstration to be held this (Saturday) after- noon. The nomination of officers for the ensuing season afterwards took place. Two visitors from the Onward lodge (Liverpool), Brothers George Lambe, D.C., and J. Wright. L.D., were present, and gave interesting addresses, for which the lodge expressed their thanks on the motion of Brother George Clarke. The session then closed in the usual manner.

THE FIGHTING AT ULUNDI.—The Standard cerrespon- dent at Durban telegraphs a description by an eye-witness of the recent fighting at Ulundi. He speaks in high terms of the courage of Usibequ and his men. Some of the latter stabbed Cetewayo, who was fleeing on foot and unclothed. His fate is still uncertain. Dabulamanzi escaped, and in his flight dropped his son, who was killed. The victors secured a considerable quantity of booty in Ulundi. FINDING OF CAPTAIN WEBB'S BODY.—The last act MAI beeu completed in the tragedy of poor Captain Webb's sen- sational end, and the wild speculations that had been cur- rent in some quarters as to the possibility of his escape have been effectually set at rest by the finding of his body four miles below the fatal rapids. The body bore evidence of the fearful violence of the struggle which the unfortunate swimmer had undergone. His bathing drawers were torn to fragments, and on the centre of the head was a deep cut which left the skull exposed.for three inches. The other bruises on the body were but slight and unimportant. A jury was immediately summoned, and an inquiry held in due form, at the close of which a verdict of "Found I drowned" was returned. • THE REVOLUTION IN HATTl—Advices from Port-au- Prince, dated July 10, state that the revolution in Hayti is making slow but sure progress. The insurgents are still confined within their lines :at Miragoane, and for upwards of three months have defeated the forces of the Govern- ment on every occasion on which they have been attacked. The latter have lost an immense number of men, especially officers. The greater portion of the south of the Republic has now pronounced in favour of the revolution ; and the rest of the country, especially the northern districts, is in so disorganised a state that there is no doubt of its joining the movement as soon as it reaches the capital, which is daily expecting an attack by the insurgents from the south, which it is utterly incapable of resisting. THE FORTUNE OF THE DIAMOND FIELDS.—A correspon- dent at the Cape announces the death of the former owner of the farm on which the Kimberley and Be Beer's Mines were discovered, and which he parted with for a sum in- finitesimally small as compared with the enormous wealth that has since been drawn from the soil. He says : " Thinking the following may be of interest,' write to inform you of the death of Johannes Nicholas de Beer, which occurred at his house on the banks of the Vaal River on the 20th June, at the age of 52 years. He was the owner of Kimberley and De Beer's, the latter being named after him. He sold this estate embracing both mines, for £6,500. J. N. de Beer was well known and much respected throughout the Free State for his integrity and the many good acts attached to his name." The annual value of the Kimberley and "Old de Beer's" mines owned by the Cape Government and by the London and South African Exploration Company is estimated at the enormous sum of eight millions sterling. From these mines 1,200,000 carats of diamonds were obtained in 1881.

- -FIGHTING IN TON(IUIN.

Tlit French have resumed operations in Tonquin, and their first effort has been crowned with complete success. For the past two months the garrison at Nam Dinh has been shut in lay the enemy, and the place has been closely in- vested. A sortie was resolved upon, and on the 19th instant the project was carried into effect. One half of the garri- son were embarked on board a junk, in which they sailed down the canal without being observed. By this manoeavre they got into the enemy's rear. The next morning they attacked the Annamites, who, taken completely by sur- prise, were unable to offer any resistance. The scene that ensued was terrible. The terror-stricken Annamites fled in the greatest disorder, which soon became a wild rout. Over a thousand men were shot down by the French. In addition seven guns were captured—a fact which shows that the army of the Emperor of Annam has taken the field. The loss on the French side was trifling, only one man being killed and three wounded. The Vienna correspondent of the Staadarcl says he has the best authority for stating that the conferences between the French Envoy and the Pekin Foreign Office representa- tive have recently taken a decidedly favourable turn. Through M. Tricou, the Chinese Government a few days ago submitted to the French Cabinet a proposal that the two Powers should enter into a formal treaty settling their future position in regard to Annam and Tonquin. These overtures found ready acceptance in Paris.

div.head: AFFAIRS OF BASUTOLA.ND.
div.p: THE AFFAIRS OF BASUTOLA.ND.

A blue book on the affairs of Basutoland was issued on. Thursday. In a despatch of June 14 last, Lord Derby re- capitulates at length the history of our connection with the Basutos, and says the Government cannot admit that the Cape Colony has a clear and unquestionable right to sur- render the trust which it accepted in 18T1 to govern Basuto- land, or that the Orange- Free State can claim more than that Her Majesty's Government shall undertake a fair share of the maintenance of peace on the frontier, or that the Basutos are entitled to claim that their old relations with the Crown shall be re-established. But Her Majesty's Government, in recognition of the strenuous efforts made by the Cape Colony to govern Basutoland are willing to test the sincerity of the Basutos' desire to come again under the Crown—provided, first, that the Basutos give satiafactery evidence of their desire to remain under the Crown, and shall undertake to provide the required revenue and obey the High C,mmissioner ; second, that the Orange Free State shall make all necessary provision foy preventing incursions into Basutoland and apprehending Basutos and others who commit offences in theYree State. Should the Free State fail in this, the Government would hold them- selves relieved from frontier responsibility; third, that the Cape Colony shall undertaks to pay to the High Commis- sioner all customs duties or other revenues which may be received on account of goods imported into Basutoland. Lord Derby, in conclusion, says it cannot be too clearly understood that in thus proposing intervene, the Govern- tnent accepts no permanent responsilsility for Basutoland. If the parties immediately concerned do not assist in every possible way, the Government will not consider themselves bound to continue their intervention.

Thirty-five workmen were killed by an explosion in a mine near Caltanisetto, a town in the interior of Sicily, on Saturday. Fifteen passengers and four railway employ6s were killed and a number of other persons were injured in a collision which took place on Saturday on the Rome, Watertown, and Ogdensburg Railway, U.S.A. Two fatal cases of cholera occurred at Alexandria during the twenty-four hours ending at eight a.m. to-day. The total mortality throughout Egypt from the outbreak of the epidemic to the present time has been eleven thousand. Another outrage as been committed in a train on a French railway. A gentleman travelling to St. Germain was attacked by a number of men who were in the same compartment, and was robbed of his watch and £2O. The robbers escaped, but two of them have since been arrested. The Jewish Chronicle publishes a telegram stating that a , few days ago 50 Russian refugees, workmen employed by the missionary, invaded the synagogues in Jerusalem. Their object, it is said, was to kill the rabbi, who was fortunately absent. One Jew was killed, and many wounded. The military quelled the riot, and 19 Russians were arrested. A treaty is orr the point of being concluded between the United States and Switzerland for settling by arbitration any differences that may hereafter arise between them. The two States will each appoint an arbitrator of a neutral nationality. Should these be unable to agree, they will ap- point a third, whose decision will be final. The term of the treaty is thirty years. FEARFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT: 140 LIVES LOST.—The New York correspondent of the Standard telegraphs :—A despatch from Chicago reports a serious railway accident. A train fell from a trestle bridge crossing the lofty palisades of the Black Canon into the Gunnison River, east of the Wahsatch Mountains, on the Benver and Rio Grande Rail- way. Out of 170 excursionists 140 are said to have been

while calling out the name of his sister. He worked on I even with bleeding hands, and rescued eleven persons. At length be heard the voice of his sister, who faintly an- swered his call. 1 He made a desperate exertion to get nee' I her, but fell and broke his leg, and a few minutes later the sister herself expired. Prince Giustiniani Badini and his son had a marvellous escape. The Prince is described as having been seated in a room in the hotel play- ing cards with a circle of friends. His son was at the win- dow drawing a moonlight scene when the table was suddenly overturned, and the falling lamp set fire to the carpet. At the same moment the Prince's son exclaimed, "An earth- quake! Save yourselves." When the second shock was felt the walls of the hotel rocked and opened, but the party managed to reach the door, and rushed outside the house, amidst clouds of sulphurous dust. They were appalled by what had happened, and remained amid the ruins until day- break. The actor Petito, who was performing at a tempor- ary theatre, escaped unhurt, as dia also most of his audi- ence. He arrived at Naples in the dress of a Pulcinella, bringing with him a number of dead and wounded persons. Unfortunately, however, such escapes were exceptional. In the cemetery at dasarnicciola 280 corpses have been buried, at Lacco 90, and at Forio 29. According to the latest information the number of deatbs is between 4,000 and 5,000. In view of the impossibility of burying all, Senor Genala, the Minister of Public Works, after holding a consultation with the authorities on the spot, has given orders that the remainder of the bodies are to be left where they lie, quantities of liquid lime being poured over the ruins. This measure has been necessitated by the exhala- tion from the dibris, which becomes mew and more noxious to human life. Casamicciola will thus be converted into a vast cemetery. Latest accounts say the number of victims of the earth- quake at Ischia is now estimated at from 4,500 to 5,000. Another slight shock occurred on Monday night, and two guards were killed.

O'Donnell, the night before leaving London, is stated to have informed some of his old Irish friends assembled in a public-house in Great Tower-street., E.C.. that he bid travelled from Dublin to London with Mrs. Carey and ber children. He said nothing as to his dostiriation, but inti- mated that he was "going to South Africa on an important mission," and that he would be accompanied be. another man "to see that the work was done all right." The opinion of O'Donnell's London acquaintances, who little suspected what his "mission " was, is that he was impera- tive bound by some secret society to take Carev's life. It is stated that O'Donnell is not actually paralysed in one arm. There is simply a stiffness of one hand, resulting from in- juries he received while engaged in mining in California. fhose who saw him whilst in London did not know that he would be accompanied by his wife or niece ; and, imbed, he made no reference whatever to one or the urea. In connection with the assassination of the informer Carey, it is stated that a curious circumstance has come to light. On the evening of the 29th of June last •a member of the Dublin Metropolitan Police left the North Wall by steamer for Holyhead in care of two little boys, stated to be Carey's children. By the same steamer there travelled a tall middle-aged man, who was seen -off by a nu:nber of male friends. He was of the artisan class, nut judging from his stalwart bearing, he had received a military training of some sert. One of his arms was withered and useless. Ile was about six feet in height, of powerful build, and very determined appearance, and his face was somewhat scarred. He conversed freely with his friends on shore, and when the steamer was leaving he waved his hat and cried " All right." The people who were seeing him off cheered and waved their hats also, and several men who were in another steamer lying alongside joined in the demonstration. The coincidence, it. is added, is remarkable in view of the statement of Peter O'Donnels that he travelled over from Dublin to Holyhead in the same steamer with Mrs. Carey and her children. The Irish Times of Thursday says the Crown lawyerr, have been considering the case of James Carey with refer- ence to the trial of his murderer. It is now Fettled that the assassination took place at sea, and that the MeiroSe Castle did not react port for twenty-four hours afterwards. This makes it a murder on the high seas, and brings O'Donnell within the jurisdiction of an english criminal court. Pru- dential reasons may, however, prevent his being hreught to trial in England. A defence fund for O'Dennell will pro- bably be started in the three kingdoms, arraneements being already on foot with this object. The relief to a'.l the families of the prisoners convicted at the late Invincible trials is being continued by the committees in Dublin, who receive subscriptions from all parts of the globe.

MURDER OF AN "INVINCIBLE" WITNESS.. The announcement of the murder at Philadelphia of the witness George Mottle' has --produced a profound sensation in Dublin, as it Was principally upon his independent tes- timony that Timothy Kelly was found guilty. The letter conveying the intelligence of his death was received in Dublin on Tuesday evening, and it was stated the deed wae committed nearly a fortnight since. Particulars of the mur- der are anxiously awaited, but it is beli.-ved that the crime would have been perpetrated sooner if it had not been for the fact that Mottley had been living under an assumed name. Deceased, while in Dublin, carried on the business of a hatter for some time, and was on terms of intimacy with Kelly, but was in no way concerned in the murder con- spiracy. The sensation caustd in Dublin is even greater• than in the case of Carey's murder, since that had been generally believed to be only a question of time.

div.head: FRIGHTFUL CATASTROPHE NEAR NAPLES.
div.p: FRIGHTFUL CATASTROPHE NEAR NAPLES.

AN ITALIAN WATERING PLACE DESTROYED BY AN EARTHQUAKE AND 4,000 LIVES LOST. An appalling disaster occurred on Saturday night in the island of Ischia, near Naples, described as the Brighton and Isle of Wight of Southern Italy. An earthquake de- stroyed in a few moments the greater portion of Casamic- ciola, and it is believed, and with too much reason, that at least 4,000 persons lost their lives amidst the falling ruins and in the tremendous fissures which opened In the ground. Many hundreds of others who escaped with . their lives received serious injuries. The Bishop of Casamicciola, Count Filipani of Rome, the Prefect of Cagliari, and members of many other wealthy Roman and Neapolitan families have perished. Assistance was sent from Naples, and steamers were loaded with the injured, who speedily filled the hospitals in the city. The scene which took place must have been ghastly in the ex- treme. Sappers and other troops were detached to dig out the dead bodies which were lying under earth and debris in all directions. Beats were plying all night bringing over terror-stricken fugitives to the mainland. Others were freighted with corpses, and one boat in particular is spoken of as having arrived with the dead bodies of twenty-four infante. Very few of the victims seems to have been ex- tracted from the ruins alive. The catastrophe is absolutely complete, and it seems impossible to restore Casamicciola. There is a not a single building standing, axcept a little church, which has been unroofed, near the harbour, and the three cottages, it which it is impossible to obtain shelter. The whole presents an indescribable spectacle. It is said.the earthquake was felt in the neighbourhing town of Forio, and in the village of Lacco Ammo. near Pezzuoli, much damage being done at both places. The shock came with a sudden irresistible violence, accompanied by a deafening, indescribable noise, while the representation in the temporary summer theatre in the Piazza Bagni was going on, and the confusion among the audieoce which filled it was frightful. The lights were thrown down and set the place on fire. A dense cloud of dust filled the air, and cries of pain and terror were heard on all sides, and shouts of "Al mare! al mare!" (to the sea, to the sea). A precipitate rush was made for the shore, and every, boat and floating thing was taken by assault. The town of Ischia has not suffered any damage. The disaster appears to have been the most serious which has occurred in Italy for many years.. In the 75 years which elapsed between 1783 and 1857, It is re- corded, at least 111,000 persons perished by earthquakes in the kingdom of Naples alone. Some of the incidents related by those who have escaped are of the most extraordinary character. One of the most pathetic is that respecting Count Sergardi, who escaped I from the wreck of the Hotel Piccola Sentinella, where he had been staying with his sister. On recovery from the aist shock he resolved to make an attempt to rescue her, and for three hours he worked among the debris, all the

div.head: ASSASSINAIIO;-OF CAREY THE INFORMER.
div.p: ASSASSINAIIO;-OF CAREY THE INFORMER.

A FAMILY OF INFORMERS. The neas of the assassination of James Carey has been received by the English public with mingled feelings. The notorious informer is said to have been a passenger on board the Melrose Castle, one of the Cape mail steamers, and while on the voyage to Natal was shot dead by a fellow passenger named O'Donnell. All who knew anything of Irish secret societies were thoroughly convinced that Carey would nit be permitted to enjoy for any length of time the security and the monetary profit which he won by his per- fidy. He himself said during the trials that wherever there was an Irishman there was a knife for him, and events have proved that his judgment in this respect was not at fault. His escape from the gallows offended the sense of justice both of the Englieh and the Irish nations. He was infi- nitely the worst of all the Invincibles. They were all of them cruel and blood-guilty men, but none of them mani- fested that utter want of moral sense and cynical indiffer- ence to every principle of honour and truth which Carey so fully displayed. It was felt on all hands that to hang the Bradys and the Curleys and to give freedom and reward to Carey were shocking necessities of the case. He deserved to die, and he is now dead. It is stated that the informer died without speaking, and that his murderer is an Irish- American, in whose possession an infernal Machine was found. The culprit denied all knowledge of Carey pre- vious to his arrival in Capetown. Mrs. Cerey and her seven children were on board the Melrose when the in- former was killed. LOCAL BANKRUPTS, &c.—(From Tuesday night's Gazette.) —Bankrupt: George Hunt, Willaston, near Nantwich, Cheshire, farmer. Liquidation by arrangement : T. Taber- nacle, Market-place, St. Helens, accountant and coal dealer. A SAD CASE —On Monday, at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, a young man, named .James Webster, was charged with being the father of the illegitimate child of Mary Ann Stanley, of Eccleston Lane Ends. Mr. Mackenzie, of Prescot, appeared on behalf of the com- plainant, and said the case was a very sad one. Since the birth of the child the complainant had been very ill and it was not likely that she would get better. He would there- fore have to ask the magistrates to attend at her house to take her depositions.—Dr. Brindle said be was attending the complainant, who was suffering from acute consumption, and he had me hope that she would ever recover. She was utterly unable to attend at court that day. The con- sumption complainant was suffering from was a family com- plaint, her mother having died of was arranged that the case should be adjourned till Tuesday, when it would be further dealt with at Prescot.—The defendant admitted being the father of the child. A NEW DISINFECTANT,—A correspondent of the Standard directs attention, in view of a possible outbreak of cholera, to a new disinfectant which was introduced to the medical profession by the late Dr. Goolden. The correspondent says that he has used it constantly for eight years, and can fully endorse all that Dr. Goolden claimed for it as a most power- ful disinfectant, with no smell of any kind. "Half a drachm of nitrate of lead should be dissolved in one pint or more of boiling water. Two drachms of common salt dissolved in a bucket of water. Pour the two solutions together and let the sediment subside. A cloth dipped in this solution and hung up in a room will sweeten a foetid atmosphere instan- taneously, or the solution thrown down a sink, water-closet, or drain, or over a heap of rubbish or manure, will produce a like result. Clothing worn by a patient with infectious disease, or bed linen, can be put at once into this solution without injury to the material, thus destroying the risk of infection for those persons who wash the clothing. Although it is a strong poison taken internally, it does not injure the skin. A room could be scrubbed with the solution, and would be sweetened at once by the process."

RIVAL LODGING-HOUSE KEEPERS AND THEIR QUARRELS. —An involved series of assault cases, summonses, and counter-summonses, which seemed to have originated in the rivalries of lodging-house keepers, were dealt with by the St. Helens bench on Monday. On the one side were Mar- garet Bradley and a young woman named Kennedy, and on the other three females named Jane Russell, Catherine Russell, and Catherine Flynn. It seemed, as far as could be made out of very contradictory evidence, that for some time past an animosity which only needed a slight aggrava- tion to make it take an active form bad for some time existed between the keepers of two lodging-bouses. This aggravation was given by a case which came before the police court about three weeks ago, and in consequence on the 21st ult. the Russell clan bore down upon Mr. Bradley's premises in full force. An encounter, whit:h seems to have Lirgelv consisted of the throwing out of foul imputations, then took place, with the further result of the summonses and counter-summonses referred to. After a prolonged hear- ing, the Bench decided to bind Jartr) Clthnriiic 1tu.311 over to keep the peace.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. At the next meeting Mr. Webster will move that the appointment of a law clerk to the Board be taken into consideration; that the salary of Mr. Copeland, the engineer, be reduced to £l5O per annum; and that the salary of Mr. Allen, the clerk, be reduced to £350 per annum. Mr. Allen's present salary is £450. BRANCH POST OFFICE FOR RUNCORN.—As We stated a few weeks: ago, the Commissioners have received a letter from the General Post Office, stating that a Branch Post Office with Money Order Office and Savings' Bank will be established near to Waterloo bridge, ald the pillar box re- moved to Lord-street. The arrangements have not yet been made. ST. LUKE'S CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUN. CORN.—In bright and sunny weather the scholars attending this school, accompanied by the teachers and a few friends, had their annual treat on Tuesday. On five lorries the children, numbering 130, were conveyed to a field at Keck- wick lent by Mr. Done, farmer, and a most enjoyable after- noon was spent, both journeys being accomplished without mishap. ODDFELLOWS DEMONSTRATION AT WIDNES.—The annual demonstration of the members of the Loyal Royal Oak Lodge (No. 4,405) 1.0.0. F., M.U., took place at Widnes on Monday evening, and being favoured with fine weather, was attended with great success. The members assembled at the Volunteer Hall, and forming into processional order, p.a., ceeded at six o'clock through the various public thorough- fares, headed by the Ditton Orldfellows Brass Band. Ac- companying the precession were Bro. Bennett, Grand Mas- ter of the Order, from Chester; Bro. Hughes, CS., Liver- pool; Tunst;ll, trustee ; C. Hartland, PG.; F. Hartland, P.G. ; J. Hartland, P.G.; Collier, P.G.; Hesketh, P.G.; Pilling, P.G. ; T. Atherton, P.G.; Quinn, P.G.; Kent, trea- surer; Dr. MacDougall, surgeon to the lodge, ik.c. The route taken was along Victoria and Waterloo-roads to the end of Mersey-road, thence back along Widnes-road and Deacon- road; returning to the starting point through Newtown. At the hall an excellent tea to which about 200 sat down, was provided by Mr. J. W. R. Fowler. Subsequently a short meeting was held, Bro. Beanett, Grand Master of the Order, presiding, He delivered a b:ief but appropriate address, concluding by presenting the emblem of the Order to P.G. Donaldson and P.G. F. Hartland. The secretary's report and balance sheet were submitted and considered satisfac- tory. The lodge, which was established in 1852, is regis- tered under the Friendly Societies' Act. It has 295 mem- bers, and possesses a capital of £2,546 17s. 9td. The average age of members is 31 years, and the average sick pay per member is 10s. id. The room was then cleared for dancing, which commencing at 9 o'clock, and was continued till an early hour on Tuesday morning. The Ditton Brass Band supplied the music, and the refreshments were provided by Mr. Fowler, of the Central Hotel.

I BUILDING OPERATIONS IN RTINCORN.—At their meeting 1 on Wednesday, the Board of Commissiners approved plans of niue houses in Bentiuck-street, and nine houses in Lein- ster-street for Mr. W. Statham. EXCURSION TO BLACKPOoL FROM FARNWORTII. The annual excursion in connection with Farnworth Parish Church took place on Saturday, when about 300 persons travelled by train to Blackpool, where a pleasant day was spent among the manifold attractions of that popular watering place. A number of the excursionists alighted from the train at Lytham. BRINGING THE LAW INTO CONTEMPT.—On Tuesday, at the Liverpeol Assizes, John Howard (15) and James M'Cor- mick (14) were indicted for breaking and entering the dwell- ing-house of David Hatton, and stealing dates, nuts, tarts, and "prize" packets, value 2s 3d, his property, at Widnes, on the 3rd June.—After the evidence had been given, his Lerdship said there was no doubt the windows had been broken, and the boys were afterwards seen eating dates and toffee, and these things, so to speak, brought it up to the line of burglary. But to call these boys burglars was almost bringing the law into a kind of contempt. There was a maxim in the law of England to the effect that the law did not trouble itself with trifles. The boys had done wrong, but it was only a boyish freak rather than a man's crime.— The jury then returned a verdict of not guilty; and his Lordship advised the parents of the boys to give them a good thrashing. PRECAUTIONS AGAINST CHOLERA IN RUNCORN. The Highway and Sanitary Committee of the Runcorn Commis- sioners have considered the cholera regulations issued I by the Local Government Board, and instructed the secre- tary to communicate with the Port Sanitary Authority I of Liverpool, asking them to ass.gn an area within the port of Liverpool for the mooring or ane.orage of vessels infected with cholera. Messrs. McDougall, Steele, Shaw, Pritchard, and Meadowcroft have ben appointed a sub- committee to consider the circulars from the Local Govern- ment Board relating to cholera, and draw up such regula- tions and directions in reference to the same as they think necessary, and submit them to the committee for sanction as early as possible. This sub-cammitteetets also to consider I a circular from the Local Government Board with reference to the Artisans' Dwellings Acts. " Musagoomiercs "AT Sue' mg.—At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. Benj imin Parkinson and Thomas Johnson were charged with having, on the 25th July, at Sutton, wilfully committed damage to the extent of is. by tramping down grass growing in a field belonging to Thomas Bate, and also by breaking the fences.— elr. Bate stated that he had had over £1 worth of damage done to his field by people tramping over it in search of mushrooms. He caught the defendant engaged in the same pursuit.—Thomas Jack- son and Walter Caldwell were summoned on a similar charge, the damage having been done in this case to land belonging to Mr. S. B Ceadwick.—P.C. Egerton, and Walter Taylor, farm bailiff, proved the case.—Parkinson and Johnson was fined ss. and costs us. 61 including damage, and C sldwell was dismissed on paying the costs 7s. 61.-1 warrant was issued for the apprehension of Thomas Jackson who did not appear. SCHOOL TREAT AT WIDNES.—On Saturday afternoon the children attending Widnes Parish Church Sunday School had their annual treat. To the number of about 300 they assembled in the school about one o'clock, and, being formed into processional order, paraded West Bank, beaded by a beautiful banner. They then proceeded along Waterloo and Victoria-roads to Appleton House, where by the kindness of Mrs. Deacon a capital field had been provided. During the afternoon large numbers of senior scholars and parents of the children entered the field, and viewed with interest the various sports in which the young people engaged with much zest. At five o'clock a capital tea,of which about 1,500 persons partook, was provided, the arrangements being car- ried out with order and comfort. Before leaving the field at eight o'clock, the children sang "Now the day is over," and the Rev. J. Wright Williams expressed his apprecia- tion of the kindness shown by Mrs. Deacon, and his remarks were loudly cheered. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH. Blogg, M A., vicar of Frodsham. The choir rendered several anthems in good style, the solos of "0, Lord our our Governor" being sung by Masters Clarke and Mack. THE FEARFUL ATTACK ON AN IRISHMAN AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John and Mary Connor, man and wife, were brought up on remand charged with having, on the 7th July, unlawfully and maliciously wounded Martin Welsh, a labourer, living at Widnes. From the evidence of the prosecutor and James Gibson, it appeared that Welsh lodged at McGarra's lodging-house in Mersey-street. He went to Widnes on the afternoon of the day in question, and returned Lome about eleven o'clock at night in a state of intoxication. The male prisoner pushed Welsh from the house into the street, causing him to fall and injure his leg. After the lapse of some time he again entered the house, when Connor felled him to the ground with a blow on the eye, and then battered him about the head and face with his fists, while Mrs. Connor struck him violently on the head with a poker. He was also savagely kicked about the body. At last he became insensible through illusage he had received, and the great quantity of blood he had lost fmm his wounds, his head being one mass of bruises. Ot Sunday, when he was lying in bed, Mrs. Con- nor threatened that if he did not "clear out" she would "chuck" him through the bedroom window. Subsequently the prisoners were apprehended by P.C. Bossons,and brought before the magistrates and remanded. Welsh was conveyed to the Workhouse Hospital, where ke has remained ever since.—The prisoners were committed to the quarter sessions for trial.

BRIDGET KILDARE AGAIN.—Bridget Kildare was on Monday at the St. Helens Police Court, committed to gaol for one month, for having been druck and disorderly in Liverpool-road, on Sunday. Ibis wis her 129th conviction. —Ann Monaghan, a young woman, was aiso sent to gaol for one month, for having been drunk and disorderly. Thi was her 28th conviction.
PRESENTATION TO CAPTAIN HAZLE-
MR. MIDWOOD'S ALLEGATIONS AGAINST MR. KERSHAW.
HURST, J.P., OF RUNCORN.

Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, of the 2nd C.R.V, enjoys much popularity among the officers and men of the F and G companies of that regiment, which are stationed at Run- corn. His tine, handsome presence and genial manners have won for him the admiration., and esteem of the men he has the honour of commanding, and it is not, therefore, sur- prising that they should have desired to commemorate his recent marriage in a suitable style. The captain, on his part, had determined that the volunteers should participate to some extent in the joyousness of the nupti tl occasion, and on his return from the Continent he invited them to a knife and fork tea, to take place on Saturday, when a bat- talion drill was held. The men assembled at the Drill Hall at three o'clock, and having gone through the customary exercises, proceeded through the town to the Grange, headed by the band. Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton was in command, the other officers present being Adjutant Kerr, Captains Hezlehurst and Jolliffe, and Lieutenants Timmins, Joule, : and Rhodes. At the Grange the corps were put through battalion drill, and we may state that Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton subsequently expressed his satisfaction at the efficient manner in which they went through the movements. The men then returned to the Drill Hall, where they were formed in half circle two deep round a platform which had been erected at the west end. The building had been elaborately decorated, the effect, heightened by the scarlet coats of the volun- teer, being very imposing. Captain Hazleleurst, ac- companied by his wife, Miss Keen, Lieut.-Col. Ashton, Captain Jolliffe and Adjutant Kerr, ascended the platform, which was embellished by ctimson cloth and beautiful hothouse plants and flowers. He was greeted with a great outburst of cheering, which was renewed when Captain Jolliffe advanced to make the presentation. This consisted of a "-presentation sword" made of silver and an address, written in tasteful style by Mr. J. H. Joyuson. The sword, which is of grelt strength and beauty, was enclosed in a plate-glass case upholstered in satin. A silver plate on the case bore the following in- scription :—'• Presented to Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, J P., by the officers, non-commissioned officers, and men of the F and G companies of the 2nd C.R.V. (Earl of Chester's Rifles) on the occasion of his marriage, June, 1883." The blade is embellished by some artistic scroll work, and is similarly inscribed, the crest and motto of Captain Hazle- burst being added. The address read as follows :—'l'o Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, J.P. We, the officers, non-corn• missioned officers, and privates of the F and G companies, 2nd C.R.V. (Earl of Chester's Rifles) beg to congratulate you upon the occasion of your recent marriage, and trust you may be spared to enjoy a long, prosperous, and happy life. We also take this opportunity of asking your acceptance of a small token of our esteem, and hope that the harmony which has hitherto existed between yourself and fellow officers may be maintained in the future." [Then follow the signatures of about 100 subscribers.] In a few appropriate remarks Cap- tain Jolliffe performed the duty which devolved upon him. —Captain HAZLEHURST, on rising to reply, was received with loud cheers. He heartily thanked the corps for the great honour they had conferred upon him, and accepted their gift with feelings of deep pleasure. He had a keen and true sense of their kindness, and be should certainly strive to do his utmost to promote the efficiency of the corps, and to keep up in the future the admirable standard attained in the past. He hoped the men would maintain the good con- duct which had marked their past career, and further merit the high enconiums of those by whom they were com- manded. He hoped, too, that a larger number of recruits would join the corps, while fewer mon would leave, so that the efficiency of the corps might be more evenly balanced. After again thanking the volunteers for their handsome present, he resumed his seat amid loud plaudits.—The tea was then proceeded with. The tables were set out with beef, mutton, chickens, ducks, tongue, and a variety of other edibles, which, it is needless to sty, rapidly disappeared before the knives and forks of the assembled volunteers.

PRESENTATION TO THE REV. J. J.
BRYANT, OF WESTON.

For a period of five years the spiritual necessities and many of the temporal wants of the congregation of St. John's Church, Weston, have been ministered to by the Rev. J. J. Bryant, M.A. His genial manner and straight- forward conduct have endeared him to his parishioners, and when a few weeks ago he was appointed in- cumbent of Christ Church, Weston Point, the congregation determined to show their regard in a practical way. A committee, consisting of Messrs Ford, Aaron, Claudet, Tudor, and W. Armstrong, was appointed to make all arrangements, and yesterday afternoon the Sunday school scholars had a field day, Mr. Thomas Ford, of Cavendish Farm, placing a meadow at their disposal. The young people spent an enjoyable time in a variety of amusements. At six o'clock a tea party was held in the schoolroom, and there were about 150 persons present. The following ladies presided at the tables:— Mesdames Barclay, Tudor. Aaron, Armstrong, John Poole, Barrow, Griffi:hs, and Moores. Subsequently a public meeting was held under the presidency of the vicar, the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A. There was a large audience. Mr. Thomas Ford read the following address, which had been composed by Mrs. Ford : " To the Rev. James Jones Bryant, M.A., incumbent of Christ Church, Weston Point. Reverend and dear sir,— We, the congregation of St. John's Evangelist Church, Weston, respectfully request your acceptance of the accom- panying clock and ornaments as a mark of our appreciation and esteem for your past and faithful services, both spirituel and temporal, which you have at all times cheerfully ren- dered to us, and although you are leaving us, we trust that our friendship will remain unbroken, and that you may be long spared. Wishing you every blessing and success in your new undertakirg, and our very best wishes for your future happiness and welfare, we are, dear sir (signed on behalf of the congregation), Thomas Ford, Joseph Tudor, churchwardens." The presents consisted of a handsome and richly ornamented gilt clock in glass shade, and a pair of beautiful vases. These were presented by Mr. Tudor in a very appropriate speech, and the Rev. J. J. Bryant replied in suitable terms.
Mr. Percival Rine O'Hara, son of Mr. W. 01lara, of Annamore, Sligo, has announced his intention of becoming the Conservative candidate for the county.

At Warwick Assizes yesterday David Mackie, machinist, was sentenced to 10 years' penal servitude for the attempted murder of his wife at Birmingham on June 6th. Large numbers of iron workers in South Staffordshire having expressed their willingness to accept the masters' terms, work will probably be generally resumed on Mon- day. Sir Robert Cunliffe Bart., M.P., was thrown from his horse at Wrexham yesterday, and fell under the wheels of a waggon, from which, however, he was fortunately rescued. lie was severely cut on the head and bruised. At a special meeting of the Dundee magistrates yester- day it was unanimously resolved to confer the freedom of the Burgh on Earls Rosebery, Camperdown, and Dalhousie, ma the occasion of the inauguration of Dundee University College by Lord Rosebery next October. A special meeting of the Town Council has been called for Tuesday to con- sider and approve the magistrates' proposal.

div.head: ALLEGED MURDER OF THE WITNESS MOTTLEY.
div.p: THE ALLEGED MURDER OF THE WITNESS MOTTLEY.

The Central News says :—A careful search of Philadel- phian and American papers reveals no trace of the murder of Mottley, or any person answering his description. In fact, nomurder or manslaughter of a stranger is recorded at Philadelphia anywhere near the time at which it is alleged the crime took place Mottley's mother denies emphatically having received any letter announcing his murder, and the police are now confident the story is a ho 4x. DEATH FROM HYDROPHOBIA.

John Fearnley, a coachman, of Bryn, near Wigan, died on Thursday from hydrophobia. About six weeks ago Fearuley was bitten by a large mastiff dog, the property of his employer, which, up to then had not shown eyAence of ferociousness. The dog was shot the following day, and Fearnley's wounds were dressed, but the aff lir preyed very much on his mind, and on Tuesday distinct signs of hydro- phobia presented themselves, and he died in great agony. DEPUTATION TO EARL SPENCER.

A deputation, headed by the Mayor of Norttampton, has waited upon Earl Spencer, at Althorp, to express their ap- preciation of his Excellency's c treer in Ireland. His lord- ship, in reply, said there was fl) place from whiei such a compliment could be mere acceptable to him than North- ampton. He was aware of the great responsibility ; but. he had to do duty to his Queen amd his country, and he should indeed have been faint-hearted if he had refused the sum- mons. Things in Ireland were now much better than they had been, and he thought he was justified in stating that improvements had taken place. lie had endeavoured to meet the difficulties which faced the Government there with fair dealing and firmness, and the result was greatly due to Mr. Trevelyan and others.

DYNAMITE OUTRAGE IN SCOTLAND. A FACTORY THREATENED WITH DESTRUCTION. The Press Association Cupar correspondent telegraphs that a box of dynamite with the fuse lighted was found yesterday morning in the large linen factory at Cupar Fife, owned by Mr. John Honeyman, and was observed just in time to prevent the building being blown up. Great excite- ment has been caused in the district by this circumstance, it being locally attributed to Fenianism, and the police are active in investigating the affair.

div.head: REMARKABLE TRAGEDY IN BELGIUM
div.p: REMARKABLE TRAGEDY IN BELGIUM

The Brussels correspondent of the Globe gives full details of a most distressing domestic tragedy which has just taken place at Marcinelle, near Charleroi, where a family of four persons—father and mother, a girl of 17, and a boy of 13 attempted, in the most determined manner to commit suicide. M. Aton, the father, was head cletk at the Marcinelle branch office of the Union du Credit, and had living with him a nephew named Jules Pirson, employed at the head office of the bank at Charleroi, who has b3en arrested for forging a cheque for 20,000 francs and the disgrace thus cast upon his family so francs, his mind that after a search had been made in his house by the police, he prevailed upon his wife and children to commit the rash act which has proved fatal to his wife, ard from the effects of which his daughter is not ex- pected to recover. It was after supper that having drunk a litre of gin between them, the fatal resolution was carried out. The boy, who had lived with a cousin at Charleroi, had been fetched home on purpose. They went up to a bed- room, and there tried to cat with a razor the veins of each other's arms at the elbow. They lost a deal of blood, but as death did not come they attempted to produce suffocation by burning a quantity of paper and shavings in the room, of which they had hermetically closed the doors and windows. Finding that this did not succeecnhe father proposed that they should drown themselves in tbe cistern, which was agreed to. The cistern , is in the cellar, and its opening near the ceiling is reached 'by a ladder. Before going down they had tied each other's wrists to prevent escape. First the mother, then the two children, and the father went up the ladder and threw them- selves into the ice-cold water. There was only two feet of water in the cistern. The boy began to cry out that he had become conscious of what he had been doing, and now said that he would not die. His father untied his wrists and helped him to get out, when his cries for help attracted the attention of a neighbour, who came to the rescue, and got the daughter out, and also the father, who then helped him to get out his wife, but she was already dead. The authorities were at once communicated with. Medical ( assistance was procured, and the wounds of the survivors, which are stated not to be mortal, bound up. The father was quite eutof his mind,and possessed of but one idea, that of making away with himself. Ever- since ten o'clock ht said they bad been tryinet to kill themselves, and that only one had died instead of four. He had remained beside the body of his wife, under the care of a garde champetre, but had managed to make his escape, and it is feaied he has thrown himself into the Sambre.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the offices, Bridge- water-street, on Wednesday morning. There were present —Messrs. John Simpson (in the chair), Rev. Father Fen- nelly, P. Briscoe, and F. Rigby (clerk).

div.head: WASERLOO ROUSE.
div.p: WASERLOO ROUSE.

The CLERK observed that he had forwarded the resolution with reference to Waterloo House to the Board of Corn- missioners but he had received no reply. There had arisen a very nice question. In Runcorn there were about 40 householders who paid no School Beard or poor rates, but who had an interest in Waterloo House, and it was alleged that if any portion of the building was let either to the School Board or any other tenant for a term of 41,- years with- out rent these householders would be prejudiced. A portion of their property would be let for nothing, and it was stated that the School Board would receive the benefit, their reply would be" We have nothing to do with the School Board." —The CHAIRMAN : They would not only be prejudiced by letting the rooms without rent, but they would have to pay their quota towards the cleaning.—The CLERK: It is a very delicate question.—The CHAIRMAN: It is a very small ques- tion, but it is one which is very awkward. We are very comfortable as w.: are, and if the Cotnmissioners cannot ar- range it for the present I don't know that anybody will suffer. (Hear, hear.)—The CLERK thouaht there would be , a way out of the difficulty, but did not wish to state it ,

div.head: VISITOR'S UNIFORM.
div.p: THE VISITOR'S UNIFORM.

On the motion of Mr. BRISCOE, seconded by Father FENNELLY, it was resolved that the tender of Mr. Thomas Leach, tailor, Church-street, for the Visiting Inepector's clothing, be accepted. TISITORS' REPORT.

Mr. BOWYER, the visitor, reported as follows :—" Returns from the Public Elementary Schools for July, 1883. Certi- fied Government accommodation. 2,716; total number on the rolls, 2,947; number on the rolls corresponding period of last year, 2,816; increase in the ,number on the rolls, 131; total average attendance, 2,207; average attendance corresponding period of last year, 2,013 3; increase in average attendance, 193 7; average attendance for the year 1874, 1.252; increase in average attendance, as compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, 955; accommodation in excess of average attendance, 509; Inumber on the rolls in excess of accommodation, 231. The returns for the past month ending July 27th show a slight decrease in the average attendance as compared with the preceding month. This I attribute to part of the school being kept open longer than usual, after the examinations had taken place. I also beg to report that all the children required for examination were present on the day of inspec- tion that could possibly be got to attend, with the excep- tion of two, several were absent through sickness, and a few others were away ith their boats and at sea. So far as I have been able to ascertain, not one per cent, of the children required for examination were absent on the day of inspec- tion, and the various teachers, I may say have been well pleased with the attendance during the examination time. The two who were absent through the parents' neglect deserve to be summoned, as I visited the parents specially and requested them to have their children at school in time, as they were required for examination. This was all the business.

THE ST. •HELENS CHURCH-STREET DRAPER AND KIS 1 WirE AGAlN.—George Barrow, draper, Church-street, was summoned before the St. Helens magistrates, on Monday, for having threatened to assault and ill-beat his wife on the 26th July.—On being asked if he were guilty, defendant replied: lam not guilty; she is a perjured woman.—Com- , plainant said that on the day in Question her husband used. 6lthy language regarding her, and also was so violent in his threats that she had to leave the house. One of his remarks was that he would "do" for her, and she considered her life was not safe. Her husband, she said, had not earned a halfpenny during the last 14 years.—Defendant, who be- haved in a very violent manner, said his wife told him twenty-two years ago, that when she got certain money left her she would go and leave him. Now she had got the mon,,y, hut she would not go. If she would give him £1,50 he would go and leave her. (Laughter.) Superintendent Johnston said the defendant had been before the court on previous occasions on similar charges.—The Chairman said he would be bound over to keep the peace, himself in £/0, and two sureties in £5 each, or in default 14 diys. racr •lefendant said he hiAd only one surety, a Mr. Rose, public:an, ' mit he wouid ha bound for £lo.—Superintendent Johnston: ' You will have to find two sureties or go to gaol for 14 clay% —Defendant ; I haven't two sureties.

On Wednesday, report on the Corrupt Fractices Bill would be considered, and on Friday report on the Bank- rupbci Bill. The adjournment of the House would be moved to-morrow a fter the Government butineez was dis- posed of; LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.—OD the motion sor the second reading of the Local Government Board (cotland) Bill, Mr. DALRYMPLII opposed. He thought tim Bill a poor weak thing, which wou;el.' do neither good nor harm, and as for the appointment of Lord Rosebery. he did not think that would prove a remedy for a block in the transaction of Scotch business in that House. The bill he connidered absolutely unnecessary, and if necessary a better measure ought to have been introduced. He moved the bill be read a second time that day three months.—Mr. JAMES STENVARY supported the bill, because he believed it would be productive of good results, and because it hal the approval of the people of Scotland.— Mr. COCHRANE PL•rnicii declined to vote for the rejection of the bill. He supported it as an acknowledgement on the part of the Gcvernment that something was necessary to remedy the deplorable condition into which Scotch legisla- tion had fallen in that House.—Sir E. COLEBROOK did not believe the measure would materially advance the progress of Scotch business. He thought that instead of a Peer being created president of the Local Government Board, it ought to be held by en influcntial Scotch member in that House.

r-2-SC-L-A. E-IZ:B00—T11.- considered the Bill-C(;nit-line-ci.intici;-ti; at was uncertiin and unsatisfactory, without the Government disestablished the Board of Supervision in Scotland. The president of the new Local Government Board would be of no more use to that House than the Lord Privy Seal. He should, however, not vote against the second reading of the Bill.—Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT defended the Bill, and said that between himself and Lora Rosebery there was, and always had been, perfect accord. As regarded the measure, he was somewhat surprised at the opposition the Bill had met with after the reception given it, he firmly believed, by the majority of the people in Scotland, and Scotch members in that House.—Sir Cnosn thought it would have been much better bad an ad- ditional Secretary of State been appointed. He condemned the Bill as crude and unsatisfactory.—Mr. ANDERSON sup- ported the Bill, and Mr. Balfour, Sir J. Hay, and Sir H. Maxwell o posed the Bill.--Mr. Warton also opposed, and talked the Bill out.—The sitting was suspended. The Speaker resumed the chair at 9-5, and the House was count d. Forty members not being present. the House ad- journed at seven past nine until twelve to-morrow.

div.head: RIVAL WARRINGTON BOOTMAKERS.
div.p: RIVAL WARRINGTON BOOTMAKERS.

SCANDALOUS PROCEEDINGS. At Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, a scandalous case of assault, winch occupied the court a long time, was heard.—Joseph Sudlow, a young man, residing at Latch- ford, was summoned by Frederick Jenkins for assaulting him on the evening of the 13th July. Frederick Jenkins and Henry Jenkins were summoned for assaulting, and Sarah Jenkins for using provoking language towards, Joseph Sudlow; while Sudlow was also summoned for assaulting Henry James Williams; and there was a cross-summons charging Henry James Williams with assaulting Joseph Sudlow.—Mr. J. 0. Swift (St Helens) appeared for the Jenkinses and Williams, and Mr. Percy Davies for Sudlow. —The chairman (Mr. Edward Greenall) after hearing Mr. Swift, said he thought the parties ought to settle the case, which c insed Mr. Davies to observe that the parties were rival bootmakers.—lt was ultimately decided that the case should go on, and that the summonses be heard toge- ther.—Frederick Jenkins then said be was a bootmaker living at Latchford and carrying on business at Warrington. Sudlow was also a bootmaker, ana resided next door to him. On the evening of the 13th Ally., witness, his wife, and several members of his family, rode from Warrington to Latchford by train. When they were proceeding down the slope at Latchford Station, they met young Sudlow and a friend of his. Sudlow said to witness,." What have you been saying about me leaving Leicester? " and witness re- plied that he had said nothinte, neither did he wish to say anything then. Sudlow then gave his hat to his friend, and saying he would "have it out" with him (witness), pushed him against the hedge, and gave him a blow on the mouth, cutting his lip. Witness and his family then got past Sudlow, and when they reached the wicket-gate at the bottom of the slope, they found standing there Sudlow's festers, one of whom used very disgraceful language to them. When he got into the house, he told his children to come in and take no notice of such " rubtasky people." Sudlow, who had returned down the slope, on hearing that, ran into his (witness's) garden, and :laying he would let him know whether he was "rubbish " or not, struck him a blow, %necking him to the ground. His son and Williami were also struck by Sudlow. The latter " hammered away " at Williams for about live minutes, and Williams at last fell to the ground with a thud and became unconscious. He was taken into the house, and ten minutes elapsed before he regained con- sciousness. Sudlow was taken into his own house by his father.—By Mr. Davies: Miss Sadlow was not in his garden.- but she said " Give it him, Joe ; give it him, Joe." His son did not go into the house to fetch a poker.—Sarah Jen- kins, wife of the last witness., gave corroborative evidence, and added that when they reached the wicket gate one of Sudloe's sisters "danced all round her, and came out with some nasty stuff." By Mr. Davies: She did not say to Joeeph Sudlow "Go and get a wheelbarrow and wheel your sister home drunk as you did a short time since."—Mr. Davies: Did you tell your son to fetch a poker? No, sir, I never said such a thing; we hadn't a poker in the house then. She admitted she had la!en bound over at Warring- ton Police Court for an assault, but said it was about ten years since.—Henry J. Williams, shopman for Mr. Jenkins, and several other witnesses also gave evidence, after which Joseph, Sudlow was called. He denied having assaulted Frederick Jenkins in the railway slope. When the quarrel arose at the house, Frederick Jenkins said, "Come away, and don't speak to that scamp and imposter," meaning witness. Mrs. Jenkins said, "Tell your father to pay 20s. in the pound," and used other offensive expressions. Mrs. Jenkins scratched him on the face, and Williams kicked him--A young man named Parkinson, who was with Sud- low at the time, was then cdled, and he said he did not hear Sudlaw use any bad language to the Jenkinses.—Other witnesses gave evidence, and one of them said he saw the .acuftte in Jenkins's garden, but he was not pre- pared to sat who struck blows and who did not. Mrs. Jenkins used the language complained of. He did not think Williams was insensible, because he spoke.—Mr. Swift: What did you hear him say? I heard him say he was dead! (Laughter.)—After Miss Elizabeth Sudlow had given evidence. the Bench said they were of opinion that Sudlow had committed two assaults—one in the railway slope on F. Jenkins, and the other in Jenkins's garden on the shopman. He would be fined 103. and costs in each case. Mrs. Jenkins would be bound over in her husband's recognisances of £10; and the other summonses would be dismissed.

FAneesrowN AND TELE PARCELS POST ARRANGEMENTS.. —The Parcels Post came into operation on Wednesday last, hut so far as fearlestown is concerned there has been very little increase in the amount of business transacted by the postal atethorities. The parcels will be delivered by the present letter carriers, but it should be borne in mind that parcels- for other places should be handed in at the Eatles- town office before nine o'clock in the morning and five o'clock in the afternoon. Any parcels posted after, the latter hour will not be despetelled until the following mornine. The members will assemble at their re- spective schools and mach in procession to the. Market' ground, where two hymns will be sung. ihe anted pee- cession will then be formed and led by the Edge. e Pride of Latchford ,shepherds (AU.) On Saturday the members of t'Ls Lodge of the Loyal Order of Ancient held their annual dinner at the house of Bra.:'ther Thomas Ireland, the Cheshire Cheese. About 50 perverts' ~,Itt down Ito an excellent repast, provided by the host and L'ostess, and after ample juetice had been done to the good ttOngs supplied, a meeting was held, at which D.P.C.S. Echnu&d Wrigley presided.—The District Secretary read a .letter' from the Chief regretting his inability to attend ow,ng to business arrangements.—The CHAIRMAN then gave the " Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds," to which P.P.CS. LAWRENCE GILLOOLY responded. He stated that the Order was composed of some 91,00 t, members,- with a balance oc some £145,865, having gained during the year £10,349. Ir consequence of the arrangements mado by the Order and carried out so care:ully by the districts, he did not believe , the time would ever come when a workingman, would be re- fue„ed the full amount of his slob pay.—Replying to the toast of the "Warrington District," Pro. MILLITGTON, sec., in responding; said the lodge was composed of some 50 members, with'a good fund at the:r back, and was healthy, having no side on the funds.—The toast of the "juvenile Burial Society aud Widow and Orphans' Fund" having been given, P:P:C&. JAMES DELOO3I3, secretary, in responding sad the JuVenikt Burial Society was established for the purposo of protecting children until they became of 013 age to be n-ansferredlo- the adult Order, when their entrance fee would be horns by the society. It was a good institution and wet: t worthy the- support of all members of the socie:-T It was anproached, by the payment of id. per week, and'the benefits 3iven were. equal, if not better, than any other society. It was com- posed of some 1,206 'members, and had at present Sa3l 14.9.,• Bd. to its credit. With regard to the Widow and Orphans' Fund, he said it was composed of ewe 65 members, with a balance of £99 188 4.d. This society, he argued, was one calling for the sympathy of all members, established as it was for the purpose of providing for the widow and orphans at the death of a member. The contribuLion of 7d. per ! quarter, with a graduated scale of entrance, - which was small, was all that was asked of members, and the benefits, namely; £5 for the widow and 103. for each child under 14 years of age were given in return.—The toast of the "Lodge Surgeon" was responded to by Dr. Jas. CANNELL —The Criminal.; gave the "Town and Trade of Warrington and ' District," which was ably supported by Bro Tom BARBER. —The "Host and hostess " was responded to by Bro. T. Tgiter to the editor.. OUR NATIONAL CHURCH. `Sir,—Adverting to a letter under this heading, printed in your issuer di Saturday last, may I be permitted to say a few words relative thereto. Being bat a y,oung Churchman, I do not presume to reply to, or answer in'any way the points raised by your correspondent "Clifford Dix," but it does seem to me that we are entitled to a substantiation of the statements be has made, and it is with the atm of obtaining this subtantiation that I trespass on your space. In the first place after a short preface to his remarks, he says "Orange 'Lodges, Church Defence Associations' and kindred 'bodies care nothing whatever for the glory of God or the salvation of His people. To be the rulirg sect, to have their bisheps in the House of Lords, to be looked upon in each town and village as the leaders of society, to hinder all common-sense legislation,—this is all the Church and its supporters aim at and exist for." Now, sir, may I ask ' "Clifford Dix" what proof be can offer of such a statement, - and what he means by " common-sense legislation," such -as, whether the Bradlaugh Relief Bill would come within the definition? Again, " Clifford Dix" writes,—" One of the main arguments relied upon by Dissenters in their en- deavours to disestablish the Church is, that the parsons look too much after the loaves and fishes, and neglect their flock." "This has now become proverbial," he goes on to say, but he avoids expressing his opinion thereon, and does not state whether they are justified and have any grounds for setting up such an empty plea. This is one of the state- Assents such as those I have quoted at the be- ginning of my letter, which are the easiest in tise world to make, but the hardest to prove. I don't suppose for one moment that Dissenters will like me to accept the authority of your corresßondent on this point; -but if this is one of the " main " arguments for the Dises- tablishment of the Church it only shows how weak and frail their arguments are, and I am no great prophet in say- ing that if such be the case, the Disestablishment and Die- endowment of the Church of England is an event too distant to be imagined. As to its being proverbial that par- sons look too much after loaves and fishes does this apply exclusively to the clergy of the Church of England? How do the reverend representatives of the "New Jerusalem" and "Little Bethels" conduct themselves whenever they get a chance? I know a few little episodes connected with the circuit dinners of a certain Dissenting body. Yet, another statement to quote, and I have done. "Look any Sunday inside Trinity Church," says "Clifford Dix," "and you find a mere handful of people, the officers of the church outnumbering the congregation. Let this church be turned into a lecture hall," he says again, "the living diverted from the wasteful channel through which it now flows, into pay- ing able and learned lecturers, and we should see an altera- tion in the grim looking pile." What a "wasteful channel" the education supplied to "Clifford Dix" must have flowed down, and what a pity it was not applied to a more fertile soil. For what an exhibition of ignorance does he here disclose. Let me challenge him to mention, not only a Sunday, but any week- day service which will bear out this statement. As to the living sf the church going down a wasteful channel, this needs defining, surely. Can your correspondent mention another clergyman, no matter of what creed, who is more worthy of his hire than the Vicar of Holy Trinity? I think not. The proofs of his work are the increased congregation and Sunday school attendance. Is there another clergyman in town who has stood the brawlings, and the insults of our local Atheists—or rather Ft eethinkers as they prefer to be called—a term which may signify, as Lord Derby said of Liberalism, anything or nothing. I wonder if "C. D." has ever been in Trinity Church, or indeed into any place of worship, for I think from the latter part of the last state- ment I have quoted it can fairly be gathered what manner of man he is. One of the greatest hardships which the 'Church has to battle with at the present time is misrepre- sentation. Of this there are instances innumerable. Mr Joseph Arch, speaking at Newcastle recently, made a state- ment that a Sussex clergyman had turned out of his day school the children of some Dissenters who did not attend his Sunday school, but when written to twice by Mr. Byrom Reed for either the name of the clergy- man or his parish it proved to be a myth, a mere invention I for his ignorant Newcastle audience (and it was accordingly " golloped down" like the promises of 1880), as no answer has ever been received in reply. Then again, the Arch- bishop of Canterbury the other day stated that when the recent religions census was taken, to his own knowledge, out of a diocese which was supposed to have been faithfully recorded, 39 churches and some odd missions had been omitted. And now come the statements of Clifford Dix, which are an insult to all thinking and intelligent people. I have no doubt that had Mr. Joseph Arch been addressing an audience of ordinary intelligence he would not have dared to utter what he did. As to the numerical attendance at public worship, Clifford Dix must remember that religion is not like agriculture or commerce. It is not a thing where the -demand refatlates the supply, it is an intruder, a thing against the grain. Religion will therefore not be in demand. "The carnal mind is enmity against God." God has given divine orders that religion shall be supplied though there be no demand. For this purpose an established and an endowed church is necessary. " The grand end and aim of an established and endowed church," says the Rev. Charles Marshall, "is the providing of scriptural, that is to say Evangelical and Protestant ordinances for the land and for the poorest of the poor in every corner of the land." Bishop Watson ssys : "He must be a narrow-minded, short- sighted statesman who does not see and acknowledge that national morality proceeding from religious ptinciple is essential to the peace, the prosperity, the permanency of this and of ewery other Christian country." On the other hand, I think that the destruction of the established, en- dowed Church will tend to promote infidelity. Sir Walter Raleigh has said: "When all order, discipline, and Church government shall be left to newness of opinion and men's fancies, soon after as many kinds of religion will spring up as there are parish churehes in England, every contentious and ignorant person, clothing his fancy with the Spirit- of God, and his imagination with the gift of revelation; inso- much as when the truth, which is bat one, shall appear to the sinful multitude' no less variable than contrary to itself, the faith of men will soon die away by degrees and all re- ligion be held in scorn and contempt." With an apology for the lengthiness of my letter, I conclude without adopt- ing a none de plume as a shield to the statements I have made.—Yours, &c, H. J. WESTBROOK. Stockton Heath, August 2, 1883.
