div.p: THE FENIAN CONSPIRACY- THE ST. HELENS AND LIVERPOOL PRISONERS. Mr. Justice Stephen, in charging the grand jury at the opening of tha Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, said there was a prosecution against a man named Featherstone and others who were to be proceeded against on a threefold charge—in the first place, for conspiring to murder certain of her ISLijesty's subjects, or at least some of them were so charged. Secondly, for kaowingly having in their pos- session explosive substances with intent ta commit and en- able others to commit certain felonies. Thirdly, they were charged with conspiring together to destroy houses and public buildings by the use of the said explosive sub- stances, and lastly, which was the most serious of all, they were charged with wkat was usually described as treason-felony; that was to say, conspiring to depose the Queen and to levy war against her Majesty in the United Kingdom, in order to compel her to change her councils, and to intimidate and overawe the two Houses of Parliament, such intention being mani- fested by certain overt deeds and acts. The prisoners against whom these charges were made were Daniel Feather- stone, O'Herlihr, Denis Deasy, Patrick Flannigan, and Henry Dalton (otherwise known as John Henry O'Connor). The depositions relative to the charges were, as the grand jury might see, very voluminous, and a large number ef documents had been produced in evidence. He had read them carefully, and might inform the grand jury that al- though the case looked extremely complicated and difficult the facts really fell into a comparatively small compass. There appeared in the depositions formal evidence of certain facts of great notority, which facts he presumed were put in evidence, as being the materials from which, if they thought it right, they might draw the conclusion that a conspiracy did exist for the purpose of blowing up important buildings in different parts of the country, in order, he supposed, to intimidate the Government of the country, the Queen, and the Houses of Parliament, and by that means to procure the conversion of Ireland into an independent kingdom. His lordship then related the facts of the case, which laave been frequently given, and said that if these per- sons agreed together for any of the purposes he had men- tioned, and having agreed together, they constructed their machines and procured these explosive substances to carry out that purpose, it undoubtedly would bring them within the meaning of• what was known as the Treason-Felony Act, passed in 1848. He saw there was also a charge .against them of conspiring to murder certain of Her Majesty's subjects, but he did not see how a person could be guilty of conspiracy to murder unless he really intended to murder. The grand jury must be satisfied that these men really agreed among themselves to put people to death, or to do that which must necessarily cause death, though he himself did not see much evidence of it.

She was shouting and waving her hands at imaginary persons, and at length in the height of her excitement aimed a violent blow at one of these unaubstantial individuals, and then fell to the ground. On rising she shouted out in a menacing tone to the same aery personages that she would let them know what she would do if they continued to follow her.—The prisoner said she had walked from Liver- pool on Monday and had not been able to find lodgings She lived in Coburg-street, Liverpool.—She was fined 53. and °pets or seven days.

A WOLF STUNG TO DEATH BY BEES. A remarkable scene was witnessed at Middlewich one afternoon last week. For some time past a wolf, brought from America a few years ago, has been kept at the Milk Factory. A number of bees are also kept at the factory. As the honey was being moved from one of the hives, the wolf came out of its kennel, and the bees swarmed upon him in great force. The animal beat a hasty retreat, and in its kennel rslled over, apparently in great agony, Dulling off large quantities of its hairy coat, but the bees still stuck to him and swarmed with greater force. The scene was one of considerable interest, but as it was evident the wolf was getting the worst of the attack, efforts were directed to draw off the bees. The kennel, into which the anim d had retreated, was closed and smoked ; hut this had not the desired effect, and in about three hours the wolf died. A horse and some dogs were also severely stung. MOORE.

On Tuesday, at the Liverpool Assizes, William Corbett, alias Hammond (59), tailor, pleaded guilty to breaking into the dwelling-house of Thomas Crompton, and stealing certain linen and other articles, his property, at Ashton-in- Makerfield, on the 9th of May, and was-sentenced to eighteen months' imprisonment with hard labour. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A LAD. On Thursday week a serious accident happened to William Henry Cook, six years of age, son of Mr. Henry Cook, manager of the Edge Green Colliery. The lad was playing on the line of rails with other children, when, by some means, a number of waggons commenced to move, and before Cook could get out of the way his right arm was run over, being lacerated in a fearful manner, and the bone smashed. His father, who had been a regular attendant at the St. John Ambu- lance class, conducted by Dr. Latham, promptly applied tourniquet, which prevented the loss of blocd. Drs. Latham and Hannah have since attended the little sufferer, but tha arm has had to be amputated a little below the elbow. The lad, however, is now progressing favourably. MEETING OF THE ASHTON CHARITY TIIJSrEES.-4 meet- ing of the trustees of the Ashton Charities was held at the offices of the Local Board, Bryn-street, on Tuesday last. There were present the Rev. W. J. Melville (in the chair), the Rev. H. Siddall, Messrs. Ashton, A minall, Melling, Knowles, Livesley, Bromilow, Clarke, Flannah, and James Hill (clerk). The meeing was called to consider the report of the committee appointed to meet Mr. Rowe. the Seneley Green schoolmaster, in reference to his reappointment.—Mr. Melling reported that the committee had met Mr. Rowe on the previous Thursday evening, amid they explained the wishes of the trustees to him. He promised to give his reply in writing.—Mr. Rowe's reply was then read. He stated that before committing himself in any way he should require something tangible to be placed in his hands, and suggested the f ollowing provisions :—That the trustees should bind themselves to reinstate him before his notice expired; that any attempt to remove him should be for abuse of the charity or misconduct, and should be decided without referring the same to the Charity Commissioners or any other Board.—Mr. Clarke thought the letter contained provisions which they could not accept, and the Rev. H. Siddall said the only terms on which he should be willing to pledge himself to the reappointment of Mr. Rowe would be the terms which all other masters entered into, and which were contained in the minute book of the Ashton Charities. —lt was afterwards resolved that the conditions should be copied from the minute book and forwarded to Mr. Rowe, and that Mr. Rowe be informed that the trustees would require three months' notice from him; at the expiration of which they would reappoint him on the original conditions. —The question of repairs to the Fleece Inn, Ashton, was left over for future consideration, and a cheque for £6O was ordered to be made out in favour of Mr. Rowe, on account of salaries.

A POLICEMAN ATTACKED BY A DOG AT MOORE —Oll Tuesday, at Daresbury Petty Sessions, Edwin Field, of Marsh Gate Farm, Norton, was summoned for being, on the 27th June, the owner of a dangerous dog. and not keeping it under proper control.—P.C. Hoyle stated that about half- past two on the afternoon of the day named he was on duty at Moore, when he was attacked by a large dog bolouging to the defendant. The animal first jumped at his thro it, but he prevented it getting held by knocking it off with his arm. The dog sprang at his throat a second time, and succeeded in catching hold, but owing to a cape he was wearing it lost its grasp and fell off. He did not remember anything after that until about half an hour h.:d elapsed, when he found himself on the ground just recovering con- sciousness. The dog would be about two miles away from home.—Defendant promised to k-ep the dog under proper control in future, and was let off on paying the costs. NANTWICH.

CHESHIRE CUEESE FAIR.—At the Cheshire Cheese Fair, at Nautwich, on Thursday morning, there were about fif- teen tons (mostly of medium quality) of cheese on offer. There was a keen demand for dairies of fine-flavoured ripe Cheshire for London consumption, but the supply was limited. For inferior dairies the quotations were 45s to 50s middling, 50a to 603 and fine 60s to 72s per cwt. - R AINFORD.

PRESENTATION TO A TEACHER AT HALTON. 011 Sun- day afternoon the teachers of the Halton Parish Church Sunday school presented to Miss E. A. Addis a teacher's Bible, on the occasion of her leaving Halton to take charge of the Darwen National Schools, after having acted as assis- tant mistress at the Halton school for two years. An illu- minated address in the Bible ran thus :—" To Miss E. A. Addis, from the Vicar and teachers of Halton Parish Church Sanday schools, as a small token of esteem and regard, to- gether with their good wishes for her future temporal and spiritual welfare. 29 July, 1883." The Vicar, in making the presentation on behalf of the teachers, regretted the re- moval of Miss Addis, but he hoped the change, as expressed on the first leaf of the Bible, would be for her "temporal and spiritual good." At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, Wright Yates was fined 2s. 6.1. and costs for being asleep while in charge of a horse and lurry at Haydock on the 11th July. John Kenny and Thomas Williams pleaded guilty at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, to playing at pitch and toss in Lyme-street, Haydock, and they were each fined 2s. 6.1. and costs. STEALING COAL AT HAYDOCE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Margaret Callin and Mary Burchal!, two widows, pleadd guilty to a charge of stealing a quan- tity of coal-slack, value 2d., the property of Messrs. Richard Evans and Company,—They were ordered to pay a fine of is. and costs. A HAYDOCH COLLIER AND HIS WlFE.—Thomas Moran, a collier, residine. at Haydock, was summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions, fast Saturday, ter assaulting his wife, Ann Moran, on the 12th July.—the complainant said that her husband had deserted her on six occasions, and was in the habit of going about "spreeing " with his wages. She had to work in order to provide for their four children. On the date in question he threw her down and kicked her twice— on the hip and on the knee. He also threatened that he would take her life.—Fined 10s. and Costs. HELSBY.

LIGHT WEIGHTS.—On Monday, at the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, Samuel Tweedle, shopkeeper, Helshy, Was charged with having certain unjust weights in his possession on the 12th June.—Superintendent Naylor said he found a one pousd weight in defendant's shop which was two drachms deficient, and a half-pound weight similarly deficient. A pint and a half-pint measure were also unjust—Defendant said be was short-sighted, and "no scholar," and that he was not aware the authorities held a periodical adjustment. —Sergeant Johnson, who had accompanied Superintendent Naylor, corroborated, and added that defendant had had previous experience in a butcher's shop, and had received due intimation regarding the necessary adjustment of weights and measures.—Fined ss. and costs. THE STATE OF THE CROPS.

We are indebted to several agricultural correspondents for the following reports on the state of the crops in this dis- trict, from which it will be observed that the prospects of the farmers are more favourable than they were at the time the last reports were publish; d in June PRESTON Buocur.—Hay crop not much over one-half the average; wheat not heavy, still an average; oats good; potatoes heavy, and free from disease; turnips not regular, good in places. ANTROBUS.—The corn, grass, and root crops ia this dis- trict are unusually good. Our correspondent adds:— Having been through most of the Midland and Southern Counties of England within the last three weeks, I have seen no crops equal to those in this district. GREAT SANKEY.—The hay crops have been light in general. Wheat is doing well, Considering most of it has been spring sown. Oats are looking well, and there will be an average crop. Early potatoes are getting up very well, and the later sorts are looking uncommonly well. Turnips are also looking •Vir ell. Du-rm.—The first crops of hay and clover have been stacked in very fair condition, but crops, with few excep- tions, have been light. The second crops of hay and clover are looking very well. Oats, wheat, barley, vetches, beans and potatoes are all in fine condition, and premises well for good crops. The produce of cottage gardens has so far been good, and promises to continue so. WOOLSTON.—Wheat a fairly good crop, except in some instances, where mildew will cause more or less deprecia- tion. Oats very gooi, but late. Hay grass a light crop, but on the whole well got together. Pastures wearing well. Potatoes exceptionally good, and no disease showing yet. Swedes good where early sown. Masgols thin on ground, but showing better than for some years past. ITIIICTON.—Wheat and oats look well, but the latter are rather short in the straw. No barley worth mentioning is grown. Hay grass is about half an average crop, but is stacked in good condition. Potatoes look remarkably well, but a few grown early for own use have been diseased. Turnips and mangolds have made most satisfactory progress the last two or three weeks, and appear as though there would be a fair average. WINDLE.—Wheat, not much sown on account of the very wet autumn; most of what is sown looking well, though some fields are thin and short in straw. Barley is looking very well, and will be more than an average crop. Oats are short in straw, and the crop generally is light, and not an average. Potatoes are looking well, and every appearance of a heavy crop. Turnips and mangolds are a good average. The hay crop has been generally light, and not near an average. ,
ALLEG„ED TRESPASS ON NEWTON
COMMON.

A matter of considerable i _iiterest to the public of Earles- town and district was, considered at the Newton Petty Ses- sions, on Surday, before George McCorquodale, R. Houghton, T. I. Gillespie, and A. C. McCorquodale, Esqs. Twe young men, named William Sutton and John Sutton (brothers), were summoned at the instance of Wm. Water- north for trespassing on land in his occupation, on the 14th July.—The complainant was represented by Mr. Moore, solicitor, Warrington; while the defendants, who pleaded not guilty, were not professionally represented. Mr. Moore stated the complainant was the tenant of a farm and some land at Newton Common, which be had leased from Mr. W. J. Legh. The two defendants were also leaseholders under Mr. Legh, and resided at another farm. For some time prior to the date named, the, com- plainant had fenced in a portion of land near his house, and had been much troubled with persons going on the land and doing damage. He told the defendants that they were not to go over the land, but they wilfully did so and committed damage, for which the sum of ld. was claimed. It was not to punish the young men that the case had been brought, but simply to show to the public at large that the Common was really the property of Mr. Legh. Wm. Waterworn, the complainant, was then called. He said: I remember Saturday, the 14th July. I have a cot- tage and Borne land adjoining leased to me by Mr. Legh. It i 3 a cottage for which I pay rent, and I have the ground attach'ed. The two defendants got over a fence which I have put up. They said they had as much right there as " owd Legh" himself.—The Chairman: That is not leasehold is it ?—Mr. Moore: Yes, sir, it is . leasehold.— In reply to the Chairman, the complainant added that he had paid rent for the land for six months, and he had been lin the house four years.—The Chairman: Why did you I not pay for the land during the three and a half years ? The complainant: I paid for the cottage.—The Chairman: But about the land ?—The complainant : Because it was not fenced off.—The Clerk: How long has the fence been put up ?—Complainant: Since the 11th March last.—Mr. Moore : You say you paid rent for it the last six months. —Complainant: Yes. The Clerk: And before that it was a common. What made you pay this rent to Mr. Legh for the last six months ? Complainant : Because the agreement was made for me to pay the rent, and I fenced it in,—Mr. Moore: There was an agreemententered into between Mr. Legh and this man four years ago. There was a provision in it that whenever be fenced this portion of land in he was to have it on a rack- rent—The Clerk: Has this common been controlled by the Commissioners?—Mr. Moore: It is private property.—The Clerk: 'They say it is not.—Complainant: I have built six houses on it.—The Clerk: That might be. Did you pay for the land before you did so.—Complainant: I. got my lease from Mr. Legh's office.—ln reply to Mr. Moore, wit- ness subsequently added that the land was mentioned in the lease, and it adjoined his house.—The Chairman: You call it the common and it may involve a point that we are not : competent to decide upon,—Mr. Moore: The question of title will not arise in this case, your worships.—The Clerk replied that it had already arisen, anl asked the defendants what their objection was.—The Chairman said he had known the common a good many years. The defendant John Sutton said at the beginning of th e quarter the complainant commenced to fence along the highway, enclosing a portion from where they got their water. Last nursday he began to rail and board the common. He (the complainant) had said they got over the boards, but there was not a board there to get over at that time. There was a place there from where they had to get their water. It was a piece of a wild plot which had never had a spade nor plough in it for the last hundred years. _ _

Hairrox.—Potatoes are plentiful, without signs of disease. Oats look well, and are very promising. Wheat is forward, and show signs of plenty both in ear and stalk. There is very little barley grown in this neighbourhood, but what there is cannot fail to g,ive satisfaction to the growers. Beans held out greattopesOrat the black insects have made great havoc. Farmers have, generally speaking, no room for complaints; and the harvest of 1883 may already be looked upon, perhaps, as more satisfactory than any daring the past seven years. BUDWORTH DISTRICT.—Wheat has improved very much of late, and with a continuance of such favourable weather for filling as we have experienced lately is likely to be a good yield. Oats will be a good crop. They are looking well, and some early fields are beginning to assume a yellow hue, reminding us that the harvest is at hand, though none will be fit to cut for about a fortnight, and I have known oats cut here before now—July 31st. Hay is hardly all got in, in fair condition, except some meadowing yet to cut. The crops, as a rule, have been light. Potatoes are looking remarkably well, and promise to be a heavy crop. I am glad to say that I have not yet seen any symptoms of blight, but have been told that it has appeared in some places. Should fine dry weather continue for another few weeks we may escape this scourge. Turnips aro looking well where ground is in good condition. Wierwrcx AND ORFORD.—Since last report, on June 9th, there has not been a rapid, but a favourable progress of the crops in this locality. Both ceriala and root crops promise well. Early potatoes have not been so weighty as could have been desired, as the rain came too late to assist them very materially. The appearance of the late Crops and roots in general, and the present aspect of the corn crops, is •good. The corn harvest has not commenced yet, only in very isolated instances; and there ire a few parts of fields (probably on the Foxbench formation) now ready, but it will be more than a week, should the weather be favourable, before the harvest will be anything like general. The crops of hay have been generally good; only in a few instances small occupiers farming their own land, who appear to be about the worst class of farmers existing, are about calling, and some have not yet commenced. No corn was cut last year before the 14th of August in this locality, and in 1881 on the 6th of August; so that we are in good time yet. Knectsuff.--Of wheat, a small breadth is sown, probably not more than half or two-thirds of the usual acreage, and that under very unfavourable circemstance, being late, and the land out of condition. Consequently it came up very thin of root, and the cold spring kept it backward; the dry May also tended to check the growth of straw. Wheat is now late, and with the most favourable weather will prove to be but a very small crop. Oats came up very well, hut were afterwards attacked with both wire worm and bot, which wade sad havoc, in some inetances destroying nearly the whole crop. These pests were followed by a dry May, which very much retarded the growth of the straw (except- ing on good deep rich soils), which will consequently be short, and in most instances not a very heavy crop. . The early kinds of potatoes have been a very disappointing crop, and in numerous instances have left the growers much in debt, this being a very expensive crop to grow. The second crop of swedes and mangolda are making very little progress, and do not appear likely to make up for the loss in the potato crop. But late kinds of potatoes are looking exceedingly well, and with every promise of bein,c,e an abundant crop, providing they keep free from disease. Early sown turnips are looking well, but late sown ones are rather patchy. Beans have nearly all been destroyed with hots, but the few that remain look well. Apples and pears are both splendid crops; in fact, to see an apple tree without fruit isan exception. The trees also are looking much better and more healthier than they have done for several years past. The late mild winter, now being followed by a dryer and warmer summer, is acting most beneficially upon most kinds of fruit trees, and will enable them to stand a severe winter—the past severe winters have killed a great number of fruit trees. Plums and damsons are a very poor crop, trees not bearing a single can be counted by dozens, and therefore plums and damsons will not, on the whole, be one-hundredth of a crop.

Complainant (to the defendants): You have no right to go on the land. Defendant, John Sutton: Yes, we have a right. It is a piece of wild common, and you cannot say it is anything more. Mr. Moore replied that the mere assertion of a thing was not sufficient. If the defendants asserted a thing they must try to prove it. Mr. Moore: It is a most important else, because it affects others. If your worships think it necessary I would sug- gest—b-ceuse I don't want the case to fall through—that it be adjourned. It affects the rights of so many others on Mr. Legh's estate. Tne Clerk: It affects no rights. Will you pay the defen- dants' expenses. Mr. Moore: Oh, no. I was only instructed at the estate office this morning. The Clerk: Call your witnesses, please. Thomas Waterwortb, a young man, said: I am the son of William Waterworth. There is no water on the portion of land that is fenced round.—ln reply to the Bench, witness continued: The land was not dug or ploughed for the purpose of growing the clover.—The Clerk: Have many people gone over that land during the last two or three years ?—Witness: Yes, sir.—The Clerk: How many, a hun- dred or two P—Witness : I don't knoev about that..—The Clerk: A good many P—Witness : Yes, sir.—The Clerk : What made them go P—Witness : I don't know that, sir. It was not fenced off two or three years ago.—The Clerk: It was open land then P—Witness: It was open land then, sir. —Mr. Moore: Since it has been enclosed have you cautioned these two men ?—Witness: Yes, sir. The Clerk then asked the defendants if they had any witnesses to call, and John Sutton replied in the affir- mative. Joseph Bury said: I live at Newton Common. I have lived there about seven years. I know the piece of land the defendants have been upon. I have been on the land myself many times—standing at the races. It is open common land. It was open to the races for 20 years. I know that other people went on as well as me. They have always been in the habit of doing so.—By Mr. Moore: I am not a tenant of Mr. Legh, but of Mr. John Wright, of Haydock. Where my house stands was once the common. I have no land enclosed. My garden was fenced when I went there haat October. The house will have been built four or five years. I saw them building it. Before then it was a common, and anybody and everybody had a right to go there.—Mr. Moore: If everybody had a right to go there how was it that it came to be built upon P—Witness : Mr. Wright is supposed to be lord of the manor, and the lord of the manor reckons to claim all waste land.—Mr. Moore: When any land has been enclosed have you known any persons to trespass on it ?—Witness: People will not trespass on it so long as there is a notice board up; but there is no board up on the land in questien.—The complainant: There has been some boards put up and people have pulled them down.—Mr. Moore again asked if persons went over land after it had been enclosed.—Witness said they had no right to go over the land if there was a notice board up, but he had not seen one up since the 14th July.—Mr. Moore: Was any notice board up before the 14th P—Witness : I have nothing to do with what was before.—Mr. Moore: Will you answer the ques- tion: Was any board up before that time P—Witness : There was none up when they were on the land.—Mr. Moore: That is not the question. Have you seen any board up be- fore then P—Witness : I think I have.—Mr. Moore: What was on that notice 7—Witness: I never looked at it.—Mr. Moore: How do you know it was a notice board then ? Witness: Because I saw the board, and I heard people say- ing that they had pulled it down.—The Clerk: The fact of the pulling down of the notice board is evidence that there is a dispute about the title. Defendant, John Sutton: We have scores of witnesses to say that there was not any enclosed land. Mr. Moore: Very well, then sir, will you— The Clerk: The case is dismissed. The defendant, John Sutton, asked that their expenses might be allowed. LORD RIPON'S INDIAN POLICY. SPEECH BY MB. BRIGHT.

There was a grrat meeting at Willis's Rooms on Wednes- day in support of the Marquis of Ripon's Indian policy, more especially the Ilbert Criminal Jurisdiction Bill, and Mr. John Bright took the chair. The right hon, gentleman said the Ilbert Bill had given rise to considerable clamour. in India and great divergence of opinion in this country The Bill was intended to admit a few natives of India— lawyers, magistrates, and judges—to the exercise of certain powers wh:ch they did not possess. It would not have the slightest effect upon three-fourths of the English population of India, viz, those resident in Calcutta, Bombay, and Ma- dras. Mr. Bright then dwelt on the equity of the proposed legislation, and quoted amid cheers the Royal proclamation issued after the close of the mu- tiny (in the Premiership of the late Lord Derby)—a " magnificent and noble proclamation "he called it. This proclamation declared that her Majesty's subjects, of whatever race or colour, should be freely and impartially admitted to offices in the Queen's service the duties of which they might be qualified by their education, ability, and integrity duly to discharge. "We hold ourselves bound," it proceeded, "to the natives of our Indian terri- tories by the same obligations of duty which bind us to all our other subjects, and these obligations, by the blessing of Almighty God, we shall faithfully and conscientiously fulfil." What after this, asked the right hon. gentleman, was to be said of the clanseur against Mr. Ilbert'e Bill. If after this clamour the bill did not become law the hope of the people of India ,a ould be blasted and their souls filled with despair. There would be a growing discontent, and with it a growing disloyalty, the result of which no one would like to face. Lord Ripon desired to advance a policy of justice and generosity to the natives of India, and for this reason the meeting should support the Governor General at the present juncture. Mr. Forster moved a resolution, which was passed, expressing confidence in Lord Ripon's Administration, and other resolu- tions approving of his Excellency's measures of reform were also agreed to. In acknowledging a vote of thanks Mr. Bright said he could not but believe that the effect of that meeting would be considerable in this country, and perhaps it would be even more considerable in India.

AN INDIAN WANDEREIL—A man named William Pym was charged at Prescot, on Wednesday, with deserting from the 4th regiment of infantry. The regiment is stationed in India and it appeared that the prisoner had sailed thence as a stowaway, and after various fortunes had arrived in Prescet, when want compelled him to give himself up to the police.

DAMAGING A TREE.—An old man, named Thos. Richard- son, was charged at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Satur- day last, with stealing a piece of wood, value 3d., the pro- perty of Mr. John Brooks, banker, Manchester.—P.C. Grundy stated that on the 7th July he heard a noise of wood being broken in Bradley Wood, near Burtonwood, and on going thither he saw the defendant with an axe and the piece of wood produced in his possession. The defendant had cut the wood (a branch) from a tree, though the branch appeared to have been previously broken.—The defendant said he simply wanted a piece of timber for a garden, and he did not think there would be any harm in getting a bit from the wood.—Mr. Kilshall, the tenant of the property, was called to name the damage to the tree, but as he had not seen it, the magistrates refused to take his evidence.— The charge was then altered to one of damaging the tree, and the defendant pleaded guilty. The damage was assessed at 2s. 6d., and the defendant was ordered to pay that sum j and the costs. 1

div.p: WESTON.

THE TENANT AND HIS RENT.—AI Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, Thomas Nolan, a young man, was sum- moned by John Houghton on a charge of fraudulently and clandestinely removing from a house at Weston, in order to prevent a distraint for rent.—John Houghton said he let the defendant a house at 3s 9d per week, payable fortnightly, but he had run sadly behind with his payments, and was now £1 193 8d in arrears. On the 19th July witness heard that defendant was removing his goods, and he at once issued the execution. When he arrived.at the house there were not goods worth 53 in the house, and he understood that the few articles there were belonged to the neighbours. —Elizabeth Murphy deposed to seeing a table and clock in the house a few days before the date mentioned in the sum- mons.—Charles Houghton, greengrocer, High-street, Run- corn, stated that he served the warrant. He found on the floor of a room upstairs a mattress, an old box with the bot- tom out, and a blanket. Downstairs there was nothing but a soap box for the cradle, in which were some old rags. On these a child was lying. In the cupboard there was a lot of empty jars, and beer and porter bottles. Witness told the defendant's wife that his father could not permit them to live in the house, as it was in such a filthy state. They must either remove or pay the rent and keep the premises clean. She swore at him. —Mr. Burton, who defended, con- tended that there had been no evidence that the clock be- longed to the defendant, and he would call the owner of the article to prove that it did not. There had been a table and bedstocks sold in order to raise money for the defendant's wife to visit her parents in Ireland, who were ill, but at that time only a few shillings for rent were owing, and they were acting within their legal right in selling the articles. Mr. Burton submitted that he had a right to put the defendant and his wife into the witness box, but Mr. Ashton (the magistrate's clerk) decided against him, and a witness not being forthcoming, the case was adjourned for a fortnight on the application of Mr. Burton. WHISTON.

DEATH FROM BURNS AT WHISTON WORKHOTISE.—On the 16th ult. a woman, 64 years of age, named Mary Burke, an inmate of Present Union Workhouse,left that institution by leave of the authorities in order to visit some friends in Widnes On Wednesday night while reposing on a sofa in front of the kitchen fire in the house of one of her Widnes friends she overs t a kettle of boiling water by which she was badly scalded, and in her agitation arising from the circumstance her clothing caught fire. Assistance was im- mediately procured, and the sufferer was removed to the Whiston Workhouse, where she died on Thursday. An in- quest will be held to-day (Friday).
The 82nd conviction was recorded against Elizabeth Tither at the St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday. Her offence was drunkenness, and she was fined 10i. and costs, or 14 days.

"A BAD CHARACTER. "—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, a young man named James Sutton, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on licensed premises on the 28th July.—An officer stated that he had been called into the New Inn to eject the prisoner. On arriving there, he found that Sutton had hold of the landlord, Mr. Hasling, and was striking and kicking him.—Prisoner: I have a bad character, and I cannot live for these policemen. They gave me 26 summonses in two years, and they would have given me 60 if I had been here longer.—He was fined £1 and costs, or in default one month's imprisonment.

div.head: VOLUNTEER INSPECTION AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: VOLUNTEER INSPECTION AT WARRINGTON.

Oa Saturday afternoon Colonel Bell, commanding the Bth and 40th Regimental Districts, made his annual inspec- tion of the 9th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers. The men, to the number of 550, paraded at the Drill Hall at 3-45, and afterwards marched, headed by the band, to a field adjoin- ing St. James's Church, Latchford, where the inspection was held. The officers on parade were Lieutenant Colonel Cireenall, Captain and Adjutant O'Leary, Captains Bolton, Litton, Bridge. Ridgway, Ilepherd, and Widdows, Lieu- tenants Thompson, Gooch, and Buckton, Surgeon Gornall, and Sergeant Major Fennelly. The afternoon was beautifully tine, and the movements were watched by a large number of spectators. After receiving the inspecting officer, the regi- ne !nt marched past first in double column, then in column of double company and quarter column, in quick and double time. As the men went by the saluting flag at a steady pace they presented a pretty and effective sight. Their arms and accoutrements gleamed in the sun- shine, and the scarlet uniforms appeared to the best advan- tage. After marching past, the men were put through the manual and firing exercises by Captain Bolton, and then through various movements by Lieut.-Col. Greenall and Captains Litton, Ridgway, and Bridge, as well as through several critical movements. In the latter evolutions fre- quent mistakes were made, and showed that the men were not conversant with the drill, but taken altogether the in- Ispectien was very creditable. At the conclusion of the inspection, Colonel Bell, in addressing the men, said he waaglad to be able to say he was very well pleased with what he had seen that day on the whole. He would also say this: he had inspected a good many regiments this year, but he had not , seen one better dressed and better regulated as regarded their beim. The accoutrements were very well put on as a rule, and they fitted well not loose. He noticed going down the ranks that their belts were smartly put on. and he was pleased to be able to say that, because it was one of the particular faults that he had to find sometimes that a thin man would put on a belt that would have fitted ten—(laughter)—and that would not do. As regarded their drill, their marching past was very good, and on the whole the drill had been satisfactory. The officers might do a little more. He wanted to see the officers have a thorough knowledge of their drill, and he had per- haps not given them orders just according to what they thought, but still he had done that on purpose to see whether they knew it and whether they were able to apply the knowledge they obtained from the book on the drill field. Amongst the men there was a great deal too much talking, end that was the result of the men not knowing what to do. Every man who came on parade must pay at- tention to his drill, and he should have known by heart everything that was done that day, because he had only got to obey the words of command; se that there was no excuse for the talking, particularly if the officers knew and kept their men in hand. That was what he must impress upon them, and he hoped to see a great improvement in that respect next year. But on the whole he was very pleased, and he must say they were much steadier, and they had drilled much better that day than they did last year. There was one thing that he wanted to , mention, and that was as regarded the attendance. He thought the attendance would be better if it was not all crowded into the last week, because they klust put a great number of others to a great deal of inconvenience. When there were battalion parades ordered, and no one attendei except in the last week, it put all those who did come up to a great deal of inconvenience. Every man who was a volunteer should be able to attend his nine drills to make himself efficient before the inspection, or . else it was no use his being a volunteer. 4 He only wanted to see regiments in his district that were really good and useful men, and therefore it was desirable that everyone should do all he could to make himself as effi- cient as possible previous to the inspection. He hoped some of them would pay attention to that matter, as some of them had not been attending as regularly as they might. It was no use having members of the force if they did not take a pride in being volunteers. However, he would not say anything against the regiment because one man did not choose to behave himself properly, because on the whole he wan pleased with the regiment, and he hoped to see an equal improvement next year. They could not do better than go on in the same way. Lieutenant-Colonel GREENALL afterwards addressed his men. He said time pressed, but he was anxious to say a few words before he dismissed them from their duties. He was very well pleased at the attendance during the past week. The attendances had been better than ever they were before, and he considered that the drill during the week had been very muck steadier than ever he uea They had -laboured uncle, ei-ea....aeges that day; in the first place, the ground was new to them, and in the second place the words of command had not been heard by all of them. But he thought the inspection that day had passed off very well under the circumstances—namely, the strangeness of the ground, and the very nying ordeal to which they had been put by Colonel Bell. Same of the movements were of a most intricate character indeed, and lie very much questioned whether a line regiment, if it was called upon to perform the movements they had been called upon to do that day, would have been able to do them with- out mistakes. Under the circumstances he considered the inspection had been a very good one. The muster had been very great. They had on parade 550 men, and he thought that was very creditable. He hoped they would alwaye maintain that strength, and higher if possible. At all events, 550 was no mean number for Warrington. He was very pleased at the remarks Colonel Bell had made respect- ing the uniform. First impressions were most lasting, and no doubt Colonel Bell's eyes were attracted when he first came on the ground by the way their uniform, accoutrements, and the rest of the paraphernalia were put on. He was pleased to think they had turned out in such a clean, soldier-like manner that day ; and if they had made all the mistakes imaginable—he spoke, recollect not as a young volunteer, but as having been connected with the force for many years, and he said if they had made more mistakes than had been made, as many again, he should have been pleased at their appearance aloe, and should have been satisfied with it, because he should have judged of them, if he had came on the ground as a stranger, by their appearance. The appearance of a soldier was a very great thing, indeed, and he was delighted that Colonel Bell had noticed the way in which their uniforms, &c., were put on. They had hada very long drill, and it only remained for him to thank them one and all for their attendance during the week. He was very pleased to have met them, and he was happy to think there had been no complaints of any moment made against any of them. But he should be guilty of great injustice if be claimed to himself the credit of their appearance that day. He claimed none of it. He thought the credit of the regi- ment was due in a very large measure to the attention which Captain O'Leary and the staff had given them— (hear, hear)—and he thought he should be guilty of a great omission had he not said that before the men, because his thanks were especially due to him and the rest of the , staff. He wished them all a very "goodbye' ; but he hoped they might meet on some future occasion, and that that meeting might be no less successful than the one had been that day. (Applause.) , The men then marched back to the Drill Hall, where I they were dismissed and subsequently provided with supper.

ALLEGED EXTENSIVE THEFT OF JEWELLERY AT ST. HELENS. At the St. Helets Police Court, on Saturday, Mark New- combe, who lives in Lyon-street, St. Helens, Was charged, in custody with having stolen six silver watches, one gold guard, one gold albert and seal, one gold wedding ring, and one hair albert,ug ether worth about £44, the property of Messrs. R. Woodroofe and Sons, watchmakers and jewellers, 130, Duke-street, Liverpool.—Mr. Walter Swift appeared on behalf of the prisoner and asked for a remand, bat this was opposed by Superintendent Johnston, who said he-had a great number of witnesses present, some of whom had come at considerable inconvenience.—The Bench decided to go on with the case.—Mr. R. Woodroofe was then called and said he engaged prisoner on the 13th June as a traveller to sell goods on commission, which was to be deducted from his cash. He was to give a full account of his proceedings on the Tuesday of every week and to come to witness's office on the Thursday. On the 13th June prisoner received a silver hunting watch, which was afterwards found pledge.d at Mr. Bardsley's, Liverpool-road, St. Helens ; on the 15th Jane he received a silver watch, gold albert and seal, and a gold chain, and witness afterwards found the watch and gold albert and seal pledged with Mr. Pennington, Church-street, St. Helens, and the chain pledged with Mr. Bardslev. On the 22nd June prisoner received three silver watches and a hair albert, one of the watches and the hair albert being afterwards found pledged at Mr. Camniack's, St. Helens. Another watch pledged with Mr. Moson, St. Helens, and the third with Mr. Cohen, Byrom-street, Liverpool. On the 26th June prisoner received the gold ring from witness, and on the 28th another silver watch, both of which were found pledged with Mr. Bardsley.- Witness's. suspicions were aroused by no account being sent in by the prisoner on Tuesday, the 10th July, and he came to St. Helens on the Thursday morning following, and suspended him. Prisoner then said the missing goods were lying at Wigan on proof, but witness afterwards found that although some goods were at Wigan. none of the articles named in the charge were there.—Cross- examined by Mr. Swift, witness said previous to prisoner's suspension he had bad £203 worth of goods, and had sold £142 worth. It also tppeared that the prisoner had been committed by the Liverpool magistrates on the charge, but was after- wards discharged for want of jurisdiction.—Robert Brown, the keeper of the Brunswick Dock Bridevvell, Liverpool, said that the prisoner came to the door of the bridewell on he 13th July and said he wanted to give himself into custody for stealing three watches the property of Wood- roofe, Witness gave him into the charge of a policeman.— I?.C. Hughes, of the Liverpool city police, said he received :be prisoner it custody from last witness, and on the way

Whilst it was perfectly true that three gentlemen voted against the proceedings in the early part of the matter, an alternate course suggested by the law clerk was adopted by the com- mittee, reduced to writing, and submitted to a meeting of the Board at which he (Dr. MacDougall) was not present, but he nevertheless fully shared the responsibilities of what that meetine thought proper to do. He recognised the re- sponsibilities of silence as well as discussion, although Mr. Shaw did not. There had been a great deal said with re- gard to the resolution, and he was reminded of the fable of the mountain in labour which brought forth a mouse. The doctor ridiculed Mr. Shaw's action now, two years after the event, and when the whole matter was approaching finality, and shid it was for the chairman to decide whether the motion was regular or irregular. They must remember that whatever errors of commission and omission had been made, were the errors of the whole Board, who were responsible. The law clerk did not proceed until authorised by the board, but since then there had been a distinct and determined inten- tion of someone—he would not say who—to draw aside from toe particular question which should have above all others engaged the attention of the Board. Whatever might have been said at the committee meeting, the Board had before them the reports of their own surveyor and inspector, and if they did not act upon those reports surely no person could be-held answerable for any defect in the proceedings of the Board. Therefore, whatever defect there was it was an error of the Board and not of a single individual. They had come to a meet painful part of the matter, but he was bound to justify himself because he bad been so broadly accused of taking an unusually active part in this case, without a tittle of evidence except hearsay evidence, which had been made strong use of. Every member at that committee meeting in question spoke their minds strongly and freely. Everyone admitted and stated that they thought they had had wrong done them, and were sincerely anxious to find a way out of the difficulty. Various suggestions were offered, and the committee acted upon what he believed was a suggestion from the law clerk. They now came to the subsequent proceedings, and be called upon the law clerk to read an extract from the plain- tiff's bill of costs.—Mr. SHAW: I beg to move that he read the whole of the proceedings.—Dr. MACDOUGALL : I am perfectly willing for him b read the whole of them if he I chooses to do so. The bill is here for every person to examine.—Mr. &Lew contended that Dr. MacDougall should finish his speech without reference to the bill, but the CHAIRMAN ruled that he had a right to conduct his case as he thought fit.—Mr. Swim: No member at present knows I anything of the bill.—Mr. LINA.KER: Oh. yes. The de- fendants have been to my office and insisted upon seeing the bill. The doctor is one of them. The CHAIRMAN: I don't think the law clerk should give any information without the consent of the Chairman.— The Lew CLERK said he could not refuse any individual person in the action.—The CHAIRMAN thought application should have been made through him.—Dr. MACDOUGALL said charges were made against him, and it was his duty to get at the truth.—The Lew CLERK then read an item from the Bill, dated March 30, 1882, stating that the solicitors received a letter from "defendant Shaw" stating that he knew nothing whatever of the proceedings taken by the Commissioners against Mr. Beasley, and requesting them to write him that he need not eater an appearance to the writ. —Mr. SHAW: This is very entertaining, gentlemen.—Dr. MecDoutteLe (said some people were like the Israelites, in whom there was no guile. There was evidently no guile in the course Mr. Shaw thought proper to take on that occa- sion, according to his (Mr. Shaw'e) view of the case.—Mr. LLMAKER explained that before the plaintiff's solicitors de- livered a statement of claim the Commissioners received letters. Certain Commissioners replied and said they were not present at either meeting and too:r no part in the pro- ceedings. He understood that then Messrs. Jones and Pride withdrew action against Messrs. Philip Speakman. G. Marshall, E. Timmins, R. Shaw, J. Dobson, I. Williams, J. Meadowcroft, Samuel Collier, and S. Taylor, Mr. Linaker then read as follows :—" March 24, 1882. Attending defendant Mr. P. Speakman on his calling when he disapproved of the resolution directing the Commissioners' law clerk to take proceedings against Mr. Beasley, and that he had voted against it, and we requested him to write us a letter to that effect as soon as he had re- ferred to the minute book, es. Bd. Writing Mr. Beasley thereof and of our interview with Mr. Speakman, 3s. 6d. March 29.—Attending Mr. P. Speakman on his calling with Mr. Hitcben, his solicitor, conferring with them when Mr. Speakman stated he had voted against the proceedings of the Commissioners against Mr. Beasley, and he arranged with Mr. Hitchen that he should write to that effect, and we would then discontinue as against him, Os, Bd. Mr. SHAW, in accordance with the notice he had given, 'proposed that "Dr. MacDougall and those members of the Board who acted with him in the institution of the proceed- ing against Mr. Beasley be requestei to refund to the Board the amount of costs already paid and to be paid by the Board in connection with the action Beasley v. Commis- sioners."—Mr. SHAW said it bad always been acknowledged in that room that when members of the Board exerted them- selves for the public benefit to them the thanks of the Board were due, and time after time the Board had singled out gentlemen who had brought forward business •which had been for the benefit of the ratepayers. That being the acknowledged principle of the Board it was onlyright that if particular members brought forward some- thing which was not for the benefit of the town, and which was a costly thing, their acts should be brought home to them, and they ought to take the responsibility, and bear the blame. Now the first intimation they had of the sub- ject of the resolution took place on the 27th of June, 1881, over two years ago, when a special sub-committee of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, called the "Properties Committee," passed a resolution that proceedings should be taken against Mr. Beasly. The Board would agree with him that at that particular meeting the foundation of the ease, which apparently was not yet finished was laid, and it therefore ought not to be a very difficut matter to find out who were responsible for the squandering of about £BOO or

.Cl,OOO. He aid not intend to ao into the merits of the case ..at tbe.present time—that would be more in order when the bills were before them. If anything good had been done :they would have gentlemen coming forward to claim their :mead of praise, but they did not find any of •‘ these gentle- l!men"comine forward to accept the responsibilties of the 'business that had been transacted. They had advanced one step. Dr. MacDougall did not deny his responsibility, but he said he had an answer to the charge. for one, should be glad to hear the answer.—Dr. llonDouseis, said the meaning to be put upon his observe- ion at the last meeting was that he was a member of the B 'oard, and did not deny being one.—Mr. SHaw said he el, stply raised the question to bring out the truth. Somebody dic 1 begin this business. Many members of the Board knew very little of it. They were told in the public prints that eem eof them did, but so far as he had been able to gather tiiei embers knew comparatively little of this important and costl r transaction. The Properties Committee had never yet tt. lid the Board openly how this business begun. He musts soafese that that day be had to deal to a great extent with rt moors, and dealing with rumours he should expect some c, ocrections of the case be had to put before them. The Hit *way and Sanitary Committee, he was informed, acting u. icier the strong advice and recommendation of Dr. Mac Doug 'aftpassed a resolution to take certain proceedings against M r. Beasley. This meeting was a special meeting, but not by Mr. Norman, who was chairman t of the cc ounittee. Dr. MacDougall and his friend called this particular meeting together.—Mr. LAKE: Can you give us the name of the friend while Yu are at the first intit out it ?—Mr. Snevr, continuing, said edition the chairman of the committee got vras a notice to attend the meeting. At that meeting there was a long disc, iseion and he believed that some of the mem- bers then preen t were not anxious to take the course that was suggested by 'the doctor and the friend who was acting with him. But tl. He (Mr.i Shaw) thought that if this was so t was cert!inly bringing this question cant of the ordinary business of the Board and putting it into another atmosphere. He took it that the ordinary business of the Board and of committees N ,as to transact the business to the best abilities of the metmbers, leaving entirely aside , any feelings of animosity, split!n, and vindictiveness. If this was the origin of the meeting, and the way in phial this costly businesswas commenced and pressed, then he thought it was a case in which the ratepayers of Runcorn ought not to be called upon to pay feoo or £l,OOO to gratify the spleen and vindictive feelings of any member of the Board. If these rumours were not true it was unfair that any member should rest ader the allegations. But all of them knew that at the partZcular time in question Dr. MacDougall was smarting under a serious loss that he had stained, and private feelings beNg imparted in the case,
