30. Attending Mr. Beasley in his calling when we informed him of our interview with Mr. P. Speakman arid his solici- tor, and he stated that the matter ef the in,pection of the minute books would be brought up again before the Commissioners on Monday next, and he recuiested us to make a copy of our correspondence with Mr. Linaker on the sub- ject, and forward same to Mr. Speakman, who would refer to same at the Commissioners next meeting, 63. Bd."—Dr. MacDougall read a newspaper extract of a Commissioners' meeting held on March 6-.11, 1882, when Mr. Shaw moved that Mr. Beasley be allowed to inspect the inmate books • but it was decided to furnish Min with an extract.—Mr. SAW: It would have saved you £5OO if you had taken my advice.—Dr. MACDOUGALL quoted from The Examiner of April 3rd, 1882, which con- tained a report of a Board meeting at which Mr. Shaw again made a proposal that Mr. Beasley inspect the minute books; but eventually deferred it. The doctor remarked that there hid been too much of the monkey and the chestnuts in the whole proceedings of the Board in this matter. It had been pitiable. In that bill of costs they had undoub'ed evidence of a strongly confirmatory character that there was com- plete incidence between Mr. Srakman and Mr. Shaw about the whole proceedings. Mr. Speakman had informed them that he opp )sed the Commissioners' action, but they had no evidence that he took the proceedings mentioned in the bill in the interest of the plaintiff or the reepavers. SPEAKMAN: The fatep ayers.] He would refer to what had now more potent results, and quote an item from the bill for July 20t, the eve of the trial. He had never had to do a more painful thing in his life —Mr. SPEAKMAN : Don't be p tined on any account. Don't keep anything back about me. —Dr. MacDousam, (reading): "July 20th. Attending Mr. P. Speakman, when he made an important statement to us affecting the liability of the Commissioners. Drawinz further observations to counsel, including Mr. Tremlett's proof, 193." (To Law-Clerk): I ask you is that a correct abstract from that bill?—Mr. I,INAKER : Yes.—Mr. Non- MAN (in surprise): You refer to the very night before the trial took place at Manchester?—Dr. MACDOUGALL : Yes.— Mr. NORMAN : Good gracious! Will you give us the infor- mation.—Dr. MACDOUGALL : I cannot tell you anything beyond what is in the bill. I offer its comment upon that item. I have placed the matter very fairly before the Board from the first. With regard to what has been said on rumour, I take it that the information Mr. Shaw has thought proper to bring forward here on hearsay is just exactly on a par with the proceedings that we have recorded in the bill of costs which Messrs. Jones and Price have furnished the Board with, and for which we have had to pay. Therefore it is not worth while to follow up the question very much further, and seeing that Mr. Shaw's information earns from such an exceedingly impure source, it is not too much to say.—Mr. SHAW said that remark was scandalous, and at the request of the chairman, Dr. MacDougall withdrew it. Speaking further of Mr. Shaw's resolution, the doctor characterised it as paltry. It had, he alleged, been brought forward by two or three individuals who thought proper to throw dust in the eyes of the public, and to tarnish the fair fame and public reputation of several members by accusing them of taking a course they never did, and could not have taken had they been willing. He coecluded by moving that the meeting adjourn for a month.—Mr. LINAKER then read from his diary the following entry'. of consultation with counsel on the 21st July, the date of the trial:—‘• Attend- ing counsel, Messrs. Gully, Shand, and Seger, in consulta- tion on the whole case, when Mr. Gully, having gone fully into the circumstances of the case, informed me that from what cont.sel for the plaintiff had said to him certain individual Commissioners were going to give evidence for the plaintiff, and had spoken in such strong terms as to what had taken place at the meetings that he could not . advise the Commissioners, seeing that they were going into court as a divided body, to go on with the case."—Mr. NORMAM : That's awful.—Mr. RHODES: It looks to me that one portion of the Commissioners has committed the other portion.—Dr. STEELE seconded the motion for adjournment; and Mr. P. SPEAKMAN said he made a strong charge against the doctor at the last meeting, and he had net altered his opinion. But it was no use going round by Frodsham to get to Runcorn Hill ; and he asked Mr. Barker what mem- ber he went to when he found these things missing ?—Mr. BARKER: When I went to Waterloo House and found the things missing, I saw Mr. Handley at the shop door, and I told him what had taken place.—Dr. STEELE: Is Mr. Handley No. 1 then? (Laughter.)—Mr. BARKER said he did not know. Mr. Handley sent down to the office for the keys of Waterloo House, and in a short time he sent them back. What he did with them he (Mr. Barker) did not know. —Mr. SPEAKMAN went on to say when the committee meeting was held he was aware of the different feelings that were agitating people at that time. He felt very strongly on the subject because he knew that Mr. Beasley was a man very easily moved to law, and he said at the meeting that when the Board went into the matter they should leave any vindictive feeling out of it altogether. He then got I one of the soundest dressings that he had had for a long I time from Dr. MacDougall, whom the cap seemed to fit ex- actly. It was only by the members of the committee taking the matter up that he got out of the difficulty. At a sub- sequent meeting the members had a letter from Mr. Beaeley, who stated it was not fair that the Board ma- chinery should be put in motion so that private members mie;tat vent their spleen upon others. He (Mr. Speakman) again got another dressing from Dr. MacDougall.—Dr. MacDounau, asked at what meeting this took place, but Mr. Speakman was unable to say.—Mr. SPEAKMAN said at the special meeting that had been referred to the members seemed to be encompassed in a very great cloud, and at last he was requested to see Mr. Beasley, and at:certain if anytH.g enobi ha done to stop proceedings. Before he could see Mr. Beasley a search warrant had been taken out, and the ship was fairly on the ocean. He alleged that these proceedings were taken without the knowledge of the Board, for it was never in- tended that they should be until he had had the interview. Dr. MacDougall, the Liw Clerk, cr whoever took out the warrant acted without the sanction of the Beard. Therefore the Board bad to pay the costs. With regard to the different charges that the doctor had broaght forward against him, , he might say that like other members of the Board he had a letter from Messrs. Jones and Pride, and attended by his lawyer, he had an interview with them. From that time to this his lawyer had done the work. With regard to the statement contained in the bill of costs, all he could say was that he gave it a most solemn and flat denial that any such statement was made by him in Manchester on the eve of the trial in Manchester. It was a thing he had never heard of in his life before.—Mr. NORMAN: What in the world is that thing doing in the bill, then ?—Mr. SPEAKMAN: It doesn't matter what is in the bill. That is all I say.— Dr. STEELE expressed his regret at these recriminations on this unfortunate business, and the LAW CLERK in answer to a question, said the resolution authorising him to take action was not qualified as stated by Mr. Speakman.—Mr. Slaw said the members who launched the Commissioners into this vast expense for the gratification of their private feelings ought to pay the bill, and stated that he did not think the course Dr. MacDougall took in the matter was honourable or could be justified. He again asserted that pressure was brought to bear upon the law clerk, a state- ment which Mr. Linaker again denied.—Mr. LIORTBURN : What time elapsed between the passing of the resolution and the issue of the warrant P—Mr. LINAKER : A week or ten days.—Mr. LIGHTBURN (to Mr, Speakman): In that time had you seen Mr. Beasley P—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN: I could not see Mr. Beasley and therefore I could not report. At the next meeting proceedings had been taken. Dr. MacDouciam. then withdrew his motion for the adjourn- ment, and the meeting terminated.

WARRINGTON CLERGY INSTI 11J- TIONS• ANNIVERSARY MBE rINCr. Ott Thursday the anniversary meeting in connection with the Warrington Clergy Institutions for Clergy Widows and Orphans and Clergy Daughters school was held at the insti- tution. There was a large attendance, and the Lord Bishop of Manchester presided. Amongst those preeent were the Lord Bishop of Liverpool, Bishop Kelly, very Rev. Dean of Chester, Ven. Archdeacon Daroy, Canons H onword, Penrhyn, Stowell, Birley, Gore, Hornby, Heron, Fielden, Whitley, Revs. G. London, A. Blencowe, J. Cheetham, W. Champ- neys, S. Wilkiuson, E C. E. Carleton, A. Jones (Daresbury), C. J. Quirk, U. Livingstone, T. R Matthews. E. Marston, J. H Sunning, J. Williams (Euxton), G. Tripp. D. Ellison, P. R. Rabin' C. Marshall, Mr. E. Greenall, Mr. J. Tinsley, Rev. Canon Greenall (hon. sec.), Rev. M. Stevenson (hon. sec. of the school). Conon GREENALL (hon. see.) said he had received letters of apology from Mr. P. E. Warburton, M.P. (who was ex- pectol to preside), the Bishop of Chester, Sir G. Greenall, Col. Blackburn, M.P., the Ven. Archdeacon of Warrington, Ven. Archdeacon Anson, and about 120 other gentlemen. ANNUAL REPORT. The HON. SECRETARY read the annual report of the Clergy Widows and Orphans' Pension Fund, which was as follows :—This is the IS3th anniversary of the present in, stitution. Founded in 1697, for the diocese of Chester, it belongs now to the three dioceses into which the old see has been divided, except that in Manchester diocese (as that is a similar institution in the archdeacenry of Lancaster), only the archdeaconries of Manchester and Blackburn are in- cluded in its operations. Three urgent cases of distress have been relieved during the year, to the amount of £26. £25 came from the funds of the charity; the additional £1 was added by the kind liberality of one of the members of your committee. Since the last anniversary two of the old pensioners, b )th belonging te Liverpool diocese, have died. One lady from Manchester diocese, not requiring further assistance, has withdrawn her name from the list. There are eleven ne v applicants (7 widows and 4 orphans). Of these three widows and one orphan are from Chester, two widows and three orphans from Manchester, and two widows from Liverpool. Tile numbers now on the list are 23 Ches- ter widows, and 6 Chester orphans; 31 Manchester widows, and 17 Manchester orphans; 12 Liverpool widows, and 14 Liverpool orphans, making a total of 93-66 widows and 27 orphans. Three widows from Chester, and three from Nianchester apply for grants to give their daughters free board and education at the Clergy Daughters' School. The subscribers ought to understand that each of these grants means £45 per annum from the Pension Fund. In conse- quence of a deficiency of funds in 1881 the committee were very reluctantly obliged to withhold the bonuses of 15i per cent, which it had been customary to add to the grants. Last year they were glad to be able again to make the ad- dition, but only to the amount of 10 per cent. You will be asked to-day to sanction pensions, donations, and bonuses, of 10 per cent. to each pension and donation, and payments to the Clergy Daughters' School to the amount of £2,563 10s. The committee venture again to repeat what they say in the annual report that they would gladly increase the whole of the grants (the average amount of each is very small) but they find that this is impossible under present circumstances. There is no legacy to report. The special donations only amount to £B3 ss. Of this Miss Anson, of Chester, gave £5O, and £5 came from one of the old pensioners in the Liverpool diocese as a thank- offering for what the charity had done for her in her days of need. The committee beg to call the particular attention of subscribers and friends to the statement in the annual report in reference to offertories and subscriptions. It is to these sources that they chiefly look for a permanent increase of income. Such an increase is loudly called for. They are persuaded that it might very easily be secnred by the friendly co-operation of all who are interested in this insti- tution. They earnestly invite all the clergy to be kind enough to make the charity known in their several parishes, and to appropriate to it at least one offertory in the year. The committee have further to report that in obedience to the resolution which was passed at the August meeting, 1881, as holding meetings in the large centres such as Manchester and Liverpool, in order to excite more public interest in the charity, they have agreed to the plan which the sub-corn- mitten appointed to consider the question recommended— viz, 1. That an annual service be held in one of the three cathedrals of Chester, Manchester, and Liverpool in addition to the anniversary services at Warrington ; and that the ser- vices of an eminent preacher and of the cathedral choirs be solicited, 2. That a notice of the anniversary meeting be circulated among all subscribers and the clergy of the three dioceses, requesting them to make it known to their friends." These two suggestions will be submitted to you for formal approval; the second of them has already been acted upon in the notices that have been sent out for this anniversary. It is gratifying to be able to report that a large number of those to whom these notices have been sent have acknowledged them most kindly and expressed their thanks for receiving them, and that they have gained for us several new friends. It will be noticed that the new appli- cations far exceed the vacancies on the list. As this has happened before, and is not unlikely to occur again, the committee cannot but regard it as an additional reason for increased sympathy and support. They earnestly hope that both will be forthcoming. Canon GORE moved the adoption of the report, which was carried with the exception of that part referring to the hold- ing of annual services.

ffERMCINTS The Right Rev. CHAIRMAN said that at the annual meet- ing in August, 1881, a resolution was carried that the annual meeting be held as heretofore, at Warrington, and that steps be taken by the committee to hold influential meetings in the large centres, such as Manchester and Liverpool, in order to excite more interest in the charity. On the 29th March in this year the committee met, and they reported, in obedience to the resolution, they had agreed to a plan whicn the sub-committee appointed to consider the question recom- mended so that what they were asked to approve was something different to the resolution originally carried. Canon GREENALL moved a resolution in favour of annual services being held. The Right Rev. CHAIRMAN said the idea was, he pre- sumed, that by an attractive service of a musical character, with an eminent preacher, a large congregation might be gathered, and interest stimulated in the society. Canon STOWELL did not think services of any kind would answer the purpose of breaking up new ground, as was con- templated by the resolution of 1881, and he moewl the following amendment That this meeting censidering that the proposed plan will not fully answer the end designed by the resolution of August 4, 1881, remits the question to the committee and requests them to make arrangements for holding meetings in the three dioceses in order to make known the claims and aims of the charity, and that this experiment be tried during the current year." Rev. G. LIVINGFSTONE said his experience of public meet- ings in Liverpool was that there were not likely to be so attractive as a sermon. After some discussion, the words "and that this experi- ment be tried during the current year" were struck out of the amendment, which was eventually carried by 17 votes to four.

ment that from one of the best-known presses in France there had lately been issued what he might call a cheap people's edition of the Vicar of Wakefield." There were a few pages of introduction to the book in which the ekrgy of the Church of England were spoken of as men of kigh walks in iife, who held three livings and only preached

three sermons a year; whilst the curates were kept to de all the hard work, and were so wretchedly paid that they were not able to give a proper education and position to their families, and those families were spoken of in terms which

he would not pollute that assembly by quoting. A gather- ing like the one that day was, he hoped, calculated to reply to all such insinuations of the laity in supporting the clergy, and he hoped Warrington would more and more feel its indebtedness to the three Bishops, and that these insti- tutions would more and more prosper under their benign and kindly assistance.

The Bishop of LIVERPOOL responded. He said he did not suppose there was any set of men more called upon to do everything and go everywhere than the clergy of the Church of England. He did not know very much about the bishops of the southern counties, but the northern bishops had so much work to do that they required to have their health desired, wished, and even prayed for on every possible occasion. Referring to a French edition of the "Vicar of Wakefield," to which the previous speaker had alluded, be did not know what sort of people the French might be in supposing the upper clergy in England did not work, but neither the Bishop of Manchester nor himself would ever be what Bishop Latimer called " unpreaching prelates." (Loud applause.) He knew that he had to preach twice every Sunday of his life, and very often more than that. He did not know that they were quite as popular as the proposer of the toast said they were, for they were often called over the coals whenever anything happened which excited public interest. They saw many things they could not mend, and oftentimes peo- ple imagined the bishops were to blame when really the law of the land was responsible. At the same time he was not quite sure that it would be well for them to have more power. Power was a dangerous thing, and he was not quite persuaded that it would be used well by all bishops. As bishops they had always taken the deepest in- terest in the Warrington institutions, which were of ines- timable value to the three dioceses. He was old enough to remember when there was only one diocese, and that reached from the Dee to the borders of Westmoreland. In his diocese there was a greater number of poor livings than in any other in the country; there were a great many new livings, nearly 1,200,000 of a population, and an immense proportion were Roman Catholics and Nonconformists. During the past six years their pockets had been drained. They had to support a bishopric of which he was the first occupant, next year a university exceeding .£lOO,OOO, a new infirmary another year exceeding a similar sum, so that they might well imagine their pockets were not as full as they used to be. Then they had a cathedral to build which some said they would not be satisfied unless a quarter of a million were spent upon it. The Ven. Archdeacon DARBY proposed the " Health of the Rt. Rev. Bishop Kelly," which was heartily drunk, and the Bishop briefly responded.

The right rev. CHAIRMAN then proposed" Success to the institutions." He stated that the Clergy School had been established nearly fifty years, and that the pension fund for widows and orphans in the dioceses of Chester and Liverpool, and in the two largest archdeaconries of the diocese of Manchester, had now completed the 186th year of its existence, from which he presumed it must be the oldest of their post reformation societies. During that period the institution had been doing valuable service in the special department of Christian work which it had undertaken. (Hear, hear.) He did not think the societies were suffi- ciently well known. He quite accepted all that the Bishop of Liverpool had said about the pressure which there was on the clergy in finding means to carry on various other works ef Christian enterprise, and which must be carried on if the Church was to hold its own, bat still he could not exonerate Churchmen from the particular responsibility of supporting those institutions. The Church had not been vary largely endowed by the present generation. Ile did not mean to say that this generation had not increased considerably the old endowments left by our fore- fathers, but still the modern proportion of endowments was very small compared with those which had come down to us from previous generations. As churches and parishes were multiplied to meet the spiritual demands of the age, so it seemed to him the laity were bound to consider the temporal condition of those who were to minister in the new and poorly endowed parishes, and who, he thought, were by the general body of English Churchmen always expected to marry. (Laughter.) He had brought upon himself some- times a good deal of severe criticism because it had been supposed he was against the marriage of the clergy. But he had set a different example since he came into the diocese—(laughter) ; and as a matter of fact he had never said one word against the marriage of the clergy. He had, however, spoken against imprudent marriages, and to what he had said on that subject he still adhered. In ordinary cases, where a clergymen married a wife suitable to him— which he was sorry to say the clergy did not always do—(renewed laughter)—where he married a woman who would go about with him among his people, bringing that womanly sympathy, and that counsel which women alone could bring, and who thereby enhanced the clergyman's own usefulness, no possible objec- tion could for a moment be raised. That was the position he took on the matter, and he thought it would pass with- out gainsay in any assembly of Chum chmen. (Applause) The funds at the disposal of the Widows' and Orphans' In- StIGULIOU Weir HULdlo ati cuacyuaLll. 11.0 14111 t,.eau Ltr aog that they ever refused any fair case brought before then, but they were obliged to manage the resources of the society with exceedingly great economy in order to make them hold out. That day they had voted away £2OO more than they had in hand, in faith that bdore the end of the year sub- scriptions would come in and enable them to meet their ob- ligations. It might be interesting if he were to state what they had been doing that day. They had granted pensions to 68 widows from the three dioceses-29 out of the 66 from his own diocese, 12 from Liverpool, and the remainder from the diocese of Chester; they had also made grants in the cases of 27 orphans, the total amount thus distributed being £2,563. Ninety-three grants had been made altogether, including three educational grants of £45 a year for the daughters of deceased clergymen. The pensions were small, no doubt. (Hear, hear.). He be- lieved the largest of them was £4O a year, with a donation of £2O, and a bonus of £6, maxing a total of £66, but in that case the widow was 71 years of age ; moreover she was des- titute of any income at all, and had seen children, who were not able to render any substantial assistance to her. It would pain them if he were to select instances showing the deplorable condition in which many of the widows were. Ihe smallness of their income, the largeness of their families, and their general condition was such as to move compassion towards them. Their cases were treated with all possible tenderness and delicacy in every way. No in- quiries were made except such as were absolutely necessary in order that those who had the distribution of the funds might feel satisfied that they were applied to proper cases. Having got that information, they endeavoured, according to their best judgment, to apportion the funds at their disposal. If £2,563 were divided by 93 it would be seen that the sum they were enabled to grant was really very small ; in many cases it was lamentably small. (Hear, hear.) But if they made it larger in some cases, that could only be done by denying relief to other cises equally necessitous. The widows' and orphans' fund appeared to have an invested capital of £13,500 which produced some £5OO or £6OO per year. The collections in the three dioceses amounted last year to £Bl5, the subscriptions to £836, and the donations to £B3, making a total of £1,734. The Clery Daughters' School had an income from collections, subscriptions, and donations of £951 ; therefore the total annual income of both charities from subscriptions and from ccllections in churches was during the past year £2,685. That certainly did not represent a very great amount of liberality when one considered the wealth, the populousness, and the extent of the area over which these institutions dif- fused their benefits, and he could not but think that if the general body of churchmen at all realised the condition in which so many of the clergy lived, and in many cases were obliged to live, they would support those institutions more liberally. In some cases no doubt proper economy was not ex,rcised, for some clergymen lived up to their income and did not even take the precaution to insure their lives. Those were perhaps the most painful cases of all, for he could not conceive a more crushing re- velation for a poor widow, the mother perhaps of five or six children, who after suddenly losing her husband, who had perhaps an income of £4OO or £5OO a year, found herself without any means suddenly cast upon the Christian charity of others. Such cases came before those who had the care of the widows' and orphans' fund, and he thought they were , cases to be very much reprobated. (Hear, hear.) Any man who had given hostages to fortune in the shape of children ought to be ashamed ef himself if he was not doing his very best to make suitable provision for them. (Hear, hear.) The school, in which 66 girls were being trained at the pre— sent time, was an admirable pendant to the institution. The education given to each girl cost about £45 per year, but that education was given to the daughters of clergy in the diocese for £2O a year, and in some cases no charge was made. which practically amounted to a free gift of £45 per annum. Six such free gifts had been made this year. A new feature had just been introduced into the school in the form-of student teachers who remained a year or two after their proper time, and were employed in a manner somewhat like that of pupil teachers, partly in giving instruction and partly in receiv- ing advanced instruction in higher subjects. With refer- ence to the question of contributions, he must plainly admit he did not think the diocese of Manchester did its duty in that respect. That diocese had the the largest number of widows receiving help, but be was sorry to say it did not stand well in respect of subscriptions. Id the archdeaconry of Blackburn there was very few supporters of the institutions. Meanwhile, however, the institutions were sufficiently flourishing to pay their way. They had no embarrassments or debts, but those who had the care of the funds wished they could make larger pensions, and he hoped that in proportion as a knowledge of the benefits secured by those institutions became known so would the amount of public support accorded to them be increased.— (Applause.) ' Canon STOWELL proposed "the health of the president of the meeting," and Dr. FRAMER replied. Canon tioPwoou then proposed "the health of the lay friends of the institution," to which Mr. JOHN WHITE responded. The toast of "the health and prosperity of the treasarer and other officers of the institution" was given by Canon Goss, and was acknowledged by Mr. E. GREENALL.

The right rev. CHAIRMAN proposed "prosperity to the town and trade of Warrington," and ' The MAYOR responded. He said he was happy to be able to tell the Bishop of Manchester that Warrington was as healthy and flourishing as it had ever been since the year 1. (Laughter.) It was one of the oldest towns in Lancashire; it was older than Manchester; and Warrington people were considerably proud of the town in which they lived. They did make some smoke, but that was necessary for the prosperity of business, for nothing could be more melancholy than when no smoke came out of 1 the chimneys. He was very proud to be amonget them that day las MAyor of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He believed he was in his proper place. (Hear, hear.) He did not know that there was an institution in Warrington or in the country that was more worthy of support than those institutions whose anniversary they were celebrating that day. (Hear, hear.) He was old enough to remember the late Lord Bishop Powys, and he remembered him with the greatest affection. Bishop Powys was a very kind friend to him always; they played cricket together many times; and he had always looked upon him with feelings of love and affection. He never met a friend, he thought, wfth a larger heart and warmer sympathy. (Hear, hear.) He thought the clergy of the Church of England were deeply indebted to Bishop Powys for the services he had rendered in connection with that building, and providing some assistance for the widows and children of the clergy who had died in poor circumstances. He could not imagine, him- self, any institutions that were mare worthy and more de- serving of support. When he thought of the beautiful and touching sermon that morning he thought it was a pity that every person in the town could not listen to it. It was a sermon calculated to go to the heart of any man with any feeling in him. fie wished with all his heart greater pros- perity to the institutions under whose auspices they were assembled; and he thought it a disgrace, with the wealthy churchmen there were that these institutions were not more ' handsomely contributed to. He was sure the words which had fallen from the Chairman that day were enough to ' touch the heart of every man, and he was also sure that every one who had the means ought to do twice as much as ' he had done before in aid of the institutions. (Applause.) ' The BISHOP of MANCHESTER feelingly alluded to the ; absence of the Rector, and the company separated.

div.head: WARRINGTOS LIBRARV AND
div.p: THE WARRINGTOS LIBRARV AND
MUSEUM.

The Museum, Library, and Arts Committee of the Cor- poration have recommended the Council to adopt the fol- lowing rules for the conduct of the Museum and Library : Museum—The Museum shall be open to the public free of charge on three days in each week, viz., Monday, Wed- nesday, and Saturday, during the following hours :—From 10 a.m. till dusk, and from 6 to 9 p.m. [The Art Gallery shall be closed at dusk on Monday and Wednesday. Library.—The reading room shall be open free of charge to the public daily (except Sundays, Bank Holidays, and Sunday school anniversaries), from 10 a.m. to 9-30 p.m. Books, either from the Reference or Lending Departments, may be on application obtained at the counter. It is required that all persons using the reading room shall use due care not to injure or deface in any way books provided for their

Lending Department.—The terms of subscription to the lending library shall ba as follows :—For one book at a time 5s yearly, or is. 6d. quarterly; for two books 10s. yearly, or 3s. quarterly, and so on at the same rates. The subscription shall be payable in advance at the Museum, commencing on the Ist January, April, July, or October. Each suhscriber shall be responsible for all books taken out in his or her name, and shall make good any damage or loss. Each book may be kept not exceeding 14 days. If retained longer, one penny shall be paid for each week or portion of a week beyon 1 the 14 days. Books not in de- mand may be renewed. No book shall be re-entered from one subscriber to another without being brought to the library. No books shall be issued to any person whose sub- sctiption is in arrear, or who refuses to pay the charge for damaging or detaining a book. Subscribers wishing to with- draw shall give notice to the librarian and return their books, and those who fail to do so before the end of a quarter shall be liable for the subscription for the next quarter. Books from the reference library can only be taken out by permission of the committee. A printed form of applica- tion is provided for this purpose. The Museum Com- mittee shall not make any dividend, gift, division or bonus in money unto or between any of its members.

div.p: ATTEMPT TO ROB A PUBLICAN'S CASII-BOX.—A dejected looking individual, named William Nicholls, pleaded guilty at the St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday. to a charge of having been on the licensed premises of William Cash, of the Victoria Inn, Pocket Nook-street, for an unlawful pur- pose.—On Monday evening about seven o'clock, Mrs. Cash had been intent upon household affairs in her kitchen, when she heard someone open the drawer in which the money taken at the bar is kept. On looking to see who it was, she saw the prisoner standing with the drawer open before him. , She asked him what he was after, but his only reply was to look wistfully into the open cash-box, and then bolt out of the door. Mr. Cash, however, was standing like a watchful sentinel just without, and on receiving a hint from his alarmed spouse gave chase and caught the prisoner, who was not able lo decamp very rapidly.—Prisoner, who gave no exp)anation of his coriduct, was sent to gaol for fourteen days,

div.head: STATE OF THE SCHOOL.
div.p: THE STATE OF THE SCHOOL.

The ScifooL SECRETARY'S report was as follows :—The committee of management are glad to be able to report favourably of tbe state of the clergy daughters school to its friends and subscribers. The number of pupils has steadily increased since last August, and during the past term the school has been quite full. The health of the pupils during the past year has, on the whole, been very good. The death of a child on July Bth from pleuro— pneumonia has been the one sorrow of an otherwise happy year. The new infirmary is now being built, and it is hoped will be finished in two months. The usual examination of the school by a university examiner was not held last Christmas owing to the unsettlement caused by a change of headmistress, but the reports of the head-mistress and of the clerical principal speak satisfacterily of the work of the pupils. The institution of cookery classes has been welcomed alike by parents and by children. The com- mittee regret that the balance sheet of the school still shows an adverse balance of a considerable amount, though every effort is being made to promote economy without sacrificing efficiency. They appeal to the friends of the school to do their best to render the financial condition of the institution more satisfactory.
The report -was adopted on the motion of Canon HORNBY.
THE NEW PRESIDENT, &C.
Lord Lathom was appointed president for the ensuing year; and Archdeacon Bardsley was chosen to preach the next anniversary sermon.
The retiring Members of the committee of management were re-elected, on the motion of the Rev. C. MARSHALL (Harpurhey).
THE LATE LORD EGERTON.

The Brsuop of LIVERPOOL moved the following resolution, which was agreed to :—" That the Secretary be requested to address a letter to Lnrd Egerton of Tatton, expressing the deep regret with which the committee received the tidings of his late father's death; their grateful recollection of the many Bervices which he rendered to the Warrington Institu- tions; and their hope that the successor to his title will give these valuable charities the benefit of his influential support." On the proposition of the DEAN of CHESTER, seconded by Canon HOPWOOD, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Sieben of Manchester for presiding, and the meeting con- cluded.
A sermon was afterwards preached in the Parish Church by Bishop Kelly, who urgel upon the congregation the claims of the institution.
THE LUNCHEON.

Luncheon was provided at two o'clock in the dining hall of the institution, and a large number of clergy and laity sat down. Amongst the laity were his Worship the Mayor (Mr. John Crosfield), Mr. E. Greenell. Mr. Mackie, Mr. J. White, ate. The Lord Bishop of Manchester presided. The Right Rev. CHAIRMAN proposed the toasts of the "Church and the Queen," and "The Prince and Princess of Wales, and the rest of the Royal family." Mr. MACKIE gave the next toast, "The Bishops and Clergy of the three dioceses." After referring in compli- mentary terms to the Bishops of Chester, Manchester, and Liverpool, he said perhaps at no time had there been greater need for the bishops and clergy of that and of all other dioceses giving their support to institutions of the kind which had called them together than there was that day. It was marvellous the opposition that was being made to the personal character of the clergy here and there—not in our own land but in other lands. div.head: FLOWER SHOW AT LYMM.
div.p: FLOWER SHOW AT LYMM.

In the picturesque park of Lynam Hall (the residence of Wm. Battersby, Esq.) was yesterday held, under most favourable auspices, the first annual flower show for the parishes of Bollington, Lymm (with Statham), High Legb, Oughtrington, Thelwall, and Warburton. The exhibition was the outcome of a children's flower show held last year, and although great things cannot be expected from a first venture, yet it must be admitted that the display of flowers, fruits, and vegetalales was somewhat disappointing, remem- bering how favourably situated Lynam and district is for the production of the fruits of the earth. But the feeling of disappointment was to some extent lessened when it was borne in mind that the show was confined to cottagers, who, on the whole, made a good display, though the number of entries was not in any of the classes very large. Neither the fruits nor vegetables call for special remark, and the flowers which attracted most attention were those made up into bouquets. In the arrangement of the bouquets much taste had been dieplaved, and the charming floral combinations excited the admiration of the spectators, who were also greatly pleased with the more sober but none the less pretty bouquets of wild flowers. Another source of attraction were the model gardens, which were cleverly designed, but the one to which was awarded the first prize arrested attention lay its neat and natural arrangement. there being none of the straining for effect observable in the one which took the second prize. The exhibits were arranged round the sides of a large marquee, in the centre of which was a magnificent display of stove plants mostly lent by gentle- men in the neighbourhood. Conspicuous near the entrance was a splendid collection of ferns, including the Killarney and other filmy ferns, exhibited by Messrs. Watkinson .and Collins, nurserymen, Manchester; and further on were beautiful umbrageous palms, yuccas, tuberous rooted begonias, and hydrangers in full bloom ; while at the top end of the marquee were a, ranged two rare specimens of cocas weddelliana palms, caladiums, drascenas, adiantum formosum, and adiantum trapezi—forme ferns, set off with a beautiful show of single petunias in full bloom, and relieved with variegated leaves of coleuses. These latter were lent by Mr. H. Stanton, of Thelwall, and plants were also lint by Messrs. G. C. Dewhurst, J. D. Dewhurst, P. Stubs, W. Battersby, and T. P. Norris, Mrs. Crosfield, and Mre. Grundy. In a second marquee was an art and industsial exhibition —a novel featere at a flower show— containing excellent specimens of artistic work with the paint brush and the needle, and amongst them was a bril- liant piece of Brittany work executed by Miss de la Taste, of Jersey. In one portion of the marquee were stalls oc- cupied by Mr. John B. Taylor, ironmanger, and Mr. I. H. ' Evans, chemist, tastefully set out with their wares ; and in another part was shewn the art of fustian cutting,the staple trade ef Lymm. There was also a refreshment stall, under the management of Mr. Wickers, and near the flower show was another refreshment stall in charge of the Misses Bat- tersby. The Cheshire Counties Beekeepers Association exhibited a stock of bees, working in bar-frame hives, and • the association awarded a bronze medal to Mr. Cottrill, of Langley-road, Bowdon, for his show of bees, which could beseen working through glass frames ; and a certificate to of 13,11loir,ton In this competition Mr. E. G. Parker, of Bowdon, was • awarded an extra certificate by the Flower Show Committee L for a show of bees and appliances. Mr. Carr, of Newton, a member ef the British Beekeepers' Association, was the judge of the bees; Mr. Smith, of St. Helens, judged for the • flowers, etc.i and Mrs. Crosfield and Mrs. Norris were the judges of the needlework, die. During the afternoon the Chorlton-cum-Hardy brass band and elle Lymm fife band gave selections of music at intervals. The president of the I show is the Rev. G. W. Guest, M.A., the treasurer Mr. Bayley, and the secretary Mr. Joseph Smith, all of whom ' did their best to promote the comfort and enjoyment of the , visitors.
